Pop these bulbs into the ground in late fall and look forward to dazzling displays of vibrant flowers from February to May.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you haven’t got around to planting spring-flowering bulbs yet, don’t panic because you can plant all these showstoppers in November. From tiny pastel-hued muscari to alliums the size of softballs, many-petalled tulips to intensely scented hyacinths, the range of bulbs to plant in November is just as exciting as those that need planting in September or October, so don’t feel you’re missing out for a second if you're slow off the starting block this fall.

Growing blooms from bulbs couldn’t be easier, because fall and winter rain will provide all the moisture they need. The secret to getting great results when planting bulbs in November is to sit them on a shallow layer of grit to improve drainage, so creating a drier environment to stop bulb bases rotting in wet winter soil. You could use horticultural grit but poultry grit does exactly the same job and costs a lot less. Just make sure you use a product that’s 100% crushed rock like CZ Grain Chicken Grit, available from Walmart, rather than the type made from oyster shells.

My bulb recommendations will brighten up your garden from February all the way into May and beyond, and return year after year. And I’ve skipped right past the common-or-garden varieties to bring you flowers in standout shades and shapes to create a colorful stir in your yard. Grow these beautiful bulbs in the ground, in raised beds or in pots – but do just grow them! Which of these striking bulbs to plant in late fall will skyrocket your spring garden next year?

November is the very best month to plant tulips. Waiting until temperatures have lowered reduces the risk of fungal disease tulip fire, and cooler temperatures mean bulbs are less likely to rot. Plant tulips in full sun, burying them at a depth that's three times the height of the bulb. Tulips need excellent drainage so dropping a ½-inch layer of grit into the planting holes first is a smart move. If you’re planting tulips in containers then mix a good handful of grit into the potting soil, too.

If it’s a while since you shopped for these spring flowers, you’ll soon find that tulips don’t have to look like tulips anymore! All these show-off varieties are fully hardy in zones 3-8, blooming in April and May when you can expect lots of curious neighbors asking what they are.

Spring-flowering crocus are incredibly hardy so can be planted in November but pick wisely for the best results. Botanical crocus flower early in January or February so have little time to grow roots from a November planting. Crocus vernus, however, blooms February to April, and their bigger bulb-like corms are tougher and store more energy.

While botanical crocus have tiny blooms, the goblet-shaped flowers of Crocus vernus grow to a far more noticeable 5 inches high. And, whether you want to welcome spring into your garden with pristine white petals or drifts of carnival color, there’s a variety to suit. Plant Crocus vernus at a depth that’s equal to three times the corm’s height, in sun or partial shade in zones 4-8, adding ¼ inch of grit to the bottom of each hole, and the bulbs will quickly naturalize. A favorite spot for these crocus is under deciduous trees where bare branches give them the early spring sunshine they need to flower well.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

These little lovelies only grow 18-24 inches tall but they really punch above their height with orchid-like flowers in saturated colors, and florists prize them highly. Dutch iris are better planted in November as any earlier and the bulbs can start sending up their green shoots prematurely, when the tender growth is quickly knobbled by cold weather.

Because these spectacular flowers sit atop a single slender stem, Dutch iris bulbs look better planted in groups, which makes them easier to bury, too. Dig a hole around 6 inches deep in full sun, mix a handful of grit into the soil, and add the bulbs 3 inches apart. In containers, you can pack them more closely at 2 inches apart.

Iris x hollandica bulbs are hardy in zones 5-9, but in zone 5 they benefit from a mulch of shredded leaves thrown over the top to keep them cozy. You can also plant these bulbs in zones 3 and 4 in pots in an unheated greenhouse, ready to move outside when the worst of the winter is over. Dutch iris is a little later to flower than most spring bulbs from May into June, providing a seamless transition into summer.

These ornamental onions are very relaxed when it comes to when they’re planted and, although most folk get their alliums into the ground in October, as long as the soil isn’t frozen solid, they’ll flourish from a November planting. There are dozens of allium varieties with flowers ranging from small pom poms to huge spheres, lasting for up to a month then drying into structural seedheads.

As the size of the bulbs ranges as much as the blooms, use the usual rule of thumb to plant bulbs at a depth equivalent to three times their height. All alliums need full sun, where they’ll thrive in zones 4-9, and be sure to line holes with a layer of grit. While there are alliums that flower in summer, all my recommendations are late spring varieties that bloom from April into June.

There’s one big reason why you should add hyacinths to your garden, and that’s their incredible scent. As the flowerbuds open, their perfume is fresh, reminiscent of cut grass. In full bloom, an intense and intoxicating floral fragrance takes over, warm with vanilla and spicy with clove. Then as the flowers fade, the aroma deepens and becomes more musky. The scent profile can differ by color, too, with purples and blues typically boasting the strongest perfume, while whites and pinks smell a little sweeter, and yellows and oranges spicier.

Emerging in late February, hyacinths add an extra dimension to crisp, cold spring days when their scent hangs in the air. Hardy in zones 4-8, hyacinths prefer to be planted once soil temperatures have dropped, so the bulbs remain dormant but still get the deep chill they need to flower. Choose a sunny spot and plant bulbs at a depth of three times their height, dropping a ½ inch layer of grit into the hole to prevent them rotting. Hyacinths also thrive in a pot, where you can pack bulbs so they’re almost-but-not touching for a fabulous fragrance cloud on a patio or front porch.

Don’t reach for the standard pink, white and blue colors as there are now all sorts of tempting hyacinth tones to choose from.

‘Delft Blue’ does naturalize but gently, and you easily prevent it from travelling far by snipping off faded flower spikes before they set seed. ‘Fantasy Creation’ has sterile flowers so only spreads very slowly through underground division. And Muscari latifolium has a clumping habit so will stay exactly where you put it. All are suitable for zones 4-8 and flower March or April into May.

The more bulbs you buy, the cheaper they get, so if you end up filling your borders with beautiful spring flowers, speed the planting with a labor-saving tool.

The diameter of this bulb planter adjusts to fit different-sized bulbs. It automatically releases soil and is marked with measurements to make getting the correct depth easy.

This long-handled bulb planter with a serrated base is sturdy enough to perform well even in hard ground, and the raised pedal makes it simple to release the excavated soil plug.

Let your drill do all the work with these garden auger bits that fit a standard ⅜” hex shank. The 1.6” bit is perfect for tulips while the 3.5” can handle the biggest allium bulbs.

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#7932. Thor: The Golden Retriever Who Changed My Life

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

On July 5, 2025, I said goodbye to my best friend. His name was Thor.

It's strange how a year can pass so quickly and yet still leave you feeling like a part of your heart is frozen in time. There are moments when I still expect to hear his paws on the floor behind me or feel him brush against my leg as I make coffee in the morning. Sometimes I catch myself looking toward the front door, half expecting him to come trotting inside with his favorite ball in his mouth.

People say time heals all wounds. I don't think that's true.

Thor came into my life as a fluffy Golden Retriever puppy, full of curiosity and joy. Like most Golden Retrievers, he loved everyone. He had an uncanny ability to make strangers smile. We'd walk through town or down the beach, and people couldn't help but stop to tell me how beautiful he was. They'd ask if they could pet him, and Thor never met a person he didn't think was a friend.

We lived just across the street from the dog beach in Ormond Beach, Florida, and he knew exactly where we were going every time we picked up his leash. He would practically lead me there, tail wagging the entire way.

He wasn't much of a swimmer, but he loved to wade into the surf just enough to cool his paws before racing back onto the sand. More than anything, he loved his tennis ball. It didn't matter where we were or what else was happeningâif he had his ball, life was good.

Looking back now, those ordinary days became the moments I cherish most.

Then, one morning, our lives changed forever.

I had worked for a neurologist for years. If anyone should have been prepared for something like that, I thought it would have been me, but nothing prepares you for watching it happen to someone you love.

From that day forward, epilepsy became part of our daily lives.

Our world revolved around medications, specialists, emergency hospitals, blood work, and carefully planned routines. Every dosage or missed meal mattered. Every subtle change in his behavior made me wonder if another seizure was coming.

I learned to recognize things most people would never noticeâa certain look in his eyes, a slight change in how he walked, moments when he seemed just a little different.

Hope became measured in days without a seizure.

Then another seizure would come, and we'd start over.

Most people saw the happy Golden Retriever. They saw the dog running down the beach, wagging his tail, carrying his ball. They didn't see the nights spent sleeping lightly because I was afraid I wouldn't hear him if he seized. They didn't see the medication schedules taped around my life or the emergency plans rehearsed in my head over and over again.

One morning stands out more than any other.

Thor wasn't a cuddler. As much as I wished he were, he usually preferred to sleep nearby rather than pressed against me. But that morning, he climbed into bed and lay back-to-back with me.

I woke up to him having a seizure beside me and rushed him to the emergency hospital.

I didn't know then that it was the beginning of the hardest chapter of our journey.

Epilepsy is cruel because it gives you hope just often enough that you believe tomorrow might be different.

We fought with everything we had for months, celebrating every seizure-free stretch, no matter how short, because when you love a dog with epilepsy, you learn to celebrate the smallest victories.

Despite everything he was carrying, Thor never stopped being Thor.

He still greeted people with excitement, still insisted on bringing me his ball.

He still looked at me with complete trust, as if I could fix anything.

That trust was both the greatest gift and the greatest responsibility I've ever known. As the months passed, one question kept finding its way into my thoughts:

What if something happened when I wasn't there?

What if he had a seizure while another family member was watching him?

His collar carried my phone number. His microchip could identify himâbut only if someone thought to take him to a veterinary clinic or shelter to have it scanned.

Thor couldnât tell a stranger that he had epilepsy. He couldnât explain which medications he took or where to find them, or which neurologist knew his case.

After months of fighting with incredible strength, Thor lost his battle with epilepsy.

Suddenly, my life was divided into 'before' and 'after.'

His toys were exactly where he'd left them.

It's realizing that the routines you built your life around disappeared overnight.

People asked me if I would get another dog, but what they didn't understand is that another dog could never replace Thor. Love doesn't work that way.

As the weeks turned into months, I found myself returning to the thoughts that had haunted me throughout Thor's illness. Some things are beyond our control, but maybe there was a way to make sure another family wouldn't have to worry that critical information would be unavailable during an emergency.

I wasnât looking to start a business or be known for inventing something. But grief has a remarkable way of asking you one impossible question:

For me, the answer became honoring the dog who had given me so much.

Everything I've built over the past year in creating Bark-ID: The Worldâs Smartest Dog Tag has been my way of making sure Thor's life continues to matter.

His legacy isn't a product; itâs the love that inspired it.

If you've ever loved a dog, you understand that they leave paw prints on more than your floors.

They leave them on your routines. Your memories. Your heart.

Thor taught me patience, resilience, and he taught me how fiercely we can love another living creature.

And in losing him, he taught me that grief and gratitude can exist together.

I still miss him every single day, and I probably always will. But when I think about Thor now, I try not to think about the day I lost him.

The tennis ball that never stayed clean for long and strangers who smiled because they met him.

The countless ordinary moments that, in hindsight, became extraordinary.

Some dogs make the world happier simply by being in it, and Thor was one of those dogs, and I was lucky enough to be his person.

If there's one thing I hope his story reminds people, it's that we never get enough time with the dogs we love.

So throw the ball one more time. Take the walk. Let them stop and sniff.

Take too many pictures. Sit with them a little longer.

Because one day, those ordinary moments become the memories you'll treasure most.

Thor gave me a lifetime of love in the months we had together, and if his story encourages even one person to cherish their dog a little more today, let that be his legacy.

She lives with her Golden Retrievers in Ormond Beach, Florida, where she spends most of her happiest days at the dog beach. âThe Golden Retriever Who Changed My Lifeâ is her first published personal story.

Those gorgeous flowers are months away, but their buds are already waiting. The right fall care can make all the difference when warmer days return.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Azaleas and rhododendrons paint the spring garden in gorgeous shades of pink, red, orange, and other vibrant colors. But the work of protecting those future flowers starts now. Fall care before winter is essential for keeping these shrubs healthy and ready to bloom abundantly in spring.

Fall azalea care and rhododendron care are all about preparing them for winter dormancy, maintaining healthy roots, and protecting flower buds. Did you know that these shrubs form their buds in summer? Next year’s flowers are already set in buds, so now is the time to preserve and protect them.

Azaleas and rhododendrons are very similar plants with similar care needs in fall. However, keep in mind that there are deciduous and evergreen types with slightly different needs. We’ll point these out here, along with the essential tasks you should be tackling this fall for all your Rhododendron species.

Fall is not the time for heavy annual pruning of rhododendrons or azaleas. Most spring-blooming members of this plant flower on old growth. This means they set buds over the summer. Trimming too hard in the fall will prune away many of the buds that become next spring’s flowers.

The best time for heavy shaping or pruning is right after spring flowering. But this doesn’t mean you can’t or shouldn’t make any cuts in fall. Inspect your shrubs now for dead, damaged, or diseased branches. Remove these using sharp, clean bypass pruners, such as the Felco 8, available on Amazon, which can cut through woody stems up to 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. For larger branches, switch to loppers or a pruning saw.

Fertilizing late in the season can trigger new growth that only gets damaged in winter conditions. That damage can introduce disease. It’s also a waste of energy that should be going into keeping roots healthy over winter.

Most fertilizing for azaleas and rhododendrons takes place in spring, after flowering. At that time, you can use a product formulated specifically for these shrubs or for any acid-loving shrub. Also, consider the fact that your shrubs might not need feeding at all if they are healthy or thriving.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If you suspect your plants need fertilizer, a soil test is the best way to determine their nutrient needs. The MySoil Soil Test Kit measures both soil pH and nutrient levels, helping you identify any deficiencies before deciding whether to feed your shrubs in spring.

You should keep watering your azaleas and rhododendrons right up until the ground freezes, especially if you’re having a dry autumn. Ideally, the ground will be moist before real winter weather sets in. Check the soil regularly using a moisture meter, such as the Yamron 4-in-1, to see whether water is reaching the root zone. Provide a deep soaking as needed, including one as late in the season as possible before the ground freezes.

This matters because many azaleas and rhododendrons are evergreen, making them susceptible to desiccation, or drying out, over winter. Cold, dry winds leech moisture from the leaves, but roots in frozen ground can’t take up any water. This can result in curled, brown leaves and even damaged buds. Ensuring there is moisture in the ground before winter is less important for deciduous types.

Mulch insulates the soil and roots of your flowering shrubs. It helps regulate soil temperature, retains more moisture around the roots, and prevents the root damage caused by soil heaving that occurs during cycles of freezing and thawing.

Organic mulches such as shredded pine bark or partially decomposed, shredded leaves are ideal for mulching azaleas and rhododendrons. If you don't have suitable materials to hand, Garden Pro's shredded pine bark mulch from Home Depot is a good alternative. Layer the mulch around the root zones of shrubs to a depth of 2 to 3 inches (5–8 cm). Keep it a few inches away from stems to prevent trapping moisture that can encourage rot and disease.

Moist soil is important, especially for evergreen shrubs, but too much moisture can also be damaging. Poorly drained soil can lead to root rot and fungal diseases. Eventually, these diseases can kill shrubs.

Look for signs your shrubs are getting waterlogged: standing water around plants, soggy soil long after rainfall, and wilting or yellowing foliage even when the plants have plenty of water. It’s important to try to remediate soggy conditions. You can clear off compacted mulch and other plant debris, divert runoff from other areas, or regrade the surrounding soil, for instance. If the problem isn’t easily fixed, consider relocating the plant in spring.

Evergreen azaleas and rhododendrons add beautiful color and texture to the winter garden, but they are also more vulnerable to winter damage. Winter burn happens when the leaves lose moisture faster than the roots can draw up water to replace it.

Cold and dry winter wind is a primary cause of winter burn on evergreen shrubs, so creating a windbreak can protect them from much of the damage. Set up a barrier on the side of the shrubs that get hit by winter wind, using natural burlap garden fabric, like this from Home Depot, attached to wooden stakes.

Don’t let the barrier actually touch the leaves. They need some airflow to stay healthy. Young shrubs are more likely to need this kind of winter protection. Established shrubs in more sheltered areas are probably fine without it.

Finally, it’s a good idea to look over your shrubs for any signs of problems caused by common azalea pests or diseases. Managing these issues now can prevent them from carrying over into next year’s growing season. Look for stippling or black specks on leaves, which can indicate lace bugs, a common pest of azaleas and rhododendrons. A 10x illuminated magnifying loupe, like this Carson loupe from Amazon, can help you inspect the undersides of leaves, where these tiny insects and their dark droppings are often found.

An unusual number of dying branches, persistent wilting, and many or unusual leaf spots can indicate fungal diseases and root rot. Keep in mind that some spots are normal and that leaf drop is expected in deciduous varieties.

If you do see issues or unusual damage, remove diseased plant material and dispose of it. If issues persist or you don’t know how to identify or treat a particular pest, check with your local extension office for advice.

Fall azalea and rhododendron care isn’t extensive, but it will help you protect next year’s flowers, safeguard vulnerable foliage, and keep roots healthy. Simple steps now help your shrubs enter winter in better condition and improve the chances of a healthy, colorful spring display.

#7929. The Resentment of Being the Parent Who Can Never Clock Out

Maybe it’s a lack of freedom, unequal responsibilities with a partner, or both, but you’re big mad.

You had a certain expectation for what new motherhood would look like: Friends and family stopping by, your partner playing peek-a-boo with the baby, and even yourself feeling calm, patient, and present when the baby cries.

Reality might look a bit different, though. You blink, and your partner heads back to work, reading a newly cracked novel on the commute. Your friend drops by with pastries, then jets off to a yoga class. Everyone’s gone but you and the baby.

You’re at home, wading through a pile of burp cloths and hoping the baby naps long enough for you to choke down a sandwich. If you’re feeling a little ragey about that, you’re not alone. In one 2022 cross-sectional survey, nearly a third of new moms reported feeling intense anger.

But who are you actually angry with, and are you even mad, or — let's be brutally honest for a second — just jealous of their freedom and spontaneity? What’s really going on is likely more complicated than that, but there are things you can do things about it besides screaming into a pillow.

Anger is often underrepresented in research on the postpartum period, and tends to fly under the radar when moms get screened for perinatal depressive and anxiety disorders, as it can occur without elevated depressive symptoms, says Christine Ou, Ph.D., lead author of the aforementioned survey, assistant professor at the University of Victoria in Canada, and founder of the school’s Parent-Child Lab. “So asking only about depression may miss mothers who are struggling [with anger],” she says.

In a 2018 review, which Ou co-authored, researchers found that several factors contributed to moms’ anger, including a feeling of powerlessness and a misalignment between expectations and reality.

But you can also feel angry simply because having a newborn is hard. Moms were often mad because “their needs were compromised, and they were exhausted or stressed,” says Ou, as to why many new moms reported feeling anger. That’s pretty par for the course during the newborn haze, but being stuck at home — especially without help or breaks — can intensify those emotions.

Babies can bring a lot of joy, but staying at home around the clock with one is no picnic. First, newborns operate on an unpredictable schedule and demand constant supervision, making it feel like a logistical nightmare to get out of the house. Compounding that, mothers have historically been cast as the ‘default parent,’ says Paige Bellenbaum, L.C.S.W., founding director of The Motherhood Center, a clinic in New York City that provides care for women with postpartum depression (PPD). In traditional families, they’re “the ones physically with the baby most of the day and night, carrying most of the mental and emotional load, and managing the logistics, often while preparing for their own return to work,” says Bellenbaum.

Even if parents split duties pretty evenly within their own orbit, external factors can still throw that balance off. Take the fragmented, inadequate, and deeply unequal parental leave in the US: Often the dad or non-birthing partner ends up returning to work first. When that happens, the parent who remains at home “may feel envy, anger, or a sense of abandonment,” says Bellenbaum. Being home day in and day out with a baby can be isolating, even if you do get help from family or well-meaning visitors, she adds.

It's not just one person returning to work that creates this isolation. Reliable childcare can cost as much as your monthly mortgage these days, which means many birthing parents may make the tough but economical decision to stay home with the baby. “Everyone else can come and go, while she remains responsible for the baby, with no real opportunity to step away,” says Ou.

You could argue that the parent who’s heading into the office doesn’t necessarily want to be away from their family nor view it as an “escape.” Nevertheless, they “get to step back into their former life, stopping for coffee on the way into work, using the bathroom when they need to, and feeling useful and connected to the outside world,” says Bellenbaum. Plus, heading back to work can restore elements of their pre-baby life they may have been missing, like adult conversation, structure, control, and a sense of mastery and accomplishment, she adds. Meanwhile, the mom at home takes a 30-second shower and sings Wheels on the Bus for the 40th time in a row.

It’s normal to feel a lot of emotions in the postpartum phase — joy, frustration, rage, loneliness, anxiety, sadness, gratitude, you name it, says Ou. But that mix can make it hard to figure out exactly what you’re feeling.

While postpartum anger can happen independent of PPD, the two are clearly linked. For instance, Ou’s survey found that anger and PPD can also occur at the same time; in fact, those who screened positive for depressive symptoms had almost four times the odds of reporting intense anger. (But the survey couldn’t establish which came first.)

It’s not surprising: Imagine telling people you’re feeling trapped in your house — and no one seems to care. “When the circumstances behind a mother’s anger don’t change, when she remains overwhelmed, unsupported, or unheard, she may start to feel helpless or hopeless, which could contribute to depression,” says Ou. Maybe your partner acknowledges the struggle but doesn’t actually change anything, or you don’t feel comfortable or safe expressing your anger. Both can contribute to the development of PPD.

You might feel guilty for feeling trapped in the first place. After all, aren’t moms supposed to want to soak up as much time as possible with their babies? And, in a country where parental leave isn’t guaranteed, isn’t it a privilege to be at home with your newborn? Despite these arguments being flawed — they’re ignorant of the realities of newborn needs and nonexistent help for moms — this narrative can put a lot of pressure on moms, or even make you feel like you’re not doing right by your child. “Guilt and shame about being angry can add to that distress, potentially contributing to or worsening depressive symptoms,” says Ou.

First, know that it’s normal to be angry or irritable—period. But if you notice yourself getting worked up, take stock of how often you get angry, and how mad you get. If anger is frequent, intense, difficult to manage, or affecting your relationships or everyday life, that warrants a discussion with your doctor, says Ou. As is “feeling scared by your anger, or that you have little control over your reactions,” she adds. Postpartum Support International offers a peer support group for postpartum anger and rage, which may be a potential resource.

A screening from your healthcare provider can also be helpful since it may factor in other symptoms like crying and sadness, changes in sleep or appetite, a lack of interest in the baby, a sense of hopelessness or helplessness, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, according to Bellenbaum. “When these are present along with the anger, PPD may be at play,” she says.

However, getting professional help is not a replacement for making changes in your home and routine, if needed, stresses Bellenbaum. These tactics can help.

Since anger often stems from a lack of equality, it helps to start by looking at the division of labor in a partnered relationship. “Who gets more opportunities to sleep?” says Ou. “Who can leave without making arrangements? Who notices what needs doing, and who is responsible for making sure it happens?” Assessing this together allows you both to see who’s shouldering more of the work. “When that load is shared more equitably, resentment tends to ease, and a sense of shared responsibility emerges,” says Bellenbaum.

If and when you identify the areas of inequality, the partner should take “more ownership of tasks, night shifts, and the mental planning, not just ‘helping’,” says Bellenbaum, who recommends a card-based system called Fair Play that helps partners rebalance household work and divide invisible mental labor (like remembering to schedule doctor appointments). “Instead of splitting every chore 50/50, each partner takes full ownership of specific responsibilities, divided in a way that both people feel is fair,” she says.

“Genuine off-duty time means someone else is fully responsible for the baby,” says Bellenbaum. In other words, mom’s not on standby. She’s not listening for cries or manning the monitor, and she’s also not checking her phone or expecting a call because her partner feels the baby “wants mommy,” she explains. That can be hard, especially if the mom is afraid to leave the baby or feels guilty about being away, but it’s a worthwhile exercise for everyone. Otherwise, it “can make it harder for her partner to learn to care for the baby on their own,” she says.

Non-partnered parents need breaks, too. “Friends and family can bring food, do laundry, or hold the baby for half an hour,” says Ou. Run errands alone one evening while the baby stays home with a loved one. “A grocery run might be a chore, but it can also mean getting out of the house, being alone, and deciding what happens next without having to respond to a baby and their needs,” she says.

If a new mom in your life is dealing with anger or isolation, there are ways you can support her. Instead of asking what she needs, be specific and offer choices, like "I can do some laundry for you or bring over food for you. Which would help more?” says Bellenbaum.

If going out with friends or on a date night feels like too much for the mom, that's okay. "Separating from the baby is hard, and it often takes small steps before big ones,” says Bellenbaum. In this case, offer to watch the baby while she goes for a walk, go grocery shopping with her while you push the stroller, or hold the baby at the salon while she gets a haircut.

The bottom line? Feeling angry because your world feels small right now doesn’t make you a bad mom. “You can love your baby and resent having so little freedom over your own time,” says Ou. “Both things can be true.” It just means you need more sleep, a conversation with other adults, or an hour or two out of the house, and having those needs met only makes you a better parent to your baby.

#7928. Pyometra: Signs, Causes, and Care (Vet Answer)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Your female dog is drinking more, panting, lethargic, and you know something just isnât right. Never ignore that feeling. You know your dog better than anyone else, and if you think something is wrong, it probably is. And if your dog hasnât been spayed, you could be seeing signs of pyometra: infection of the womb or uterus that can turn deadly if left untreated.

Any dog with a uterus can develop a uterine infection, and, although rare, even dogs that have had a laparoscopic or âkeyholeâ spay, where only the ovaries are removed, can be at risk of pyometra. So, what is pyometra? Read on to find out.

An infected uterus or womb, sometimes referred to in practice as a âpyoâ, is a relatively common condition affecting entire female dogs. It occurs most commonly in middle-aged to older dogs, but cases have been reported in dogs as young as 9 months.

In dogs, the uterus splits into two branches or âhornsâ that allow multiple fetuses to be carried on each side. Female dogs come into season or estrus around every six months once they reach sexual maturity. This is when she becomes fertile and receptive to mating. If she becomes pregnant, all being well, she will deliver a litter of puppies approximately 63 days later. Sometimes there can be a âphantomâ or âfalseâ pregnancy, also known as pseudopregnancy, where the fluctuating hormones surrounding estrus and mating prepare the dog for pregnancy, even when fertilization hasnât occurred.

Every time a dog goes through estrus, her cervix relaxes and opens, and the lining of the uterus thickens in preparation for mating and pregnancy. Ordinarily, the cervix helps prevent dirt, debris, and harmful bacteria from entering the uterus, so when the cervix is open, the risk of contamination and infection increases. If fluid and bacteria accumulate, infection can set in over the following 2-3 weeks, resulting in pyometra.

There are two types of pyometra: open and closed.

The more common and less dangerous of the two, an open pyometra occurs when there is infection in the uterus, but the cervix remains open. Dogs with an open pyometra are often diagnosed more easily because owners notice a foul-smelling discharge coming from the vulva, or that their dog becomes obsessed with licking her nether regions.

Because the pus can drain out of the uterus, an open pyometra tends to be less of a threat than one that is closed. However, an open pyometra can become closed, and vice versa.

A closed pyometra occurs when the cervix has shut, locking infection inside the body. It is a far more dangerous situation because the problem is not always immediately obvious, and, as the infection continues, pus fills and stretches the uterus. This can bring a risk of septicemia (infection of the bloodstream) and uterine rupture, both of which carry a high risk of mortality.

The signs of pyometra usually appear around 2-3 weeks after estrus. As mentioned above, dogs with an open pyometra may have a yellow, greenish, or brown discharge from the vulva which, if you get close enough to discover, smells pretty awful. However, dogs that are quite clean may lick up any discharge before you notice, so itâs important to be aware of the other signs of pyometra, which include:

With each season a dog experiences, her risk of uterine infection increases. At each estrus, the cervix opens, and the repeated thickening of the uterine wall reduces its ability to contract and expel fluid and contaminants. Dogs over 7 years old are typically at higher risk, but pyometra can affect even young dogs.

The most common bacteria involved in pyometra is Escherichia coli (E. coli), responsible for around 90% of cases, usually from fecal contamination.1 Obesity, recessed vulvas, chronic diarrhea, and thick coats that regularly become soiled increase the incidence of fecal contamination of the vagina and uterus, putting dogs at a much greater risk for pyometra.

Studies have also shown that diet can affect the growth of pathogenic E. coli and therefore influence pyometra risk.2

The use of synthetic hormones to prevent embryo implantation or induce abortion in the case of accidental mating, or to suppress or delay estrus, has also been found to increase the risk of pyometra.3

Your vet will diagnose pyometra based on a combination of the history, clinical signs, and examination. They will usually perform a brief abdominal ultrasound. Pyometra appears as fluid inside the uterine horns, visible on ultrasound as discrete black circles or tubes.

pyometra in dogs,ultrasound findings and diagnosis

They will also perform some bloodwork to check for signs of septicemia and assess kidney function, hydration status, and rule out any other underlying issues.

The fastest and most definitive treatment of pyometra is to perform an ovariohysterectomy â spay the dog.

The first step in treating pyometra is to start antibiotic therapy and intravenous fluids. Depending on the severity of the situation, your vet may recommend that your dog stay overnight on these treatments before proceeding with surgery, or they may want to go ahead right away.

Occasionally, mild cases of pyometra can be successfully managed using a combination of hormonal treatments and antibiotics. However, dogs that have had one episode of pyometra have a much higher chance of having another, which is why surgery is usually recommended. Once the ovaries and uterus have been removed, a dog can never get pyometra again.

The surgical removal of the ovaries and uterus will completely eliminate the risk of pyometra. Dogs that are spayed earlier in life also have a significantly lower risk of mammary cancer.

In the last decade, advice regarding the timing of spaying has changed, and most vets recommend waiting until after the first season to ensure she has reached sexual maturity. For small breeds, the first season might occur at around 6 months, while for large or giant breeds, the first season may not happen until they are at least 12-18 months old.

In a keyhole or laparoscopic spay, only the ovaries are removed (ovariectomy); the uterus is left behind. This has become a popular option due to the perceived reduction in pain, discomfort, and recovery time. However, when performed on young, healthy dogs, the most challenging part of a routine spay is trying to convince the patient to stay quiet and calm after surgery!

Theoretically, by removing the hormonal factor, ovariectomy should prevent pyometra. However, in the case of ovarian remnant syndrome, where fragments of ovarian tissue are left behind, uterine infection can occur.

Breeding from a dog that has (or has had) pyometra is not recommended. The circumstances that allow pyometra to form â open cervix, thickened uterine walls, contamination â can also make pregnancy riskier for the dog.

Additionally, pyometra can damage the uterine lining, reducing fertility and increasing pregnancy risks.

Before surgical spaying became common practice, allowing dogs to mate and have litters was likely seen as the best way to avoid pyometra. This is probably where the old wivesâ tale that âyou should let your dog have puppiesâ originated. These days, with millions of unwanted puppies in need of homes, and surgical sterilization being a relatively safe routine procedure, there is no longer any real justification behind the idea that dogs should have a litter.

If you think your dog might have a pyometra, do not delay treatment â the longer you wait, the worse things will get. If you are worried about costs, reach out to local charities or speak to your veterinarian â there may be payment plans or charitable funds available to help.

A dog is never too old to get a pyometra, so even if your dog is considered elderly, unless they have health conditions that make surgery or anesthesia too much of a risk, itâs far better to have them spayed when theyâre healthy rather than risk them getting a pyometra in old age.

Pyometra is a relatively common â and entirely preventable â disease in female dogs. Infection of the uterus can make your dog incredibly sick, and if left untreated, can even be fatal. Signs of pyometra usually appear 2-3 weeks after a season and include increased thirst & urination, lethargy, inappetence, fever, discomfort, and, in the case of an open pyometra, vaginal discharge.

If you suspect your dog may have pyometra, contact your vet immediately â do not delay.

If your dog hasnât been spayed, talk to your vet. Remember, prevention is always better than cure.

#7927. A Change of Scenery Should Be Part of Your PPD Recovery

When the walls start closing in, a shift in your surroundings can help.

Even 13 years later, Graeme Seabrook can still vividly remember how she felt when she got home from the hospital with her newborn son.

“It was like a gray wall had come down between me and the world, and everybody else was on the other side,” she says. “I was on this side with this tiny baby who depended on me for everything. And I felt all-consuming rage, like 24/7; nothing made me happy. Nothing made me even peaceful. It was really hard to sleep. Breastfeeding was torturous. It was scary.”

Seabrook, now a mom of two, says she felt claustrophobic in her two-bedroom home in Charleston, SC, where she lived at the time.

“It felt like I didn't have any air in that house because there was baby stuff everywhere,” she says. “I had no place to go. I had no way to get out. And even when I tried to, my anxiety was so bad that I couldn't leave.”

Seabrook was ultimately diagnosed with postpartum depression (PPD) and generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and, with treatment, was able to emerge from the fog. She now lives in Colorado and created Whole Human Mama, an online support space for moms.

But you don’t need a diagnosis to know what it’s like to feel trapped. It’s common for new moms to feel stuck at home, even without PPD, says Catherine Monk, Ph.D., psychologist and division chief of Women’s Mental Health in the Department of Obstetrics & Gynecology at Columbia University.

Postpartum brings on a dramatic lifestyle shift. During pregnancy, you may still be going to work, meeting friends for coffee, and generally living on your time. Once the baby arrives, your world gets a lot smaller, and it’s often just you and the baby following the same routine day in and day out.

“Feeling trapped in one's house or apartment … can just really amplify the stuckness of the mood,” says Monk. Plus, if you’re already in the thick of PPD, getting out of the house, or even off the couch, can feel impossible.

But even the littlest of wins can make a big impact on how you feel, says Monk. This isn’t about uprooting your life or your comfort zone. A small change of scenery can do wonders to improve your mood.

You know how a smell can take you back to your grandmother’s kitchen? The same can happen with certain environments. Memory research has long shown that the brain connects memories with places, and memories bring emotions with them, says Monk. Now picture a new mom whose whole day happens in the same couple of rooms (probably covered with burp cloths, diapers, and breast pads). It makes sense that emotions would get tangled up in those surroundings.

Taking care of a baby means routines come alongside chaos, says Monk. “People's worlds can start to feel centered in maybe the bedroom or a baby's room or the living room,” she says. “People can get quite planted and rooted.”

Science has also looked into whether how a home looks and feels can alter your mood. A 2011 study of about 2,100 mothers found that moms whose homes were crowded or noisy had slightly higher odds of screening positive for depression. A small UCLA study in 2010 also showed that women who described their homes as cluttered and full of unfinished projects reported feeling down as the day went on, while those who described restful, relaxing spaces reported feeling less down.

A natural solution for getting out of the house is going outside, and it works. Spending time in nature, whether that’s hiking a trail or simply taking in the scenery, could help you feel better, says Gina South, M.D., M.S., associate professor of emergency medicine at Penn Medicine, who studies how nature affects mental health.

“There is something very specific about nature that we connect to at a very deep level that impacts our brains and our experience,” says South.

One reason lies in something called fractals, or repeating geometric patterns found organically in nature. Consider a tree: The trunk splits into big branches, which split into smaller branches, which split into twigs, and those twigs split into leaves with leaf veins — all those splits follow a similar pattern.

Research shows our brains can process these patterns with little effort, which may ease mental fatigue, reduce psychological stress, and improve attention, says South. In fact, a 2015 study found that healthy adults who took a single 90-minute nature walk showed lower activity in the region of the brain associated with rumination than those who walked just as long on a busy road.

In her own randomized controlled trial, South and her co-authors surveyed the mental health of residents living near vacant lots in Philadelphia before and after some of these lots were planted with grass and trees. Those living near the new green spaces reported fewer feelings of depression and worthlessness than those near the untouched areas. “It showed that if you change the environment, it could change the trajectory of someone's mental health,” she says.

Getting outside is also associated with socialization and physical activity, both of which have been shown to improve mood, says South. “Those social connections are very important for mental health, for depression, including for postpartum depression where people can feel isolated and [that they have] low social support,” she says.

So what exactly counts as “being in nature”? It can be taking a walk by a green space, sitting at a park bench, going to a nearby lake, or even as simple as stepping out to your backyard for five minutes.

“Include nature in your toolkit,” says South. “Going outside is not going to prevent [or treat] depression, so it’s also important to talk to your physician. It's so hard to change behavior; it's so hard sometimes to get out of a rut, but start small.”

Even if you desperately want to get out of the house, planning an outing with a newborn — even if it’s just a walk around the block — can be overwhelming. If the thought of getting outside paralyzes you with worries about blowouts and meltdowns, there are ways to change your environment without leaving home.

Create a list of things that please you, even if they seem silly or insignificant, suggests Monk. They can be as simple as drinking tea in a special mug, eating a meal at the dining table instead of the couch, taking 15 minutes to call a friend, feeding your baby in a different room, or lighting your favorite candle. Small actions can break up your routine and remind you this stage isn’t forever, she says.

If you feel like you have nowhere to escape in your own home, just taking a step to transport your mind can help shift your mood, says Monk. This can look like opening up a book, streaming a favorite TV show, listening to music or a podcast, she says. These are “things that can both be distracting [and] focus the mind elsewhere but are taking an action,” she says. “That underscores, ‘Oh, I can do things to help myself feel better.’”

Determined not to feel trapped again, Seabrook created a place that she could call her own when she was pregnant with her second child. She transformed her screened-in back porch into a colorful, cozy oasis, which served as a visible reminder that she was going to be OK, she explains.

“That was my safe space,” she says. “I had a scheduled C-section, and I knew when we were going to the hospital that morning that I had that [space] to come home to no matter how bad it got.” She didn’t experience PPD with her second birth, but that porch still became her favorite place in the house.

This tactic has now become her go-to advice for postpartum moms who feel boxed in. Simply put: Claim a spot, she says.

“And it needs to be clear of baby stuff …. It doesn't have to be a big spot. It could be a chair,” says Seabrook. “If there is enough room, make it a room. You're worth that. Who you were, who you are now, and who you are going to become — you need space for all of that.”

#7926. 16 Easy Christmas Recipes For A Crowd That'll Sleigh Their Appetites

You have to feed the people, but it doesn’t have to be hard.

The best part of the holidays is being together with your family, all of them, in one place (yes, it can also be the worst part, but we’re not talking about that right now). But when everyone has flown in and unpacked, you do have to keep them fed and happy. Part of the joy of having a house full of people is cooking and baking together — hello, holiday memories. When you have a small army to feed, you and your crew of cooks need some Christmas recipes to feed a crowd. These entrees and sides will yield large amounts of food to fill up your holiday table and stash in the fridge so guests can reheat them at their leisure.

Did someone say fresh garlic bread? Grab a premade pizza dough from your local grocery store to simplify the process, a la this recipe from Damn Delicious, and then watch your family members flock to the kitchen as the smell of baking bread and garlic waft through the house.

Salads are a great dish to feed a crowd because you can size it up as much as you need to, as long as you have a big enough serving bowl. This one from Averie Cooks is delicious as an appetizer or part of a larger winter spread. It’s got apples, pears, walnuts, pomegranate, and feta, all doused in an easy sweet balsamic vinaigrette.

You just recovered from brining and roasting an entire turkey a few weeks ago, so we need not go there again. Damn Delicious’ recipe for sheet pan chicken thighs and stuffing will give you all that herby, wonderful seasonal flavor with way less work involved.

If you need a 9x13-sized vegetarian main or side dish, try Foodie Crush’s spinach and ricotta baked pasta. It’s easy to make and easy to bulk up with the protein of your choice. Personally, I’d grab a rotisserie chicken at the store to shred and toss in with everything else.

Averie Cooks’ mashed potato recipe involves caramelized onions and plenty of cheese — hell to the yeah. If you want to simplify it, though, just skip the onions and follow the instructions for getting perfectly tender, mashable potatoes in your slow cooker. She’ll tell you exactly how much broth, half-and-half, and sour cream to add to get the perfect texture.

Pork loin is one of those meats you probably don’t make often on a random weeknight, so it feels a little extra special served around the holidays. Laughing Spatula’s recipe will show you how to stuff it with seasonal deliciousness — apples, cranberries, and pecans — for a meal your family will request again next year.

Seven ingredients (most of which are pantry staples you for sure already have) and 15 minutes of prep — that’s all you need to make Foodie Crush’s candied sweet potatoes.

You could definitely order a honey-baked ham and be done with it, but if you’re game to make your own, Damn Delicious’ version is surprisingly simple. The 8-pound ham yields about 12 servings, for reference, which you could scale up or down depending on your crowd.

If you’re unfamiliar, cottage pie is kind of like shepherd pie’s easier-to-make cousin. Shepherd’s pie is traditionally made with lamb, while cottage pie is beef-based. This recipe from Our Love Language is Food will teach you how to make a delicious, comforting cottage pie in 30 minutes, and get that cheesy mashed potato crust on top juuust right.

Beans are the perfect filling food for a crowd. They’re super cheap, loaded with protein and fiber, and they hold so much flavor. Foodie Crush’s 15-bean soup looks delicious and comforting, and would be perfect served with a big, easy salad and some bread (and reheated later when the errant house guest gets hungry).

Some dishes from Thanksgiving do deserve a comeback tour, and that includes green bean casserole. Family Fresh Meals’ version comes together in the slow cooker with nearly zero effort on your part and without so much as even taking up space in the oven. It’s a Christmas miracle.

You need carbs for an army, you say? Princess Pinky Girl’s slow cooker macaroni and cheese is the easiest and the cheesiest on the internet.

If you need to make a side dish for a crowd, a massive sheet pan or two of roasted veggies will always get the job done. You could choose broccoli, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, or, in the case of this recipe from Budget Bytes, butternut squash.

Want to whip up one or two easy desserts that’ll feed a crowd? Simply LaKita’s no-bake eggnog cheesecake recipe is just a matter of measuring and mixing, and letting the cheesecake set in the fridge for a few hours before serving. You will catch your relatives sneaking bites at midnight in their Christmas jammies.

You no longer have the energy to make another thing. That’s OK. Family Fresh Meals’ Little Debbie Christmas tree cake dip requires but a whisper of effort. You just need to food-process or mash everything together and stick it in the fridge to set for an hour, and I promise, the people will lose their minds over this stuff.

Princess Pinky Girl’s cherries in the snow recipe will yield a no-bake, light and fluffy cake dessert that serves 12. It only takes about 15 minutes to assemble (you’ll get to tear up some angel food cake for the base, which is therapeutic), and it looks so pretty on the table with that bright red cherry topping.

*Siiiiigh.* Time to go buy yet another box of Christmas tree cakes.

Since 2001, October 16th has been known as National Feral Cat Day â an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and give a voice to the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. It is estimated that there are around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, and we know that it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming. Thatâs why many feline rescue groups want to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month.

Leading the charge is Mission Meow, a unique organization that supports small feline-focused nonprofits with impactful grants, helping to deliver lasting transformations for cats in need. Throughout the year, they coordinate with donors to provide much-needed funding to animal charities across the country, giving smaller groups the means to continue their vital work. To celebrate Mission Meowâs 4th Anniversary and #FeralCatAwarenessMonth, the latest round of grant recipients have been selected in recognition of the work they do to address one of the biggest challenges facing cat rescue: overpopulation.

One of the most impactful initiatives in managing stray and feral cat communities is Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR).

âTNR tackles the problem at its source by humanely reducing the number of kittens being born outdoors while improving the lives of existing community cats,â says Sally Williams, founder and CEO of Mission Meow. âWith our anniversary falling during Feral Cat Awareness Month, it felt like the perfect opportunity to shine a light on this critical work and invest in organizations creating long-term, sustainable change.â

With that in mind, five nonprofit organizations were selected for this round of Mission Meow grants:

Community Cat Welfare Network in Pinehurst, North Carolina supports the humane welfare and stabilization of existing community cat colonies in central North Carolina through the provision of food, insulated winter shelters, veterinary care, humane population stabilization efforts, and public education.

Grant funding will provide 20 winter shelters for stabilized community cat colonies.

Through the work of Fix & Feed Feline Feral in Tampa, Florida, stray cats and kittens are humanely trapped and spayed or neutered, vaccinated for rabies, and returned to their colonies, which are managed by caring volunteers. The health of these feline communities is supported through health checkups, annual vaccinations, and specific health care as needed.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment and an incubator to expand their growing community program.

Lupa Legacy Animal Rescue provides medical care to homeless pets in central Oklahoma, with a focus on owner-surrendered pets and tame, stray cats and kittens from TNR efforts.

Grant funding will help provide TNR equipment and microchip readers to expand trapping efforts to a nearby trailer park.

Hands to Paws Rescue in Georgia initiates and supports programs that extend and elevate the standards of compassionate care for companion animals in the greater Augusta area by providing educational programs, direct care, and cooperative efforts to increase access to low-cost spay/neuter, rescue, fostering, and adoption of animals.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to help expand their community cat spay/neuter transportation program.

TippedEars in Compton, California, is combating cat overpopulation through humane TNR. While in their care, community cats are sterilized, vaccinated, and treated for fleas.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to create a trap-lending program for trained community members.

Each organization stood out in its own unique way, but they all shared qualities that are deeply important to Mission Meow. They are collaborative, community-focused, and committed to TNR, addressing cat overpopulation at its source. Many work with underserved communities and focus on community cats who could easily be overlooked. Most importantly, they understand that creating lasting change means not only helping the cats in front of us today, but also working to prevent more cats from needing help tomorrow.

Even little changes can have a huge impact, and there is no such thing as a âsmallâ donation â every little bit helps. Start at home by supporting local animal shelters and TNR programs, spay & neuter your cats, and when youâre looking for a new feline friend, think adoption first.

Fresh grass seed can take longer to sprout than the bag suggests, especially as fall cools off. A slow start is usually normal, and a few simple changes can help it along...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is when a lot of homeowners get around to overseeding cool-season lawns. You rake out the thin spots, spread the seed and set the sprinkler going. Two weeks later, plenty of those patches still look like bare dirt, and it's tempting to blame the seed.

Chances are, the seed is fine. Anyone who has spent time seeding a lawn knows some grasses are just slow, and a couple of the usual fall picks can take weeks to show anything. Fall is still a smart time to seed, though. The ground stays warm from summer while the air cools off, and the rain usually picks back up.

Grab the bag and check what's in it. A blend might mix ryegrass, fescue and bluegrass, and those don't keep the same schedule. Ryegrass can be up in about a week, while bluegrass may take a month, so a new blend looks spotty at first. And green doesn't mean done – new grass still needs several more weeks to root in.

The rest happens underground. Cool-season seed generally won't germinate until the soil is above about 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and colder ground can leave it sitting there until spring. Push a soil thermometer (like this one from the Urban Worm Store) in to see where yours is. The seed also has to stay damp and reach dirt, not just rest on dead thatch.

Any lawn that slows down and browns a little in July, then greens back up when the nights cool off, is a cool-season lawn. Bermuda, zoysia and bahiagrass are the opposite; those warm-season grasses do better seeded in late spring or early summer, after the soil has warmed up.

Across the upper Midwest and other northern areas, the ground cools early, so the window runs from mid-August to mid-September and has usually closed by October. Farther south, in places like Tennessee, there's room to seed into mid-October. Anything sown late has less time to get established before the first hard freeze.

Perennial ryegrass is what you want when a bare spot has to look green before winter – a worn strip by the mailbox, let's say, or the patch where the dog cuts across the yard. It's often up in 5 to 10 days. Sow it early in the fall window. One option is Pennington Fairway Supreme perennial ryegrass from Lowe's, which comes in a 50-pound bag with fertilizer mixed in. It's at its best in cool, moist weather and doesn't take drought well. In the South, it mostly gets sown over dormant Bermuda for winter color, not as a permanent lawn.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your USDA Planting Zone is somewhere between Kansas and the Carolinas, your lawn may well be tall fescue already. Bluegrass struggles in those hot summers, but fescue's deep roots carry it through dry spells. Seed usually comes up within a week or two. GreenView turf-type tall fescue seed, available on Amazon, comes in 7-pound bags. Fescue grows in clumps rather than spreading, though, so thin spots won't fill in by themselves and need reseeding in early to mid-fall.

Bluegrass asks for patience up front. It usually takes at least two weeks to sprout and can take closer to a month. Once it's up, it spreads by underground rhizomes into a thick, soft lawn that can fill worn spots back in. It does best where summers stay fairly cool. Get it down right at the start of your fall window. Home Depot stocks a 5.6-pound bag of Scotts Turf Builder Kentucky bluegrass mix.

Keen for your grass to get a move on? Look this way...

Get down and look closely at a patch that still hasn't come up. You'll often find the seed sitting on top of old thatch or dead leaves instead of on the soil. It dries out between waterings up there; indeed, its first root may never reach the soil. Before you seed, mow the grass you already have down to about 1 1/2 to 2 inches (4–5cm), rake out the loose debris, then scratch up the surface until you can see bare, crumbly soil.

On small areas, a stiff 16-tine steel bow rake like the one Walmart carries will break up a crusted surface. Once the seed is down, rake over it lightly to work it into the top 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3–6mm) of soil, or press it in with the back of the rake. Don't worry if some seed is still showing, since bluegrass actually sprouts better with a little light.

On a breezy afternoon, soil watered at breakfast can be pale and crusty by the evening. Seed that's begun to swell can dry out and fail. Short, light sprinkles once or twice a day, and one more on days like that, keep the top inch (2.5cm) damp, not muddy. Long soaks can float seed into low spots or waterlog the soil, and an overnight rain counts as a turn.

A pulsing impact head can knock seed loose, but an oscillating sprinkler lays water down in a soft sweep. With the Melnor XT turbo oscillating sprinkler from Amazon, you can narrow the spray so it stays on the seed, not the sidewalk. For days when nobody's home, the Orbit single-outlet hose faucet timer from Home Depot can run short cycles as often as once an hour. Once seedlings have roots, water less often but more deeply.

A thin layer of screened compost over the seed helps keep the surface from drying out so fast. That layer gives the seed some protection from heavy rain, too. Spread it no more than about 1/4 inch (6mm) deep. You should still be able to see a little seed and soil through it.

Thicker isn't better. Grass seed carries only a small store of energy, and seed buried too deep can use it up before the shoot reaches light —, and fine bluegrass seed may not sprout under a heavy layer at all.

If you don't have finished compost, a bag of Scotts Turf Builder lawn soil from Home Depot is made for overseeding and top dressing.

So how long should you wait? With ryegrass or tall fescue in soil that's stayed warm and damp, about three weeks is a fair wait. Before reseeding, scrape back a little soil and look. Swollen or split seed is still working, while seed that looks dry and unchanged probably dried out or never touched the soil. Old seed can be the culprit too, so check the packaging date.

Don't count on starter fertilizer to hurry any of this along. Seed carries its own food for germination, and starter fertilizer is there to feed seedlings once roots form – too much can burn tender new grass. If your fall window has closed, it's better to stop than to keep sowing into cold soil. Some people dormant seed instead, spreading it in late fall once the soil is too cold for sprouting but before the ground freezes. Otherwise, early next fall is the more reliable time to try again.

Slow grass seed usually just needs a few more weeks. Choose the right grass for your area, sow it while the soil is still warm, and keep it damp. That will do more than any quick fix. With some patience, those bare spots may be filled in by the time you mow next spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7922. 19 Easy, Cheap Christmas Baking Recipes Loaded With Holiday Magic

‘Tis the season for sweet treats that don’t require 87 niche ingredients to make.

What’s affordable is different for every family. For the purposes of this story, let’s assume you keep sugar, flour, butter, and some basic baking seasonings (like cinnamon) on hand.

Ina Garten’s rich, gooey brownie pudding recipe went viral earlier this year; this recipe is Feel Good Foodie’s take on hers. It’s less expensive because it omits the liqueur and subs in vanilla extract for vanilla bean paste, but you still get that custard-like center with crispy edges like Ina intended.

Laughing Spatula’s cranberry bars would be a great dessert to take to a holiday gathering at work or with friends. The bulk of the ingredient list relies on pantry staples, so you’ll just need to grab sour cream, a bag of fresh cranberries, and some vanilla extract if you’re out.

White chocolate chips, sweetened condensed milk, peppermint extract, and some candy canes — that’s all it takes to whip up Averie Cooks’ white chocolate peppermint fudge. Her post has great tips for first-time fudge-makers, like how best to store it so it stays fresh and how long to let it set before venturing that first slice.

Growing up, we made Rice Krispie treats for every holiday. You can add festive sprinkles, a colorful icing drizzle, or mix in something like crushed candy canes and white chocolate chips. You can even add food coloring to the marshmallows when you melt them and then shape the Krispies into whatever you want — gingerbread men, little trees, or snowmen. If you’ve never done it before, Budget Bytes explains the whole process of making your own Rice Krispies treats thoroughly.

Eggnog lovers, this one’s for you: an eggnog poke cake courtesy of Princess Pinky Girl. Again, this recipe relies on a boxed cake mix base, so you don’t need to have any flour or sugar on hand to pull it off. (Side note: her red velvet Christmas poke cake looks amazing too.)

I love how easy and cozy dump cakes are, especially when you eat them warm out of the oven with a scoop of ice cream on top. Family Fresh Meals’ recipe uses canned apples for affordability and a boxed vanilla cake mix for ease.

Something about this cake looks expensive, but you could bake far pricier cakes than this one. Budget Bytes’ recipe breaks down the cost per serving to make this fluffy, tender cake that also has a satisfying nutty crunch.

No dessert sounds cozier to me than a warm brown butter snickerdoodle fresh out of the oven (you know your whole house is going to smell amazing after baking these). All The Healthy Things’ recipe relies on pantry staples you likely already have, and if you do need to pick up a few things — cream of tartar or a new box of baking soda — they’re all pretty cheap.

A genuinely good cake that requires no eggs, milk, or butter? Believe it. Budget Bytes’ recipe is a take on a chocolate cake recipe from the Great Depression when such food items were scarce, but perhaps more than ever, families just needed a little sweet treat to get through the day.

Brb, I need to go buy marshmallows and Rice Krispies ASAP.

#7921. The Silent Health Problem Vets Say Most Cat Owners Never See Coming

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Dental disease is one of the most common health problems seen by vets, yet it's also one of the easiest to overlook. Cats are particularly good at hiding discomfort, so a cat with painful teeth or inflamed gums may carry on behaving normally for a surprisingly long time.

By the time obvious signs appear, the problem may already have been developing for months or even longer, and suddenly a minor issue is a major disaster. The good news is that dental disease is largely preventable, and keeping a cat's teeth healthy doesn't necessarily mean relying on a toothbrush alone.

Plaque is where the problem begins. It forms when bacteria mix with saliva and food particles on the surface of the teeth. If plaque isn't removed, it can harden into tartar â aka calculus â within days.

Tartar leads to inflammation of the gums, a condition known as gingivitis. This can progress to periodontitis, an infection involving the tooth root, weakening the attachment between the gum and the tooth, and eroding enamel. Eventually, the tooth starts breaking down from the inside.

These conditions can all be painful. A cat with advanced dental disease may drool, paw at its mouth, drop food while eating, or stop eating altogether. Bad breath, bloody saliva, teeth chattering, and even sneezing can also be warning signs.

Unfortunately, cats don't always make their discomfort obvious, which is why prevention is so important.

Regular toothbrushing remains the most effective way to prevent dental disease in cats. Daily brushing removes plaque before it has the chance to harden into tartar and tackles one of the main causes of dental problems.

A toothbrush or finger brush designed for cats should be used with toothpaste specifically formulated for felines. Human toothpaste contains ingredients that can be harmful if swallowed.

It's much easier to establish the habit when a cat is young, making it an enjoyable, even fun part of their routine. Older cats can learn too, although a slow approach with plenty of positive reinforcement gives the best chance of success.

Even brushing every few days is better than not brushing at all, although daily brushing provides the greatest benefit.

For cats that arenât tolerating a brush, dental wipes can be a good option.

For cats that won't tolerate brushing, dental diets and treats can provide another option. Dental dry foods contain ingredients and have a texture that are designed to help reduce plaque formation. The limitation is that not every cat actually chews its food. Some cats swallow their food with very little chewing, which reduces the potential benefit.

When choosing dental products, the Veterinary Oral Health Council seal is a useful indicator of effectiveness. Products carrying the VOHC seal have been independently tested and shown to reduce plaque or tartar.

Prescription dental diets are also available through veterinarians. They typically use oversized kibble designed to encourage more contact with the teeth during chewing and may be worth considering for cats with a history of dental problems.

Dental treats and chews have a similar action to dental diets, but are often made from more palatable ingredients to encourage cats to chew them. As a result, they can be quite high in calories, so make sure you include them in your catâs daily allowance.

More recently, powders containing brown algae or seaweed have been showing promising results in the fight against tartar formation, but some cats arenât keen on the taste.

Oral rinses offer another preventative option for cats that resist brushing and aren't suitable for dietary changes. They can be applied using gauze or a soft cloth and work by chemically reducing plaque and tartar before they build up.

The VOHC seal can again help when choosing between products. A veterinarian can also recommend an appropriate rinse for an individual cat.

Water additives are one of the easiest dental care options because they are simply added to a cat's drinking water. They work by helping inhibit plaque formation.

There are some important limitations, however. A cat that doesn't drink enough water may not receive much benefit, while some additives can change the smell or taste of the water enough that a cat avoids drinking it.

A VOHC-approved water additive can be a useful addition to a broader dental care routine, but it is unlikely to be enough on its own.

Plaque prevention gels are often used after a professional dental cleaning. They can help protect newly cleaned teeth and extend the time before another cleaning is needed.

Veterinarians commonly recommend these gels as a follow-up to professional dental treatment rather than as a standalone daily solution. Any instructions about feeding and drinking after application should be followed carefully.

Even cats receiving regular dental care at home may eventually need a professional cleaning. This is performed under general anesthesia, allowing the veterinarian to clean below the gum line, examine each tooth closely, take dental X-rays when necessary, and identify teeth that need to be removed.

The need for anesthesia can understandably concern some owners, but untreated dental disease can lead to chronic pain, infection, and systemic illness.

Senior cats and cats with a history of dental problems may also need their teeth assessed more frequently than during a standard annual examination. Finding problems early generally means treatment can be simpler and less invasive.

There has been a rise in the number of businesses offering dentals without anesthesia, at a price much lower than a dental procedure with your vet. While the idea of a cheaper dental cleaning without the worry of your cat going under anesthetic is appealing, the most significant periodontal disease happens below the gumline. Cats in particular are susceptible to a painful condition known as feline oral resorptive lesions (FORLs), in which the tooth slowly dissolves. FORLs can develop in completely clean teeth. They often form in the roots and need to be diagnosed using dental x-ray.

A catâs teeth may look clean after an anesthetic-free dental, but there could be painful problems going on beneath the surface.

Dental disease isn't inevitable, but preventing it requires more than waiting for obvious symptoms to appear. Cats can hide dental pain remarkably well, meaning a seemingly healthy mouth may already have problems developing beneath the surface.

Regular brushing is the most effective option, but dental diets, treats, rinses, water additives, and professional cleaning can all play a role. The right combination will depend on the individual cat and how well they tolerate each approach.

Keeping on top of dental care can help prevent painful problems from becoming something a cat has to quietly live with for years.
