#7920. Ask Dr. Paola - HELP! My Havanese Puppy Isn’t Eating! (October 5, 2026)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their dog's health and well-being.

Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned dog lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral issues, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your furry friend happy and healthy. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

I purchased my Havanese, Paisley, at 8 weeks. She hasnât eaten any food for three weeks now. That makes her blood sugar drop. I have taken her to the emergency vets twice and my regular vet numerous times.

They have run multiple liver tests but can't find anything wrong with her. I have been hand-feeding her the prescription sugar water the vet gave me, but I have to force her mouth open to give it to her.

Have you ever heard of anything like this?â

A tiny puppy has limited energy reserves, so when she stops eating, her blood glucose can fall quickly. This is one reason we normally feed puppies several times throughout the day. However, three weeks without eating is much more concerning than simple âpuppy hypoglycemia.â Sadly, once a puppy stops eating, this can become a vicious cycle because low blood glucose can cause weakness, abnormal behavior, and even less interest in food. Sugar can temporarily raise her blood glucose, but it does not address the underlying problem. And since Paisley has been refusing food for several weeks, this deserves some serious detective work.

Normal liver blood tests are reassuring, but they do not completely rule out every condition that can cause chronic inappetence or recurrent hypoglycemia in a puppy. Depending on what has already been evaluated, your veterinarian may also consider additional investigation for conditions such as infection, gastrointestinal disease, congenital portosystemic shunting, adrenal disease, or other metabolic disorders.

A portosystemic shunt (PSS) is an abnormal blood vessel that allows some blood from the digestive system to bypass the liver instead of passing through it normally. Because the liver plays an important role in processing nutrients and maintaining normal metabolism, this abnormal circulation can cause problems in some puppies. More specialized blood tests and imaging, such as abdominal ultrasound with Doppler evaluation or, in some cases, CT angiography, may be needed to investigate these conditions.

The Havanese is among the breeds with a higher risk of PSS, so if it hasnât already, I think this should be thoroughly investigated.

Although managing her glucose levels is very important, please be cautious;  forcing sugar water into her mouth carries a risk of aspiration (inhaling the liquid into the lungs). If Paisley is conscious and able to swallow normally, the recommendation is to place a small amount of an appropriate glucose source, like the water you mentioned, directly onto her gums or inside her cheek, where it can be absorbed through the mucous membranes. This can help raise her glucose levels without the risk of aspiration. However, if she becomes extremely weak, cannot swallow normally, collapses, becomes unconscious, or has a seizure, nothing should be given by mouth because of the risk of inhaling it into the lungs. Those situations require immediate emergency veterinary treatment.

Because Paisley has gone this long without eating voluntarily and continues to experience low blood glucose, I would discuss referral to a veterinary internal medicine specialist or hospitalization for nutritional and glucose support. Think of the glucose as a power generator keeping the lights on, but the priority is still finding out why the electrical system keeps failing. Sugar can keep the lights on for a while, but eventually we need to find the faulty wiring. Supporting her blood glucose is essential, but identifying and treating the underlying cause is what will ultimately allow her to maintain normal glucose without constant intervention.

I wish you and Paisley the very best, and I hope this helps.

#7919. 15 Cozy Holiday Shows For Bingeing With An Oversized Blanket & A Mug Of Cocoa

From very merry matchmaking to an absurd amount of buttercream, these series will put you in the holiday spirit.

Here are the cozy holiday shows I’m queuing up this season. Come live in the twinkle lights a little while with me, won’t you?

A very merry… homicide? OK, I know, but hear me out. In this Hallmark series, Sarah Drew (yes, April from Grey’s Anatomy) plays Emily Lane, a newcomer to the quaint town of Fletcher’s Grove. There, she runs an impossibly charming Christmas shop — and keeps stumbling into murders. But trust that it is full-on cozy between all the twinkle lights and flirty banter with Peter Mooney’s Sam. Plus (!), Emily has a mysterious past of her own that just seems to get juicier every season. Season 3 premieres Thursday, Nov. 5, and Good Witch queen Catherine Bell joins the fun, so now’s the time to catch up.

Where to stream: Hallmark+, Netflix (Seasons 1 and 2)

Is there anything more quintessentially holiday-esque than baking? The GBBS holiday specials give you everything you love about the lovely culinary competition (The tent! Paul Hollywood! Desserts that make you drool!), but bring back fan-favorite bakers from past seasons to whip up festive showstoppers. I love that the stakes are blissfully low here; no one’s going home in tears. It’s the TV equivalent of a warm mince pie, and the rare show the whole fam will actually watch together. Bonus: You may be inspired to bake! If you’re anything like me, you will not succeed… but you’ll be inspired, nonetheless.

This cutie-pie series has only one season, with just eight half-hour episodes. That’ll get you through a marathon night of gift wrapping, won’t it? Cynical Dash (Austin Abrams) and endlessly sunny Lily (Midori Francis) trade dares in a red notebook they leave for each other all over New York City at Christmastime. I mean, come on, you can’t ask for much cozier than that. It’s like a scavenger hunt crossed with You’ve Got Mail, minus the corporate bookstore villainy. It’s swoony and gorgeous and features the historic Strand bookstore, and I’ll never fully forgive Netflix for canceling it after one season.

I realize this isn’t technically a holiday show, but I just feel like nothing says “cozy winter” quite like this sitcom about a fish-out-of-water New York doctor stuck in the tiny, quirky, snowy town of Cicely, Alaska. It’s peak ‘90s comfort TV, aka weird in the best ways. I highly recommend watching the whole series from the start. However, if you just need a quick fix, start with the Christmas episode “Seoul Mates” from Season 3 and then just keep going until spring.

One of my favorite Christmas shows to come out of the last few years, this series sees Mae Whitman (forever Amber from Parenthood) as Kate, a perfectly content single textile designer in an English village whose best friends sign her up for a holiday matchmaking program. The gist: 12 themed dates leading up to Christmas. It’s all very Bridget Jones by way of a Christmas market with (bonus!) Jane Seymour and Mary McDonnell along for the ride, not to mention a sweet B-plot about Kate’s dad finding love again. Six episodes with a satisfying ending and no cliffhanger? Total bliss.

Since we’re on the subject of Hallmark holiday series, might I put you on to Hallmark’s official first-ever holiday series? This one follows six families on one cul-de-sac as they navigate the chaos (and, yes, joy) of the season. It’s a totally stacked cast, too, thanks to Ian Harding, Erin Cahill, Rachelle Lefevre, and Dennis Haysbert in the mix. Basically, it’s a warm ensemble-cast hug of a show that’ll have you weirdly ready to head home for the holidays and straight into your family’s distinctive brand of holiday dysfunction.

Anyone who’s ever fielded “So… are you seeing anyone new?” over holiday dinner will relate to our heroine here: Johanne, a 30-something nurse who panics under family pressure and claims she’s bringing a boyfriend home for Christmas. Ah, classic setup! That means she has 24 days to find one, so the race is on. This Norwegian rom-com is funny and real and snowy and absolutely worth the subtitles.

I never thought I’d be so into a reality series about glassblowing, but here we are! Here, glassblowers make holiday ornaments, snow globes, and festive sculptures out of molten glass and, I gotta be honest, it’s oddly soothing. It’s a solid choice when you need the kind of background TV to put on that the kids won’t complain about.

Dennis Quaid is in peak Dennis Quaid form as an intense family patriarch who meets his youngest daughter’s musician boyfriend over the holidays. It’s got that classic multicam sitcom feel, laugh track and all, that nails the delightful agony of spending a holiday week trapped in your parent’s house. It’s only one season, making it an easy binge.

There’s just something about a show that takes place in a small town where everybody’s all up in your business that feels somehow inherently holiday-esque. So no, this one’s not specifically a Christmas series, but it feels right at home on the list. Anna Lambe stars as Siaja, a young Inuk mom who walks away from her marriage and tries to build a new life in the tiny Arctic town of Ice Cove. It’s a super-snowy series that manages to come across incredibly warm, not to mention laugh-out-loud funny. Season 1 swept the Canadian Screen Awards, and Season 2 lands on Netflix Nov. 5.

Was there ever any doubt? Stars Hollow in the snow is the blueprint for cozy TV. Lorelai’s love of wintry weather (“I smell snow”), the town’s over-the-top seasonal festivities, Luke’s Diner, enough coffee to kill a horse… it’s like a holiday show that happens to be year-round. Whether you’re watching for the 20th time or finally indoctrinating your teen, there’s truly no wrong time to go back to Stars Hollow. There’s definitely a right time, though, and it’s now.

How do I love this show? Let me count the ways: 1. Tina Fey, 2. Will Forte, 3. Colman Domingo, 4. Steve Carell, 5. Kerri Kenney-Silver, 6. Marco Calvani, 7. Erika Henningsen… OK, OK, you get the point. Which is that there are many reasons to love this Netflix series about a group of longtime friends who vacation together four times a year. Every season of the show includes a winter getaway, complete with cozy cabin vibes. Season 2 dropped this spring and Season 3 is in production, so you’ve got 16 episodes to work through for now.

Ugh, my heart! In this lovely series, the late, great Treat Williams stars as a big-shot New York neurosurgeon who uproots his grieving kids to a tiny mountain town in Colorado. Cue snow streets and small-town eccentrics and lots of earnest WB-era feelings! In full transparency, this one might make you cry into your hot cocoa. At four seasons long, it makes for the perfect long December binge.

I cannot stress enough how much any self-professed devotee of cozy shows should be watching this adaptation of James Herriot’s books. All Creatures Great and Small follows a young vet in the Yorkshire Dales, and every season ends with the exact kind of Christmas special your holiday-loving heart hopes for, between snowy farmhouses, roaring fires at the pub, and loved ones gathered around the table at Skeldale House. Season 7 doesn’t hit PBS until Jan. 17, 2027, so you’ve got this final stretch of the year to get all caught up.

Where to stream: PBS app (with PBS Passport) and PBS Masterpiece on Prime Video

Host Jonathan Bennett (aka Aaron Samuels) and judge Melissa Peterman put 10 aspiring leading men through festive challenges in this Hallmark holiday competition. Think Santa auditions, gingerbread builds, and scene work with Hallmark royalty like Tyler Hynes and Alison Sweeney. The goal? To crown one the next star of a Countdown to Christmas movie. It’s cheesy in the way that all the best holiday stuff is, and will actually hit you right in the feels when you least expect it.

Get your Christmas-print jammies out; it’s time to start your cozy holiday binge sesh.

From Venus flytraps to corkscrew plants, your birth month carnivorous plant might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On paper, birth month carnivorous plants sounds... well, a little twisted, especially when you compare it to the usual birth month flowers. Most of us have a side to our personality that we don't show the world every day, though, and these plants are the perfect way to shine a light on our dark side.

These remarkable plants are far from ordinary. From the Venus flytrap's sudden snapping jaws to pitcher plants luring in unsuspecting insects, carnivorous plants have developed some ingenious ways to survive. Some are bold and imposing, others are subtle and deceptive, and each and every single one has its own strategy for getting what it needs.

So how does this tie into you? Well, from birth month birds to birth month animals, nature offers us countless ways to reflect on our character. The lens of carnivorous plants, though? Why, that adds a much more intriguing twist! Behind ambition, for example, there may be a need for control. Sensitivity can sometimes turn into possessiveness, while confidence can tip into arrogance. Even our most admirable qualities can have a less flattering side... and there's no point denying it.

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month owl, birth month tree, and birth month spider (oh yes, I'm deadly serious!), but carnivorous plants perfectly pair with the traits, instincts and impulses that sit beneath the surface of your everyday personality.

You might be determined to the point of stubborn, much like the Venus flytrap; you might, like the bold pitcher plant, have a more domineering side hidden away. Secrecy, perfectionism or an almost obsessive need to prove a point? Well, sometimes it's worth reflecting on the less flattering habits you might not always recognise in yourself.

Ready to meet your botanical shadow self? Let's dive on in...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

January babies like to believe they're in control, but their biggest weakness may be their need to have things go their way. No wonder, then, that the Venus flytrap is their birth month carnivorous plant.

Like this iconic houseplant, you know when to strike, and once you've made up your mind, you can be remarkably difficult to sway. You may have little patience for people who waste your time or challenge your authority.

Your dark side emerges when determination becomes stubbornness and protecting your boundaries turns into shutting people out. You don't always give second chances, especially when you feel someone has crossed you. Why not buy yourself a Venus flytrap from Amazon, then, and spend some time watching it and reflecting on what it says about you?

February belongs to the fanged pitcher plant, which feels wholly appropriate. If this is you, then your imagination is one of your greatest strengths, but it can also help you become someone others struggle to read.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, you know how to draw people in with something fascinating, unusual or irresistible. You may enjoy being unpredictable, keeping parts of yourself hidden and making others work to understand you. And, at your darkest, you can use charm to get your way, leaving people wondering whether they ever really knew you at all.

March babies notice what other people feel, sometimes before they even say it. That sensitivity can make you compassionate, but it can also give you an advantage you don't always use wisely.

Like the sundew plant, you can appear delicate and harmless while holding on tighter than anyone realises. As such, you may struggle to let go of hurt, replaying conversations and remembering every slight. And, when you're wounded, you might use silence, guilt or emotional distance to make others feel the weight of what they've done.

You have a powerful presence and rarely enjoy being told what to do. Indeed, much like the purple pitcher plant, you can draw attention without trying, but your confidence sometimes hides a tendency to rush headfirst into situations you haven't fully considered.

You may mistake resistance for a challenge and disagreement for disrespect. As such, your darker side appears when your need to win becomes more important than understanding others, because you'd rather take a spectacular risk than admit you might be wrong.

Why not treat yourself to a purple pitcher plant from the Ragnaroc Store, then? They're colorful and a cute way to keep pests at bay, not to mention a great way to sit and reflect on the qualities you keep hidden from the world.

If this is your birth month carnivorous plant, you prefer stability... but that doesn't mean you're always as easygoing as you appear.

Like the butterwort, your strategy is subtle: you don't need to chase what you want when you can let it come to you. No wonder, then, that you hide frustration behind politeness, hold grudges long after an argument has ended or quietly keep score when you feel underappreciated.

Your shadow side emerges when patience becomes a way to avoid confrontation and kindness becomes a silent expectation of loyalty in return. Hey, that's not a bad thing; there's a reason this pretty houseplant is so good at killing fungus gnats. Time to bag yourself some butterwort seeds from Amazon, maybe?

A post shared by Lucas Brannen (@lucas_2307_)

Are you a June baby? Say hello to your (very unusual) carnivorous plant!

Always curious about people, you thrive on connection... but you may become restless when the excitement fades. Like the spoon-leaved sundew, then, you attract attention through a delicate and inviting appearance while being far more complicated underneath.

You might tell different people different versions of yourself – not out of malice, but because you want to be understood and liked by everyone. This explains why your darker side appears when the need for validation makes your loyalties unpredictable and your promises easier to break.

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Born in the height of summer, July babies care deeply about the people they let into your world, but their loyalty can have a dangerous edge.

If your birth month carnivorous plant is the cobra lily, you present a striking warning to anything that gets too close, and sometimes may convince yourself that you know what's best for the people you love, even when they haven't asked for your help.

No surprises, then, that your shadow side emerges when protection becomes control, jealousy disguises itself as concern and you struggle to accept that the people you love have the right to make mistakes without your permission. Time to pick yourself up some cobra lily seeds from Seedville, then, and pour some love into it.

A post shared by Mobile Bay National Estuary Program (@mobilebaynep)

August belongs to the white-tipped pitcher plant, which means that you (much like your carnivorous friend here) know how to make an impression, and you rarely enjoy being overlooked. Indeed, much like the white-topped pitcher plant, you have a dramatic presence that naturally draws the eye.

Beneath that confidence, though? Well, you may be more dependent on admiration than you care to admit. You might turn everything into a competition, struggle when someone else takes the spotlight, or dismiss criticism as jealousy. Perhaps, then, your darkest tendency is believing (strike that: knowing!) you're exceptional means you should always get your way.

September's birth month carnivorous plant is the rabbit-eared bladderwort, which is incredibly fitting. After all, you notice everything: the inconsistency in someone's story, the mistake everyone else missed, the detail that doesn't quite add up.

Like the water-dwelling bladderwort, your most interesting mechanisms operate largely out of sight. You may appear helpful while mentally cataloguing other people's flaws but, when things don't meet your standards, frustration can turn into criticism, and careful planning can become an obsession with controlling every possible outcome.

Your shadow side, then, is the belief that if you can find a flaw in everything, nothing can ever catch you off guard. An oddly comforting notion, right?

A post shared by Singapore Carnivorous Plants (@singaporecarnivorousplants)

Halloween month (this author's birth month, no less!) belongs to the bowl pitcher plant, a particularly fitting match for anyone who happens to be a little, or a lottle, emotionally evasive.

Oh sure, you know how to keep the peace, but sometimes harmony matters to you more than honesty. Like the bowl pitcher plant, you can thrive in ways that others don't immediately understand; think concealing your real feelings, avoiding difficult conversations or telling yourself that keeping your options open is better than making a decision.

Your darker side emerges when diplomacy becomes avoidance and your desire not to upset anyone leaves others guessing where they truly stand with you.

November babies get a twist on a classic carnivorous plant, in the form of an all-red variety of Venus flytrap. Why? Well, because you rarely feel things halfway. When someone earns your trust, you can be fiercely loyal; when they betray it, you may find forgiveness far more difficult.

Like the Red Dragon Venus flytrap, your dark coloring conceals a mechanism that reacts decisively when triggered. You might dwell on betrayal, replay old arguments or become fixated on proving that someone underestimated you, which means your shadow side appears when you stop seeking closure and start wanting the other person to feel the same hurt you experienced. Eek.

A post shared by 8 Billion Trees (@8billiontrees)

Last but not least, December belongs to the corkscrew plant, which means you are something of an escapist as you crave discovery, freedom and the feeling that something exciting is just around the corner.

Like your birth month carnivorous plant, whose unusual traps lead prey through a one-way route, your own curiosity can take you further than you intended. You may chase new experiences whenever life becomes predictable, abandon plans when they start to feel restrictive or use humor to dodge uncomfortable truths.

Occasionally, your darker side emerges when freedom becomes an excuse to run from responsibility, as every new beginning becomes a way to avoid finishing what you started.

Whichever birth month carnivorous plant you are, and whatever shadowy trait it holds bare to the light, rest assured that you are still a wonderful person (just check out all of your amazingly positive traits in your classic birth month flower).

Still, there's no denying that it can be fun to embrace our dark sides every once in a while... especially if it helps us embrace a whole new world of plants in the meantime. All hail, then, the bitey side of the botanical world! Sometimes, it's good to be bad...

#7917. As A Therapist, I Thought Caregiver Burnout Wouldn’t Come For Me. I Was Wrong.

The sandwich generation is sorely lacking in support.

Tuesday, 8:10 p.m. I’m helping my 87-year-old mother brush her teeth and change for bed. My 10-year-old calls from the room next door that he and his dad are done reading his latest Big Nate book. He asks (again) when I’m coming to his room to say goodnight. I try not to rush my mother, but I’m exhausted after a long day, and keenly aware of missing those precious minutes right before bedtime when you get the real deal from your child about everything that happened that day.

After months of juggling my work as a therapist with caring for my aging mother (who has been diagnosed with dementia), and being a present, engaged mom and wife, I had to admit that I was dropping some balls. Having all of this on my plate was clearly not working.

I knew I was not alone — I’ve been having this conversation with many friends and clients, also in their 40s or early 50s. In fact, 47% of caregivers under the age of 50 are part of the sandwich generation, those of us who are raising children and caring for aging parents at the same time. If we aren't talking about perimenopause with all its patches and pills, we’re talking about the health concerns of our parents and, potentially, our grandparents as well.

The burnout I was feeling falls particularly heavily on the shoulders of women. Even if you have siblings, most of the caregiving responsibility consistently falls on one person, and that person is typically a woman. Women shoulder the majority of caregiving responsibilities, often to the detriment of their careers. To make matters worse, some caregivers may have a complicated relationship with the parent who is now dependent on them.

Caring for your parent can be immensely rewarding and depressing. Sometimes I feel deeply honored to care for the person who dedicated her life to caring for me. Other times, my mom can’t remember why her beloved husband hasn’t come home yet — my father passed away several years ago. She really doesn’t enjoy having to be bathed by her child, for that matter.

As a mental health professional who has sat with clients going through this very thing, I expected to have more of the answers, to be able to cope and balance more than someone else due to my experience. But the truth is, nothing can truly prepare you for your induction into the sandwich generation.

No matter how we try to overcome the difficulty of caregiving as individuals, we must acknowledge that there’s minimal financial or systemic help for consistent care for the elderly living at home. Some Medicare programs can provide all your healthcare in one place, which is obviously better than driving all over town talking to doctors who aren’t talking to each other. But they often only offer last-minute daily help and, because of the high need in our country, you typically see a new caregiver each day. While better than nothing, it’s clearly not a great situation for a parent who is already confused in their day-to-day life. Some programs actually pay you, the caregiver, for your work, but that doesn’t give you back the missed moments with your own children or restore those career opportunities.

Eventually my husband and I realized that we needed help. Fortunately, we could afford to pay a nurse out of pocket, but the costs have been steep: tens of thousands of dollars annually to have carers for my mother seven days a week, and that’s with me still doing bedtime duty on the weekends. It’s simply not realistic or sustainable for most people.

And one of the challenges that we don’t often talk about is the guilt. Even if you are able to defy the odds and pay someone to come in to help, you still feel guilty about it and get caught up in the “shoulds.” I should be able to care for my parents and my children at the same time; people have been doing this forever with a lot less help. I should be grateful to be able to spend whatever time I have left with my parent. The important part missing from that is the fact that many of us don’t have villages in the way we used to — that nearby family network that would support each other during all the stages of life.

Our lack of a village came into focus for me recently when we adopted a baby into our family. She has brought us more joy than we could have imagined, and I see how much a community would change this experience for us. In my Mommy and Me classes, so many of the young mothers have discussed having their parents come and stay with them during the early weeks of having a newborn. What a stark contrast for me as a mother, in a different phase in my life, where I am taking care of my parent, rather than her taking care of me and my children.

This is a problem that is not going anywhere. Around the country and the world, people are making tough decisions every day — draining bank accounts, missing out on kids’ milestones, declining promotions and date nights with their partner — to take care of a loved one. The physical, financial, and emotional toll can cause extensive damage to the caregiver’s well-being in so many ways.

We also know what to do about this problem. Studies show that while caregiver burnout is a worldwide issue, it is less so in the countries where (surprise, surprise) there is a strong public healthcare system, flexible work environments for caregivers, and affordable private health insurance. These kinds of safeguards can be a key part of rebuilding a new kind of village and community support. The answer is there. The question is if we will take heed before we all burn out.

Dr. Patrice Le Goy is a licensed marriage and family therapist and international psychologist. She is also the research chair of Maternal Mental Health Now and the board chair of Open Paths Counseling Center, as well as the host of Like-Minded with Dr. Patrice, an award-winning mental health podcast.

Patrice lives in Los Angeles with her husband, two children, and their massive dog who is definitely part wolf. You can follow her on social media @drpatricelegoy.

#7916. Dogs on the Screen and in the Audience for Brad Pitt’s New Film

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

You know the drill. Keys in hand. Shoes on. One last look at your dog before you head out, and there they are, wagging their tail like maybe, just maybe, this time you are taking them with you.

Those hopeful eyes. That little head tilt. The expression that says, Excuse me, where exactly do you think youâre going without me?

And then you do the cruelest thing imaginable: you leave.

Sure, they have a perfectly comfortable sofa at home, but imagine settling into a movie theater seat, popcorn in hand, with your dog curled up beside you. Instead of leaving them behind, wondering where you went, you could reach down during the movie and give them a little scratch behind the ears.

Honestly, why have we been doing movie night without them all this time?

Apparently, someone in Miami had the same thought.

At a special screening of Brad Pittâs new movie, Heart of the Beast, at Silverspot Cinema in Downtown Miami on September 19, dogs were officially on the invite list.

The morning had all the ingredients of a proper dog outing: leashes in the lobby, photo ops, plenty of new butts to sniff, and a red carpet where the dogs seemed perfectly comfortable stealing the spotlight.

Then came the part that made this movie night different. The dogs got to go inside and watch the movie, too. And considering that Heart of the Beast is about the bond between a man and his dog, enjoying it in the company of dogs feels almost too perfect.

Heart of the Beast follows Special Forces officer James Belmont, played by Brad Pitt, and his combat dog, Odin, after a plane crash leaves them stranded in the Alaskan wilderness. Their survival depends on communication, trust, and their ability to work together.

The story centers on a relationship that many dog people will recognize, even if the circumstances are a bit more dramatic than the average Tuesday with a Labrador!

Directed by David Ayer and co-starring a German Shepherd named Uber, the movie is described as an adventure thriller centered on the bond between a man and his dog as they face the Alaskan wilderness together.

So while the movie tells the story of one extraordinary human-dog partnership, the Miami screening gave plenty of ordinary dog parents the chance to celebrate their own.

And really, that is part of what makes dogs such irresistible companions. They are not just waiting at home while life happens. They are woven into the little things: the walks, the errands, the road trips, the lazy Sunday mornings; even the occasional movie date.

As fun as dogs in the theater sounds, not every dog is going to be thrilled about it. Crowds, darkness, unfamiliar dogs, and those big cinematic sound effects can be a lot, especially for pups who are sensitive to noise.

Dogs hear much more acutely than we do, so a theater that feels exciting to us can feel pretty intense to them. Around 90 decibels can be uncomfortable for some dogs, and sudden bursts of sound can be especially startling.

A pup who settles happily beside their person? Perfect.

A pup who starts panting, pacing, hiding, or searching for the exit? That is probably their polite way of saying, âI vote for the sofa.â

And honestly, that is okay. Dog-friendly should mean dog-comfortable, not dog-compulsory.

The movie promotion had another very good reason to put dogs in the spotlight.

Ahead of the filmâs September 25 theatrical release, Brad Pitt teamed up with organizations including Wags & Walks Nashville to bring adoptable rescue dogs along to some of the movieâs promotional events.

At a Big Dog Adoption Event in Nashville, Pitt and animal coordinator Andrew Simpson spent time with dogs looking for homes. And at the filmâs global premiere in Franklin, Tennessee, adoptable dogs from Wags & Walks got to join Pitt on the red carpet.

And letâs face it, standing beside Brad Pitt is only going to improve a dogâs chances of finding a new home! Itâs the kind of exposure that can give a little rescue dog a better chance of being noticed. Someone who has never considered adopting might spot one of those faces, click to find out more, and suddenly find themselves filling out the adoption paperwork.

And that is perhaps the most impactful part of all this movie promotion.

The movie gives us a story about the bond between a man and his dog. For these rescue dogs, the hope is much simpler: to find their person, go home, and become someoneâs dog. If Brad Pittâs star power helps a few of these dogs find their forever home, that has to be worth more than any gold statuette.

For the dogs who got to tag along in Miami, they got the kind of movie night most dogs can only dream about: their person right beside them, plenty of new smells to investigate, and a whole theater full of things to sniff. Add a little popcorn to the mix, and honestly, what more could a dog ask for?

Plenty of garden pests spend winter as eggs or dormant adults in old vines, twigs, and leaves. Remove them during fall cleanup – but spare the helpful insects.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By late October, the vegetable beds are mostly dead vines, and the shrubs are dropping leaves. At that point, fall cleanup is usually just tidying up. Next year's garden pests are still in that mess, though. Squash bugs shelter under the old vines, moths leave egg masses on bark and lawn chairs, and beetles seal their eggs inside viburnum twigs.

Many common garden pests don't die off in winter. They spend it as eggs, pupae, or dormant adults in one spot, and they mostly stay there until spring. That makes them pretty easy to find and remove right now. A pair of pruners, a putty knife, or a rake can take out a whole tent caterpillar colony before it ever hatches.

Where you look depends on the pest. Some hide their eggs inside twigs, while others leave them right out on bark or a fence post. A few of the egg cases and cocoons you'll find belong to beneficial insects, though, and those should stay put.

Insects that overwinter usually ride out the cold in a resting stage. For a lot of garden pests, that means an egg mass on a twig, a pupa in the soil, or an adult wedged under leaf litter. Eggs and pupae can't scatter, and dormant adults barely move. Bare branches help too – egg masses hidden by summer foliage are much easier to spot once the leaves fall. One scraped egg mass in October can mean hundreds fewer caterpillars in spring.

So why not rake up everything? Good insects spend the winter in the same spots as the bad ones. Lady beetles and ground beetles burrow into leaf litter, and many native bees tuck into hollow stems. Strip every bed bare during fall cleanup, and those go, too. Focus on whatever had problems this year, and leave the rest a little messy.

Here's where some common pests spend the winter and how to clear them out.

Squash bugs (Anasa tristis) are still around after the plants die. Adults crawl under dead vines and leaf litter for the winter, and some hide under nearby boards. Clear that out once the squash and pumpkins are done. Those vines are prickly, so you'll need good protective gloves like these nitrile-coated garden gloves from Home Depot. Bag the vines rather than piling them up, or the bugs move right in.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your viburnums got chewed up this summer, the leaf beetles (Pyrrhalta viburni) probably left eggs in the twigs. You won't see the eggs, just little rows of bumps near the tips of this year's branches once the leaves are off. Those are the caps the females made from chewed bark. Cut the twigs off with sharp bypass pruning shears (these Fiskars bypass pruners on Amazon are good value for money if you need a new pair) and trash them before spring.

Eastern tent caterpillars (Malacosoma americanum) mostly feed on cherry and apple trees, so start there. Look along the thin twigs for a shiny black band, like someone dripped varnish around the branch. That's the egg mass. Snip the twig off or crush the band, and throw it out. For a big tree, Monterey horticultural oil works as a late-winter dormant spray that can smother the eggs.

Anyone in the Northeast or upper Midwest has likely heard of spongy moth (Lymantria dispar), once called gypsy moth. Its caterpillars can strip a tree bare in a bad year. Right now, though, they're just eggs, packed by the hundreds into tan, fuzzy patches on tree trunks and fences. Check sheds and the underside of patio chairs, too. Scrape each patch into a bucket of soapy water – a soft-sided tub like this Tubtrugs one from Walmart works well – and let it soak for several days.

Iris borer moths (Macronoctua onusta) lay their eggs on old iris leaves in late summer and early fall, and the eggs wait there until spring. Then the caterpillars hatch, climb the new leaves, and tunnel down into the rhizome. Wait until after a hard frost, since the moths can keep laying until then, and cut away the old leaves. Dispose of the foliage in the trash rather than adding it to your compost pile.

If you've had trouble with iris borers before, consider keeping a spinosad-based insecticide, such as Bonide Captain Jack's Deadbug Brew, on hand for spring, when newly hatched caterpillars are vulnerable to treatment before they burrow into the rhizomes.

Scale insects (Coccoidea) stay stuck to the stems and branches of shrubs and trees all winter. They look like small bumps that come off with a scrape of a fingernail. It could be an adult female, a young one, or a cover with eggs under it, depending on the type of scale. Scrub off what you can, and treat the tiny crawlers with Garden Safe insecticidal soap, available on Amazon. Look over potted citrus before bringing it inside, since scale can keep breeding indoors.

Plenty of aphids (Aphididae) get through winter as eggs on rose canes and fruit tree twigs, especially on apples. Those eggs are tiny, black, and shiny, and they're usually near a bud or in a crack in the bark. They're hard to see without a 10x handheld magnifier, like this one with a built-in light on Amazon. Winter pruning gets rid of many, and a dormant oil spray before the buds start to swell can kill more. If some still hatch, a spray of Bonide neem oil from Walmart can help.

Lady beetles, lacewings, mantises, butterflies, and native bees overwinter in the garden too. Don't remove these beneficial insects.

Lady beetles tend to bunch up in winter, and raking into the leaves at the base of a tree can turn up a whole cluster. Cover them back up and move on. Both adults and larvae eat aphids, and every beetle that survives the winter is one more working the garden next year.

Mantis egg cases look like dried globs of tan foam, sometimes as big as a golf ball, glued to a stem or twig. If one is on a stem, you need to cut below the case and tuck the stem into a shrub, off the ground. Mantises do eat helpful insects, too.

Lacewing eggs are easy to recognize – each one perches on the tip of a hair-thin silk stalk. By fall, you're more likely to find the round, papery cocoons that larvae spin in hidden spots on plants, or adults sheltering in leaf litter. The larvae are voracious aphid predators. Leave both stages in place.

Black swallowtail caterpillars spend the summer eating parsley and dill, and the last ones of the year don't leave in fall – they hang on through winter as brown chrysalises, sometimes on the old herb stems. One looks a lot like a scrap of dead plant, so go slowly when you cut those herbs back.

Native bees need a winter spot, too. Many of them nest in the ground, and bare soil is easier to dig into than mulch. Leave a patch or two uncovered. Other bees use hollow or pithy stems like raspberry canes, and their young spend the winter sealed inside. Leave those stems standing until spring warms up, then cut them back to about knee height.

A clean garden and a healthy garden aren't always the same thing. Cut the marked twigs, scrape the egg masses, and clear out the old squash vines and iris leaves. Then let the rest of the leaves lie. Next spring should bring fewer squash bugs and more lady beetles.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7914. The Cat Network, Inc. – How a $35 Bounty Started an Epic Journey

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Throughout October, we are throwing our support behind the mission to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month, an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and recognize the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. With around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, we know it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming, and one group that understands this more than most is The Cat Network in Miami, Florida.

Founded in 1995, The Cat Network is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization supported by more than 2,500 volunteers and donors, helping community cats, stray, abandoned, and homeless cats throughout South Florida while supporting the people who care for them. Through education, low-cost spay/neuter services, adoption assistance, and advocacy, the organization works to humanely reduce cat overpopulation and improve the lives of cats and the communities they live in.

The Cat Network is dedicated to humanely reducing cat overpopulation in South Florida through five core pillars: education, sterilization, adoption, advocacy, and humane public policy. Our story begins more than 30 years agoâ¦

In July 1995, the City Manager of Miami Beach contracted with a commercial trapper, Humane Animal Removal, to trap and euthanize the cityâs feral cats, with a bounty of $35.00 for each cat trapped and killed. When this became public, a local and national outcry ensued, and the media had a field day. The Cat Network, still in its infancy, helped organize local opposition to the trap-kill plan. Susan Fleming, president of The Cat Network and a Miami Beach resident, was instrumental in negotiating with the City to institute TNR instead.  With help from Animal Controlâs mobile animal clinic and SoBe spay/neuter certificates, we convinced the City to implement the more humane approach of TNR.

The following year, we began our spay/neuter certificate program with participating veterinary clinics, the first of which was Galloway Animal Clinic. Since 1995, we've helped sterilize more than 122,000 cats and assisted in the adoption of more than 24,000 cats.

What makes us unique is our comprehensive approach. Rather than simply responding to the symptoms of overpopulation, we focus on preventing future litters while helping cats in need. Our programs include the Miami Meow Mobile, low-cost spay/neuter vouchers, adoption referrals through an extensive foster network, public education, and advocacy for Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) as the most humane and effective way to manage community cat populations.

One of our biggest challenges is simply the sheer number of cats needing help. Because South Florida has warm weather year-round, kitten season never truly ends. This creates an ongoing demand for spay and neuter services, foster homes, adoptions, and community education. Every day we receive calls from residents who have discovered kittens, injured cats, or growing community cat colonies.

There really isn't an "off season" for cat rescue here, so our volunteers and veterinary programs stay busy throughout the entire year. Preventing unwanted litters through early sterilization is one of the most effective ways to reduce this constant cycle.

Funding is another ongoing challenge. Keeping our veterinary programs affordable requires significant community support, and the costs of medical supplies, equipment, and operations continue to rise.

People can make an enormous difference by:

Becoming a volunteer or foster caregiver.

Sharing our educational resources and adoptable cats on social media.

Every donation, volunteer hour, and shared post helps save lives.

Over the past 30 years, The Cat Network has become one of South Florida's leading organizations dedicated to reducing cat overpopulation. Sterilizing more than 122,000 cats and helping over 24,000 cats find homes are milestones that represent countless lives saved.

We're especially proud of the Miami Meow Mobile, which has dramatically increased access to affordable veterinary care, and our long-standing network of volunteers and foster caregivers who make our adoption program possible. Together, these programs have helped thousands of residents become part of the solution while improving animal welfare throughout South Florida.

The Miami Meow Mobile is a fully equipped veterinary clinic designed specifically for cats. Originally envisioned in 2001 and launched in 2005, it was created to make affordable veterinary care accessible to more people throughout the community.

Today, the Meow Mobile provides low-cost spay and neuter surgeries, vaccinations, testing, microchipping, parasite treatments, and basic wellness services. Originally designed as a traveling clinic, it currently operates from a fixed location in Kendall, allowing us to serve a large number of cats efficiently and safely.

The Meow Mobile remains one of our signature programs because every surgery performed helps prevent future litters and reduces shelter overcrowding throughout South Florida.

Our Spay/Neuter Certificate Program partners with participating veterinarians throughout South Florida. Residents can purchase discounted certificates that cover sterilization surgery, a rabies vaccination, and ear tipping for community cats.

This partnership expands access to affordable veterinary care beyond our own clinic. If someone discovers a stray or community cat in their neighborhood, the voucher program provides an affordable pathway to have that cat sterilized before additional litters are born.

By working together with local veterinary clinics, we're able to reach far more cats than we could alone and give residents practical tools to help solve the community cat problem.

Working with cats means no two days are ever alike. Volunteers have rescued kittens from engine compartments, construction sites, shopping centers, and backyard sheds. Every rescue brings its own surprisesâand often a few scratches and plenty of memorable stories.

The resilience of these cats never stops amazing us. Watching frightened community kittens transform into affectionate family pets is one of the most rewarding experiences we witness over and over again.

Every cat that is sterilized prevents countless future kittens from being born into homelessness. Every adoption changes two livesâthe cat's and the family's.

Knowing that thousands of volunteers, donors, veterinarians, and community members are working together toward the same goal makes every success even more meaningful.

As we celebrate over 30 years of service, our goal remains the same: continuing to expand access to affordable spay and neuter serviceswhile working toward a future where no healthy or treatable cat is euthanized simply because there are too many homeless animals.

We continue to strengthen our community partnerships, grow volunteer involvement, support foster caregivers, and educate the public about responsible pet ownership and Trap-Neuter-Return practices.

Anyone interested in getting involved can learn more by visiting TheCatNetwork.org. There they can become a member, volunteer, foster cats, adopt, donate, or schedule services through the Miami Meow Mobile.

#7913. My Parents Took Me Voting. Now I'm Doing The Same With My Daughter.

Your candidate might not always win. But, as my parents taught me, it’s important to show up anyway.

My earliest memories of voting take place at the elementary school up the street from my parents’ house. Every Election Day, my parents would bring me and my younger sister along with them to the polls. I remember standing in the long lines impatiently wondering when it’d be our turn. I remember at least one year where there was a mock ballot for kids. And, perhaps most importantly to elementary-school-aged me, I remember receiving the prized Future Voter sticker at the end.

At the time, I didn’t think of any of this as civic education. My parents weren’t necessarily sitting us down for lectures about democracy or giving us pop quizzes on the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (although that would come later during my AP U.S. Government class). My parents were simply voting and we were watching. But, as it turns out, we were learning by observing.

My parents made it abundantly clear to my sister and me that voting was both a right and a responsibility — and that this wasn’t always the case for people who looked like us. As Black girls growing up in America, that history mattered. We learned that Black people had marched, organized, been beaten and even killed for the right my parents exercised so routinely at the elementary school around the corner.

So, when Election Day came around, we went. And not just for the presidential elections every four years. My parents participated in every election — local, federal, didn’t matter. The responsibility was the same.

By the time I was finally old enough to vote myself, I couldn’t wait.

I missed being able to vote in the 2004 presidential election by a year, which meant the 2008 election would be my first chance to vote for president. And I felt elated that my first presidential vote would be for the country’s first Black president.

At the time, I was working as a reporter at my community newspaper in a conservative county in Maryland. On Election Day, a colleague and I spent hours driving around to various polling places, interviewing voters and reporting on turnout before returning to the Board of Elections to wait for results.

After work, I went home and watched the national returns with my dad. When Barack Obama walked onto the stage in Chicago’s Grant Park with his beautiful Black family, I remember staring at the television in disbelief.

Wow, I thought to myself, soaking in the moment. I just witnessed history.

But elections don’t always end with the history you hoped to witness.

In 2016, I proudly cast my ballot for Hillary Clinton and went to bed believing we were about the elect the country’s first woman president. We all know how that turned out.

Four years later, I voted for Joe Biden, but I was especially excited about his running mate, Kamala Harris, whom I’d supported in the Democratic primary. Watching a Black and Asian woman become vice president meant something different to me. Of course, representation isn’t the only reason to vote for someone and I think we’re all doing ourselves a disservice if we pretend as if identity is entirely separate from politics. As a Black woman in America, I’d spent most of my life looking at the highest echelons of power and rarely seeing anyone who looks like you.

In the spring of 2024, I picked up my then two-year-old daughter Violet from daycare, went to swim lessons and then swung by our neighborhood elementary school to vote in the Illinois presidential primary. With her little puffs and binky in tow, she naturally became the star of the polling place.

Our next-door neighbor, Mr. Steve, was working the polls that day and gave Violet a Future Voter sticker. She was entranced. To her, the sticker was probably the best part of the whole outing, which, when I thought about it, was exactly how I felt when I was her age (and, let’s be real, is also how I feel as an adult).

Afterward, we went outside to the school playground and, as I watched her run around, it hit me what a full-circle moment this had become. And then I had another thought: This could be a children’s book.

I wanted to write a book that could explain voting to children around Violet’s age: something that would talk about walking into a polling place; why grown-ups stood in line to fill out ballots; what even is a ballot; and why any of this matters anyway.

That fateful afternoon eventually became the premise of Violet Goes Voting, an early reader about a little girl accompanying her parents to the polls and learning that voting is one way we use our voices. But the book was just the beginning.

That fall, my husband and I took Violet with us when we voted in the presidential election. This time, I had a very specific picture in my head of what the moment might look like in both real life and the book version. My daughter would sit on my lap as I cast my ballot to elect the first Black woman president of the United States.

My parents had taken their Black daughters to the polls so we would understand that our voices mattered. Decades later, I would take mine with me as I helped elect a Black woman to the White House. Except, of course, that’s not what happened.

Like so many people, I woke up the next morning devastated. The history I had imagined sharing with my daughter would have to wait. Since then, I’ve thought a lot about what, exactly, I want Violet to inherit from me and learn from all of this.

Because maybe the lesson was never supposed to be that if you show up, your candidate will win. My parents certainly never promised that to me. What they taught me was the importance of showing up anyway.

Voting is a small part of civic engagement, but it was my introduction to it nonetheless. Long before I knew what a primary was, before I understood the harsh reality of voter suppression or could name any of my congressional representatives, before I was old enough to fill in a bubble next to a candidate’s name, I knew what Election Day looked like.

It looked like my parents making time to go to the polls. It looked like my sister and me eagerly tagging along. It looked like waiting our turn. And, yes, it looked like getting a sticker at the end.

Now, as a mom, I understand that those seemingly ordinary trips were teaching me something much bigger: This is what our family does. We show up. We pay attention. We responsibly exercise the rights people before us fought to secure. We don’t take them for granted.

Only time will tell who Violet will vote for when she’s old enough to cast her first ballot. And, frankly, we have a while before that happens. She’s much more interested in playgrounds than politics at the moment, which is exactly how it should be for an innocent five-year-old.

But I hope that when her first Election Day arrives, she’ll look back on our family selfie from outside the voting place in 2024. I hope she’ll remember me reading to her the book that she inspired. I hope she understands why walking into that booth and making her own choice carries a history older than the both of us combined.

But most of all and most importantly, I simply hope she shows up. Because that’s the inheritance my parents gave me and my sister. And now it’s mine to pass on.

L’Oreal Thompson Payton is an author, journalist and the founder of Zora’s Place, a Black feminist bookstore and community hub in Evanston, Illinois. Her books include Stop Waiting for Perfect, Amanda Gorman: Poet and Activist, Violet Goes Voting and the highly-anticipated memoir Infertile Black Girl (Fall 2027). Her byline has appeared in outlets such as Essence, Fortune, New York magazine and SELF. Learn more at lorealthompsonpayton.com.

#7912. What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

Bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

Unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

Impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.

Keeping a bird bath ice-free could mean life or death for your garden birds this winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we head further into fall, it’s time to take steps to stop a bird bath freezing over and depriving birds of this valuable resource. Birds need daily access to water and when natural sources freeze over, a bird bath can become a vital lifeline and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard. During a cold snap, dehydration kills birds far faster than starvation, so keeping an ice-free bird bath this winter really is a lifesaver.

Water is surprisingly necessary to so many elements of avian survival in winter, and most small garden birds must drink at least once a day simply to stay alive. As insects become scarce as temperatures fall, a diet consisting primarily of seeds and nuts means birds need to drink more to digest their food, and in sub-zero conditions, eating snow isn’t an option for small birds because of their limited body heat.

A reliable water source also enables birds to bathe and preen, zipping individual feather barbs back together daily to maintain a waterproof insulating top layer. Vital to trap body heat on cold nights, this is also essential for efficient flight – and bare winter branches can leave birds vulnerable to predators. Keep your bird bath unfrozen and you’ll also help birds preserve energy they would otherwise waste finding an alternative water source. So, whether yours is a simple DIY bird bath you made yourself or the smartest birdie bowl money can buy, here's how to stop the water freezing over.

Seems obvious, right? But while the best place for a bird bath in summer is in partial shade to prevent algae growth, a sunnier spot in winter will help to keep a bird bath ice-free. Remember that the sunniest winter spot in your garden may be different to where the sunshine hits in summer, because the sun is lower in the sky. Think about prevailing wind direction, too, as a breeze will increase heat loss from any liquid, just as you blow on your cup of coffee to cool it down, and speed the freezing process in cold conditions.

Positioning your bird bath around 6 feet from a south-facing wall is an optimum solution. Not only will the water be warmed by sunshine for most of the day, the wall will shelter the bath from cold northerly winds and also act as a solar radiator, reflecting the sun’s heat or absorbing then releasing it once the air temperature cools. Either way, your bird bath will sit in a microclimate and the water will be slower to freeze and quicker to thaw.

Solar power is also the force behind this idea as dark stones will absorb the sun’s heat during the day, then release it as the air cools, to slow or stop bird baths freezing over. To be effective, the rock needs to be at least 4 inches across, but do match it to the size of the bird bath as it shouldn’t displace more than a third of the water. The stone should protrude above the water line as an exposed surface will heat far more quickly than a submerged one. The darker and denser the rock, the more heat it will hold, and a flattish surface will absorb more warmth.

Any object that floats on the surface of the water will constantly disrupt ice crystal formation, so it takes longer for the bird bath to freeze. Tailor your choice of what to float to how exposed your garden is, as the object needs to be light enough to move on the slightest of breezes but heavy enough to stay put in stronger winds.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In a sheltered corner, a ping pong ball is best; in a windy position, try a tennis ball. But in most gardens adding a rubber duck to your bird bath hits the sweet spot, and it doesn’t have to be yellow as this Mallard Rubber Duck from Amazon shows.

To reliably prevent ice in bird baths, use a de-icer, but be smart when shopping as many products sold as bird bath de-icers were designed for chicken coops. Look for a product with a thermostat that only works when temperatures drop and automatically shuts off once the weather warms up, so it uses minimal energy. You only need to prevent the water from freezing, not keep it warm, so a product that’s rated 60-120 watts is ideal; leave those 1000W designs for the chickens!

Another important consideration is the length of the lead, as birds often won’t use a bath positioned too close to a wall. Think about the size of your bath, too. This 9” Thermostatic Birdbath Heater from Amazon with a 5.9’ cord is great for a bigger bird bath, while this smaller 100W Bird Bath Heater, also from Amazon, with a 5’ cord would be better for an average-sized bath.

If garden aesthetics are important to you, then faux-rock designs such as this 60W Bird Bath DeIcer from Walmart bring a more natural look. You can also buy heated birdbaths with options to fit onto deck posts and balcony rails as well as ground stakes.

As temperatures drop and natural water sources freeze over, your ice-free bird bath will become a magnet for neighborhood birds. All that splashing avian action will mean you’ll need to keep the bath topped up as the bigger the volume of water, the more stable its temperature. Clear out any fallen leaves, too, as tannins will leach out and make the water unpalatable and rotting plant matter will invite unwelcome bacteria into your birdy spa.

It’s vital to scrub your bird bath once a week, particularly if neighbors don’t bother to keep their bird baths ice-free and yours becomes very busy, as that higher traffic means disease spreads more easily between birds. Use a bird-safe cleaner such as Bird Saver, available from Walmart, or a dilute solution of 10% vinegar and a scrubbing brush, and rinse well before refilling with water.

All these simple ways will keep a water supply for your garden birds, and bring feathered friends flocking to your yard through winter. So, if you're switching up your bird-feeding routine for colder weather, whether that's putting up an extra feeder, adding seasonal kitchen treats or planting shrubs laden with winter berries that birds adore, it's essential to take steps to ensure there's water alongside that welcome food.

She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#7910. The Busy Mom’s Guide To Gift Shopping On Budget

Amazon and Alexa for Shopping make it easy to get it all for less.

Amazon knows how hard moms are working, and they have some ways to lighten the load. When you shop through Alexa for Shopping — Amazon’s personalized agentic shopping assistant — it all becomes way less stressful and way more affordable, and you might even get enough time back to finish your coffee before it gets cold (can you imagine?).

With everyday low prices that meet or beat other retailers across a huge selection of products, from affordable private-brands that help you save without sacrificing quality to the name-brand finds your kids have been asking for, Amazon makes it easier to find gifts that fit your budget.

Here are a few ways to use Amazon to get all the gifts you need — and stay sane while doing it.

Alexa for Shopping is Amazon’s agentic shopping assistant, and it’s really something else. It combines knowledge of the hundreds of millions of products across Amazon with info from across the web, and applies all of that to your personal shopping history and preferences. In other words, it knows all the possible gifts you could get on Amazon, and it knows you.

You can use Alexa for Shopping by asking it questions, like “What are the best toys for 5 year-olds?” or “What are teenagers asking for this year?” or even “What are some premium and more affordable brand options for a red dress and matching headband for my 3 year-old daughter’s holiday outfit?” It will give you ideas (including taking your shopping history and preferences into account) and then share a list of products to look through. So whether you’re gifting your own kids and just need some fresh ideas when you’re drawing a blank, or shopping for an older niece who lives five states away and have no clue where to start, you get tailored advice that helps you land on the perfect thing.

Budgeting during the holidays is not for the weak. Between finding the perfect gifts for your kids, your mother-in-law, and your spouse, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of holiday shopping and discover more things you know they’ll (or you’ll) love along the way.

The good news? Amazon’s prices consistently meet or beat other retailers, so you’re already getting low, competitive prices when you shop on Amazon. On top of that, Alexa for Shopping is a great tool to help you stay on track. First of all, you can use it so see up to a full year of price history for any product you’re interested in. Once you have that information, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to let you know when it drops to the right price for you. And even better, you can ask Alexa for Shopping to turn on auto-buy so it can complete your purchase using your default payment method when the item reaches your price target.

That saves you time (who has the bandwidth to keep checking back every day?!) and helps you know that when you do hit “buy” (or have Alexa do it for you), you’re getting the thing you want at a great price. And if you do that for all of your holiday shopping, you’re setting yourself up to spend less this season. That can be a huge relief at such an expensive time of year.

Bonus: the savings aren't just about gifts. From stocking up on groceries for the holiday feast to getting extra household essentials for overnight guests, the season comes with plenty of demands. With everyday low prices on fresh groceries and household essentials, plus fast free delivery, you can get the things you need at great prices that help your holiday budget go further.

A large part of the mental mom load is figuring out which [insert kid-related item here] is the best one. From onesies to bikes to pimple patches, there are so many things to choose from, and it takes time to figure out what’s actually right for your kid.

Alexa for Shopping takes that stress off your plate, too. Once you’ve found a few options that might work, Alexa for Shopping’s got you: it can show you side-by-side comparisons, highlighting the differences in features, price points, and even the reviews. Instead of digging through details, you get it all laid out and can quickly make your pick. Goodbye, overthinking.

We all know that holiday magic is really just... moms. But Amazon and the features built into Alexa for Shopping sort of feel like their own kind of magic. With Amazon, you can create a holiday season your kids will always remember, and make it look almost effortless. When you can do that without overspending or screaming into the void? We think that’s beautiful.

(And heads up, the savings go even further with Prime thanks to free delivery, exclusive deals, gas discounts, and more. But we digress.)

The best kind of holiday magic isn't just finding the right gifts at the right prices. It's getting a little time back for yourself, too. And honestly, moms deserve that kind of magic most of all.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole tackle the controversial topic of scruffing, while also sharing some fun comparisons between cats, dogs, and toddlers. Instead of treating scruffing like an absolute taboo, the hosts break down why understanding a cat's specific boundaries can make quick vet visits or home care way less stressful for everyone. Dr. Karyn brings her cat, Sirill, onto the desk to show why a timid pinch fails, how a solid hold gives cats a sense of security, and how to quickly test if your cat is way too sensitive for the technique.

Get the real scoop on scruffing catsâincluding why total bans ignore harm reduction when you just need to safely pull out a thorn or trim nails in a pinch. Dr. Karyn breaks down the biggest mistakes pet parents make, explaining why delicately pinching a bit of skin only annoys your cat and how a full-hand hold actually provides better control and stability. Youâll also learn how to check your catâs tolerance before even trying a hold so you never accidentally upset a sensitive pet.

Plus, the hosts chat about research comparing how dogs, cats, and toddlers help others, debating whether cats are truly selfish or just super selective about their time. From winning over shy rescue cats to comparing dogs to needy toddlers and cats to moody teenagers, this episode offers a relaxed, relatable look at living with felines.

Rethinking the Scruffing Debate: Dr. Karyn and Nicole discuss how complete anti-scruffing rules miss the mark on practical care. They explain that learning safe restraint acts as harm reduction, letting you handle fast tasks like pulling out a thorn or trimming claws without having to resort to full sedation.

Test Sensitivity First: Before going in for a hold, Dr. Karyn recommends checking the neck area with gentle pets and tickles. If a cat flinches or pulls away (like her cat, Zelda), you should never try to scruff them.

Skip the "Pinch": The most common mistake people make is grabbing a tiny pinch of skin, which just annoys the cat and provokes a fight. Proper restraint needs a full, firm hand on the scruff so the cat feels secure and can't wriggle free.

Never Pick Them Up by the Scruff: The hosts emphasize that while a hand on the scruff helps keep a cat grounded, you should never lift or carry an adult cat this way.

Altruism in Pets vs. Toddlers: The conversation turns to research comparing toddlers, dogs, and cats. Studies show dogs and kids will help out even without a reward, while cats generally step in only when thereâs something clear in it for them.

Earned Love Feels Extra Special: Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how dogs offer constant, people-pleasing affection, whereas a catâs love feels like an earned privilege. That conditional nature is exactly what makes it so rewarding when a quiet cat finally comes over to snuggle.
