Why settle for decorations that only last a few weeks? Create beautiful seasonal containers that can brighten your entrance well into winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Holiday porch pots are a cheerful way to decorate your home's entrance for the festive season. These outdoor winter arrangements look beautiful and welcoming when placed near front doors, steps, or entryways to greet guests during the holidays.

As October ends, the holiday season approaches. Families make Thanksgiving plans, starting a season that lasts right through the new year. This is the ideal time to start putting together natural holiday decorations that bring bright colors and greenery to your home's entrance.

If you are ready to jump into a creative gardening project for winter, we’ve got the ideas to get you started. The basic idea is to combine beautiful plants and greenery to make spectacular seasonal containers. But you should plan to have some fun while you are doing it.

The best plants for DIY holiday porch pots combine appealing structure with festive cut boughs. They should be hardy enough to survive cold weather and add winter curb appeal.

Why not start with an evergreen that nobody else on your block is likely to display? This silver Korean fir cultivar is one of a kind: a curious, fascinating dwarf evergreen with twisted, curled silvery needles. The twisted needles of ‘Ice Breaker’ Korean fir (Abies koreana), available at Nature Hills, have frosted undersides, making it look as if it is perpetually snow-covered. These little beauties grow very slowly, getting to 2 feet tall after 10 years. They are hardy down to -20°F.

It’s easy to find evergreen foliage plants without red berries, but harder to find red berries without evergreen foliage. That’s exactly why winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata) in holiday porch pots is totally intriguing. You can order a best-selling Berry Poppins winterberry holly from Plant Addicts.

These native hollies – growing in eastern Canada through the southern United States – are pretty plants all year long, but they become stunningly beautiful at the dreariest time of the year. They lose their leaves in autumn, leaving only the amazing crop of bright berries to light up your winter pots. They are hardy down to USDA zone 3.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Ornamental cabbages and kales (Brassica oleracea) are cold-hardy foliage plants that provide exceptionally vivid white, pink, red, and purple winter colors for holiday pots. They are technically edible but are not grown for eating. Rather, they are cultivated for their bright, rose-like center rosettes.

Ornamental cabbage and kale plants maintain their bright structure and color well into freezing winter months. For a festive container, they can be combined with winter-hardy pansies, berried twigs, chrysanthemums, or ornamental grasses.

Pick up a four-pack of Song Bird Red Ornamental Kale Plants from Burpee.

You may know these stunning plants as hellebores (Helleborus niger), or as Christmas roses. Whatever you call them, they make fantastic additions to holiday porch pots, with their shining white flowers and strong, dark green leaves. The only issue with hellebores is that they usually don’t bloom until January – past the heart of the holiday porch pot season. But some cultivars bloom just in time for the holidays, such as ‘Christmas Carol Early’, 'Jacob', and 'Snowbells', available at Plant Delights Nursery. The Christmas rose is usually hardy to USDA zone 3.

This dense, naturally round shrub is a perfect little ball of soft green needles. Its small size and low-maintenance nature make Little Gem Norway spruce (Picea abies 'Little Gem') a popular addition to your holiday porch pot. You can order a plant from Magic Valley Gardens at Walmart.

Norway spruce grows slowly, adding only about an inch or two in size every year and topping out at about 3 feet tall and wide. Don’t worry about winter weather – ‘Little Gem’ is hardy down to -40°F. The new growth emerges soft and bright lime, but by Christmas it will be a handsome forest green.

The flowers that give Heuchera its common name of coral bells only appear in spring and summer. By the time the holiday season rolls around, you’ll appreciate this plant's incredible foliage. Coral bells offer a wide range of leaf colors beyond green, including apricot, bronze, pewter, burgundy, and deep purple. The foliage often adds even more enchantment with scalloped, wavy, or veined edges. Select ‘Caramel’ or ‘Peachberry Ice’ cultivars, both available at Plant Addicts, for foliage with rich tones and holiday warmth.

Many trailing “spiller” plants work well in holiday plant pots, but few are better than the classic evergreen trailing English ivy (Hedera helix), available in an ivy variety pack from Plant Addicts. This hardy vine softens the edges of holiday planters and offers all-weather resilience. It stays vibrant throughout the season and works well with flowers or small evergreen shrubs to create a festive feel. The cascading leaves create a rich, full look, balancing upright or mounding holiday plants.

If you’re ready to create gorgeous holiday plant pots of your own, a few practical tips will help. Let’s get down to the basics of how to put it all together.

The base of it all is the pots or containers you select. Choose pots in materials that can handle winter temperatures, like metal, wood, or even plastic. Avoid materials that will crack when the temperatures drop. Get pots that are big enough, but not too big. Generally, front door holiday plant pots should be between 12 and 30 inches in diameter and between 12 and 18 inches deep.

You’ll want to use potting soil in the containers. Leftover summer potting soil works just fine, but it’s best to buy fresh, like Miracle-Gro Organic Outdoor Potting Mix, from Amazon.

Next, you’ll want to put in the plants, and I suggest using a classic thriller, filler, spiller design. Start with the thrillers. These are the tall, eye-catching focal plants that make guests admire the pots. You can use one of the taller plants you have selected – like winterberry holly or ‘Ice Breaker’ fir – or you can use cut boughs after trimming the stems.

Get ready to layer in the fillers. This is the place for medium-height evergreens or foliage plants. Coral bells or ornamental cabbage work well in this role. Alternate textures and shades.

Last, add the spillers, plants with draping or trailing foliage. These go around the bottom edge of the container so that they cascade gracefully over the edges of the container.

Creating your plant pots is fun, but you’ll also have to put in a little effort to keep them going strong through the season.

This starts with care immediately after you set out the pots. Give each of them a deep watering, enough to saturate the entire soil. Excess water should run out of the drainage holes in the bottom of the pot. Make sure that’s the case, or your plants will die of root rot. It helps to add pot feet to elevate the containers off freezing patios.

Don’t worry too much about freezing weather. It is normal for the moisture in the patio pots to freeze. Keep checking the soil and add more water if the top inches are dry. Mist the evergreen branches during dry winter days to rehydrate the foliage. As the weather cools, cluster the containers close to the house wall to shield them from winter winds and create a microclimate.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

If you’re planting bulbs in your garden this fall, try this simple but super-effective hack to stop squirrels digging up tasty tulips and ruining the spring show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freshly planted spring-flowering bulbs provide an easy feast for hungry garden critters as temperatures drop, and are often eaten before they even get a chance to grow roots. Tulip bulbs are always the first to be sniffed out as they taste sweet and provide the perfect high-calorie meal for chipmunks as well as squirrels. Crocus bulbs, too, are carb-rich favorites on the garden menu in fall.

If you’ve experienced squirrels digging up tulip bulbs, you’ll know what determined diggers they are. Gardeners are just as dogged, however, and popular tricks to protect spring-flowering bulbs include laying steel mesh or chicken wire over the top, disguising the appealing scent of tulip and crocus bulbs by planting unappetising allium bulbs alongside, and using bulb baskets. But there’s a far easier, cheaper and more effective way to stop squirrels eating bulbs, and it helps the bulbs grow well, too.

What’s more, this robust solution protects bulbs from rodents and other underground burrowers like voles, who also love to seek out this nutrient-dense food source in fall.

When you're planting bulbs in fall, the magic ingredient to keep these energy balls safe from squirrels is poultry grit made from crushed oyster shells. The sharp, jagged edges of crushed oyster shells means it's painful for paws to dig through, so it provides an effective barrier that stops critters eating tulip bulbs and even tempting crocus.

What's more, as well as keeping bulbs safe from sharp teeth this natural material improves soil drainage, making bulbs less likely to rot through wet winter weather. Crushed oyster shells also break down very slowly to provide plants with a steady supply of calcium, which supports strong root and stem growth.

Not all chicken grit is created equal when it comes to protecting fall-planted bulbs, however. Make sure you buy chicken grit like Pacific Pearl Oyster Shell Calcium Supplement for Chickens, available from Walmart, that's made purely from oyster shells as many products are cut with cheaper materials like limestone. Choose crushed shells (sometimes sold as chick grit) over flaked shells as this is both sharper on paws and easier for plant roots and shoots to grow through.

When planting bulbs in pots, simply add an inch-thick layer of chicken grit to the soil surface to deter squirrels from digging, where it will also act as a mulch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Opt for a double layer of poultry grit when planting bulbs in the ground. Add an inch-thick layer of crushed oyster shells to the bottom of the planting hole, and sit the bulbs right on top. This helps to protects bulbs from burrowing pests who typically attack from below, when a landslide of sharp oyster shells will send them scurrying away in search of more easily accessible food. If voles, field mice and pocket gophers are a particular problem in your garden, you can also pack a shallow layer of grit all around the bulb to fully encase it.

Fill the planting trench with soil as normal but add a second inch-thick layer of oyster shell grit an inch or two below the surface. When squirrels or other critters hit this sharp, gravelly layer, they’ll give up digging. This top layer can also help deter raccoons and skunks who don’t eat bulbs but are attracted to freshly-dug soil to look for insects and grubs.

Crushed oyster shells will naturally improve soil drainage and create beneficial pockets of air, loosening up heavy soil. The shells also release calcium as they break down, which plants need to build cell walls.

Adding a heap of oyster shells to your soil can affect its pH levels long-term but this hard material breaks down so slowly, that’s not a problem unless you have soil that’s already very alkaline. While some bulbs like camassia (wild hyacinths) prefer acidic soil, more palatable tulip and crocus bulbs both tolerate mildly alkaline soil just fine. Testing your soil with simple pH test strips like these from Amazon will instantly give you an answer if you suspect your soil is highly alkaline.

There are so many striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November, and using this clever trick will keep them safe from hungry animals in fall. Whether you view squirrels as garden pests or like to welcome wildlife into your garden, crushed oyster shells are a natural solution to prevent them digging up freshly planted bulbs in fall. Poultry grit is as economical as it is effective, too, so you get to enjoy those beautiful blooms come spring without spending a fortune.

Little leaves on an orchid's old flower spike may signal trouble – but a keiki doesn’t always mean the plant is struggling. Here's how to tell the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It usually gets spotted by accident, halfway through watering. The flower spike that finished months ago has a few green leaves sticking out partway up, and maybe a stubby root or two hanging under them. That's an orchid keiki. For a minute, finding one feels like getting a second orchid for nothing.

Then the doubt sets in. Read up on what a keiki is, and you'll soon come across the idea that orchids are more likely to sprout them when they're stressed or failing. Anyone whose plant has also dropped a leaf or two lately will find that hard to shake.

Stress can play a part, though it's far from the only thing. Heat, fertilizer, and genetics all factor in, and plenty of keikis grow on plants with nothing wrong at all. A few minutes at the sink with the parent plant will tell you more than the keiki does itself.

The name is Hawaiian – keiki (KAY-kee) means baby. Look closely at a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) spike, and you'll see small bumps along it, each wrapped in a papery sheath. Those are nodes, each holding a dormant bud, and once in a while one of those buds grows leaves. What grows is a miniature copy of the parent.

Keikis aren't an orchid disease or a parasite, and they can't spread to your other plants. They're simply one way orchids reproduce without seed. Where it grows matters more. A spike keiki sits up on the flower stem. A basal keiki comes up at the bottom, squeezed in next to the lower leaves, and on a moth orchid, that second kind can point to trouble at the crown.

A stem keiki growing on a Phalaenopsis orchid stem

Sometimes a keiki does show up because the parent is in trouble. Moth orchids grow from one point only, right in the middle of the leaves. Lose that tip to rot, or a break, and no new leaves can form up there. With energy in reserve, the plant may instead push out a basal keiki below the damaged tissue. Dendrobium canes that lose their roots, or their link to the rest of the plant through rot or injury, sometimes sprout keikis as well.

Plenty of keikis turn up on orchids with nothing wrong, though. On moth orchids, they come naturally from the middle and upper nodes of the spike, and certain species and hybrids are just more prone to it. Hormones are what flip a dormant bud into a keiki. Dab cytokinin, one of those growth hormones, on a node and it can pull a keiki out of a perfectly healthy plant. Crazy Keiki Cloning Paste, available on Amazon, is a well-rated product that contains cytokinin.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Long spells of heat as a spike finishes, heavy nitrogen feeding late in the season, and too little light or humidity have also been tied to keikis.

Some longtime growers take a keiki as a sign orchid care could use adjusting – a dim corner or heavy feeding is a good place to start. On a plant with firm, flat leaves and plump roots, a spike keiki usually isn't hiding anything. A basal keiki pushing up beside a soft, dark center is the one to worry about.

A basal orchid keiki growing on plant with some shriveled old roots

Start by checking for orchid leaf problems. Healthy moth orchid leaves are thick and firm, almost leathery. An occasional yellow bottom leaf is normal – the oldest leaves dry up as the plant ages. Several leaves yellowing at once is another matter, and so are newer leaves that have gone limp and wrinkled. Leaves that shrivel like that usually aren't getting enough water. And in fall, don't be fooled by a cold windowsill – nights below 60°F (16°C) can yellow lower leaves on their own.

Next, slide the pot off and check the orchid roots. Good ones feel firm and plump. They look green right after watering and silvery once they dry. Rotted ones are brown and mushy, and if you pinch one, the outer layer may slip off, leaving nothing but a thin string.

Now peer into the middle where new leaves come from. That's the crown. It should be firm and green. If it has gone soft, black, or wet-looking, crown rot has likely set in, often from water molds such as Pythium ultimum and Phytophthora cactorum, and rot that spreads through the crown can kill the whole plant.

One yellow leaf proves very little. Slow decline is different. If the leaves feel a little softer each time you check and nothing about the care has changed, look underground – usually at the roots, or at old bark mix that's broken down into soggy muck. Good news shows up in the same places. New leaves unfolding from the crown, or fresh green root tips near the base, mean the plant is still growing.

A basal orchid keiki has been left to grow into an established offshoot on this neglected plant

Did everything look fine? Then leave the plant alone, keiki and all. If the check turned something up, fix that and only that. Cut rotted roots back to firm tissue with something small and sharp, and wipe the blades with rubbing alcohol between plants. Fiskars' micro-tip pruning snips are narrow enough to get in between roots.

For repotting, use a specialist orchid potting mix, like Better-Gro Phalaenopsis mix, available at Home Depot, which is a fir bark blend. Use a clear slotted orchid pot, like these Holanhing pots, so you can keep an eye on the roots.

After that, water orchids sparingly until new roots reach the fresh bark, and water in the morning so the leaves dry before dark. Tip out any water that pools in the crown. Moth orchids do well in bright, indirect light, just not pressed up against cold glass or sitting above a heating vent.

The keiki itself can stay put. Without roots of its own, a spike keiki draws water and nutrients through the parent's flower stem, and snipping it off does nothing for rotting roots or a damaged crown. Many growers leave a moth orchid keiki alone until it carries a couple of leaves and roots about 1–1.5 inches (2.5–4 cm) long. Smaller ones often struggle on their own. Once it reaches that size, separating and potting the keiki is a quick way to propagate your orchid.

It depends on the damage. A moth orchid that still has some plump roots and a firm crown can come back once its care is fixed, though you may wait a while for the first new leaf. Rot through the crown is a much tougher case. So is a pot where you find almost nothing but mush. Even then, a plant with enough energy stored up can sometimes send up a new plantlet from its base.

This is where a keiki helps. It grew from the parent's own tissue, so it carries the same genetics and can keep that orchid going if the parent doesn't make it. Leave it attached while the parent holds up.

What if a declining plant has a green flower spike but no keiki? Try using keiki cloning paste, mentioned above, to coax one out, though results vary.

So it’s not time to write that orchid off, just yet, because of one odd growth. Check the plant it's growing from. If the leaves are firm and the roots and crown look good, the keiki is no warning at all, just a free second orchid hitching a ride on the first. With a little TLC, you can get that orchid blooming beautifully in no time.

Anyone else been ogling Catherine's Thanksgiving decor on Instagram?

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

You don't need elaborate floral arrangements or expensive accessories to make a Thanksgiving table feel specia; all it takes is a handful of colorful leaves, a few little pumpkins and some carefully chosen garden finds . Now if you'll excuse me, I think I'll be heading out to the backyard with a basket before all those beautiful fall leaves disappear!

Think your vegetable garden is finished for the year? Not so fast. Some crops relish cooler temperatures and can shrug off a little frost.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn’t necessarily mark the end of the vegetable growing season. While warm-season crops are definitely done for the year, you may still be able to sow and grow some of your cold-hardy favorites.

Knowing how and when to plant a vegetable garden so late in the season depends on your USDA hardiness zone, climate, and local weather. If you have milder winters, you can likely sow seeds directly in outdoor beds. In colder climates, you’ll need to provide some protection against frost and snow.

Here, I offer pro tips on late veggie growing, along with eight vegetables you may be able to start now for a winter or spring harvest. If you’re unsure about whether or not you can grow any of these in November, contact your extension office for more location-specific guidance.

Planting veggies now takes more effort than simply sowing seeds. Beyond knowing your climate and hardiness zone, you need to pay attention to the weather. For example, avoid seeding when the soil is frozen or soggy.

Prepare the soil by clearing out weeds, raking out any stones or remaining summer plant debris, and mixing in fresh compost. Seed planting depth and spacing depend on the crop you are sowing, so do check the seed packet information.

Manage your expectations for this project. Less sunlight and colder temperatures mean germination and growth will be slow. Be patient.

Although these veggies are either cold-tolerant or good at overwintering, they still will not tolerate very cold weather. If you have cold winters, you’ll need to protect your efforts. An old milk jug can give seeds some protection and act as a mini greenhouse for a few seeds. If you want to start more seeds, use a cold frame, like the Giantex wooden cold frame, which has a flip top for easy access.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As plants develop, row covers will protect winter veggies from frost, snow, harsh winds, and flying pests. This Plant Covers Freeze Protection Kit on Amazon includes hoops, clips, and a roll of frost blanket.

Apply straw, shredded leaves, or other loose, organic mulch over and around new crops or overwintering veggies. Just take care not to drown delicate seedlings in mulch.

Take care with watering, as letting soil get soggy is easy to do in winter. Check the soil before watering plants.

These are some of our favorite vegetables that many gardeners can start in November, including those that could be ready in winter and others that you’ll harvest in spring or summer.

Garlic is an example of a crop that will overwinter and provide you with a harvest next summer. As long as your soil is workable and not waterlogged, garlic is a dependable crop for planting now. Plant individual garlic cloves with the pointy ends up. Use mulch to protect the cloves from winter freezes. If successful, your cloves will grow roots over winter, foliage in spring, and bulbs in the summer.

You can plant garlic from the grocery store, though it’s usually a softneck variety grown in milder climates and may struggle in colder regions. Hardneck garlic is often a better choice for those areas. Botanical Interests offers an organic garlic flavor sampler bundle featuring two hardneck varieties and elephant garlic.

Shallots can also be overwintered and will reward you with a harvest in late spring or early summer. Plant shallot sets or individual shallot bulbs with the pointy ends up, just slightly above the soil surface. French Red Shallots from Burpee are a delicious culinary variety worth trying.

You should mulch lightly to protect shallots in colder climates. However, fall planting is best suited to milder regions, and if you have very cold winters, the planting window may already have passed. Check with your local extension office for exact dates.

Spinach is remarkably cold-hardy. The seeds will be slow to germinate in the cold, though. This Sow Right Seeds Spinach Seed Collection contains three tasty varieties. Unless you have very mild winters, use cold frames or other protections. Once spinach plants get established, they should produce leaves you can pick throughout the winter. Harvest from the outside edge of the plants, leaving the center intact.

Kale is another very cold-hardy vegetable that many gardeners can grow now for winter harvests. It’s also hard to grow from seed in the cold, so unless you have mild weather in November, consider using transplants, like these Bonnie Plants Lacinato Kale Plants from Lowe's. Use cold frames or row covers as needed, especially during hard freezes. For warmer zones, Burpee sells a four-variety kale blend.

Arugula is a mildly cold-tolerant green that is best for growing in November in milder climates. If conditions are right, it will germinate and grow rapidly, giving you a winter harvest. If you want to grow arugula in colder regions, use frames or a greenhouse and be prepared for growth to be slower. You can pick up a pack of arugula seeds for less than $5 from Sow Right Seeds.

Like arugula, radishes grow rapidly, so if the weather and soil conditions are right, you can start plants now and get a quick winter harvest. Burpee's Cooks Custom Blend Radish Seeds Collection contains red, pink, purple, and white radishes. For the best results, the soil should be workable, and November temperatures should be cool or mild. For colder areas, plant the most cold-tolerant varieties and use cold frames.

Plant carrots now for a sweet treat in early spring. Carrots generally overwinter well, but choose the more cold-tolerant varieties for the best results. Scarlet Nantes, included in this Gardeners Basics 5-Variety Pack on Amazon, can be harvested through winter with protection. It’s also important to make sure the soil is loose and free of stones, so the roots can grow deep. Use a generous layer of mulch to keep the soil warmer over winter.

Peas can also generally be overwintered for a spring harvest. Peas grow best in cooler weather, but they still need some warmth to establish. Alaska peas, available from Eden Brothers, tolerate chilly conditions, but if your November is very cold, it might be too late. In milder growing regions, this can be a good time to start peas. Be sure to plant your peas near a trellis or other vertical structure so the plants can climb in spring.

November doesn’t have to mean the end of growing veggies for the year. Depending on your region and local weather, you may be able to grow or overwinter some or all of these cold-tolerant vegetables. Choose the plants most suited to your conditions and be patient. Colder weather means slower growth.

A few thoughtful changes will keep your garden landscape looking effortlessly stylish through the cooler seasons.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While you might be thinking that the gardening season is drawing to a close this month, there's plenty to look forward to, especially if make a few simple switches to help your yard transition from fall into winter. As the year segues into the cooler months, it's time to enjoy colorful stems, textural bark, sculptural seedheads and shrubs bejewelled with bright berries, and relish the quiet beauty of this season.

Check through our landscape designer tricks to take a fall yard into winter, and add one or two to your outside space now. An injection of structural evergreens, naturalistic ornamental grasses, a tree with fiery foliage or colorful autumn bulbs can make a huge difference at this time of year now the late-season flower show is coming to an end.

Consider, too, how to make your fall garden user-friendly so you feel inspired to spend plenty of time outside still, perhaps by including a cosy gathering area around a fire pit. Which of these easy tricks landscape designers use to carry a garden from fall into winter are right for your yard?

Adding a mix of ornamental grasses is a fundamental element of fall garden design and these low-maintenance plants will continue to look good all through winter. While many annual and perennial flowering plants will happily grow through airy grasses in summer, the blades will keep borders looking full once they've finish blooming.

Choose varieties that offer bold autumn color such as Panicum virgatum ‘Shenandoah’, available from Nature Hills. Also known as switch grass, this well-behaved clump-forming grass develops stunning red and damson tones in fall, topped by wiry stems of flowers. Reaching 3 feet high, it looks fabulous planted among taller shrubs as well as with perennial blooms.

Another option favored by landscape designers is blue-green-leaved Festuca glauca 'Elijah Blue', also available from Nature Hills. Growing to just a foot high, it's perfect for border edges and winter containers.

Landscape designers often choose trees with fiery foliage to create a stunning focal point with brilliant shades of scarlet, russet, gold or burgundy. Even if space is limited, there are plenty of smaller trees that will squeeze into a compact garden.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Some of most spectacular fall color is typically associated with Acer (maple) trees, but to carry the interest on into winter, choose a type with textural bark, too. Acer griseum, the paperbark maple and available from Plant Addicts, has peeling, papery warm-brown bark. Caught in the light of a low winter sun, its peeling curls of bark are nothing short of spectacular. The coral bark Japanese maple, available from trees.com, has bark in an intense red tone that's equally eye-catching.

Another option if you're wondering what to plant in fall is a multi-trunked tree that, once the bright foliage has fallen, brings architectural interest to your garden, like the Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry tree, available from trees.com.

Attractively planted container gardens are a landscape designer's best friend during the cooler months of the year. These portable pots of color and texture can be positioned wherever you want, adding a welcoming touch to an entrance or a bright splash to a patio table.

There are all sorts of vibrant plants that love life in a patio pot and last from fall into winter for a wonderful cool-season display. The go-to formula is to combine a thriller (height), filler (body) and spiller (edging) to create a full, textured look. Good choices for fall and winter include compact evergreens or ornamental grasses to add the height element, pansies to fill out the body of the planter, and ivy to tumble over the edges. For a modern look, squeezing a container full of a single variety is an even easier option.

Dwarf pine trees are enjoying a surge in popularity with landscape designers, and no wonder. While in spring, summer and fall they provide a green, textural foil to colorful flowers and leaves, once winter arrives they emerge as standout sculptural shapes. The beauty of slow-growing dwarf pines is that they naturally stay compact and well-shaped, so need very little looking after.

Dwarf Mugo pine (Pinus mugo var. pumilo) is a particular favorite thanks to its dense, dark needles. While it eventually grows to 3-5 feet high, its easily kept pruned into a neat mound. Dwarf Mugo pine, available from trees.com, keeps its seed cones all through winter, adding to the display. Adding one, or an odd number dotted through your outside space, is a great way to ensure your garden has character throughout the year, and helps avoid that sensation of sparseness that often happens in winter when many plants are dormant.

When summer perennials and annuals fade you will need something else to take their place. Autumn-flowering bulbs will pop up reliably year after year to add color and, if you choose the right sunny spot, will naturalise, gently spreading to reflect how comfortable they are in your landscape. This repetition will strengthen the planting design, as well as adding continuity.

Nerine bowdenii (also known as as Bowden lily) brings an explosion of color to rejuvenate tired fall borders. These beautiful bright blooms on sturdy stems grow to 24 inches, and can be added to pots as well as planted in drifts through a flowerbed. In addition to the standard pink petals, there are varieties from white through to a deep ruby red, and Dutch Grown stocks a good nerine selection. While it's too late to plant the bulbs this year, you can pre-order ready for planting in spring for floral fireworks next fall.

Another favorite is hardy cyclamen, which you'll likely find potted at your local garden center in fall. Plant a mix of the hardy ivy-leaved cyclamen (Cyclamen hederifolium), which flowers in fall and has pretty foliage that lasts through winter, and winter-flowering cyclamen (Cyclamen coum) which blooms winter into spring, for a long season of interest.

Even during the cooler months of the year, your outdoor space should be an inviting spot where you want to linger. A fire pit creates an ambient spot to gather around at dusk offers the opportunity for year-round entertaining, and is a go-to for landscape designers interested in creating an outdoor space with year-round usability.

Whether you want the crackle of real wood burning or the convenience of starting a fire with the click of a button, a fire pit will add visual as well as physical warmth to your fall and winter garden. Opt for a design that complements your overall aesthetic and add layers of textured cushions and throws in a palette of warm, earthy tones to garden furniture to build on the cozy vibe.

This fire pit is perfect for patio evenings, bringing friends and family together around a warm, inviting flame. Though it burns real wood, an airflow system facilitates efficient combustion to reduce smoke levels.

Fuelled by wood or wood pellets, this 7-inch diameter stainless steel mini fire pit brings the s'mores experience to a patio table. Efficient burning means it's smokeless and a removable ash pan makes clean-up easy.

Fuelled by propane gas, this stylish fire pit has an adjustable flame and can deliver plenty of warmth to keep your outdoor gatherings cozy. A lid lets it double as a coffee table and it's also available in black and stone-look.

Landscape designers often use a mix of materials to maximize texture and interest in garden design. These are automatically thrown into the spotlight during the cooler months of the year when plants die back and leave the hardscaping exposed. Gravel offers a softer alternative to bare paving slabs, and buff-toned pea gravel in mixed sizes and shapes like this landscaping pea gravel from Lowe's creates a particularly natural look.

Softening the edges of hard landscaping with plants is another landscape-designer trick that comes into its own as a garden moves from fall into winter. Use evergreen creeping thyme to blend the edges of a curving pathway and a functional garden element becomes an attractive winter feature. You can also use gravel as a mulch to avoid areas of bare border soil in winter, an option that's also easy on the budget.

Another way to maximise texture and help your garden transition from fall into winter without missing a beat is to add warm lighting from a low angle. In fall, a ground-stake spotlight will highlight foliage but then is easily moved to throw a glow through ornamental grass blades. Even a wash of light across a gravel path creates a play of shadows that shows off texture to the full, and allows you to appreciate your garden from indoors on dark evenings.

The easiest way to create individual pools of low light is with solar spotlights, although you'll need to shop smart when buying outdoor solar lights that will generate enough power in fall and winter. For a start, choose lights with adjustable solar panels so they can be angled to match the sun's lower position in the sky. Look for a high conversion rate and a large capacity battery of at least 1500 mAh, too, and opt for warm-toned LEDS that will create more ambiance than bright white lights. These Solar Spot Lights from Wayfair tick all three boxes.

From ragdolls to Bengals, your birth month cat might reveal more about your personality than you think...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sir Terry Pratchett famously declared that cats remember when they were worshipped as gods, and it makes sense; our feline friends have an extra-special hold on our hearts – so much so that, yeah, we 100% want to know our birth month cat.

If you're one of those people who spends a lot of time reading up on how to make your yard more appealing to your cats (or which plants that are poisonous for cats) rather than tips on how to repel the neighborhood's kitties, then chances are you've wondered which cat breed best matches your personality at least once. At least.

It makes a lot of sense, too; after all, from playful kitties to lap cats that just want to be left alone to their sunbeam, there is an incredible amount of variety to be found in the feline kingdom. And after looking at our birth month pets, I couldn't resist taking a closer look at cats in particular...

I know, I know; we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month bird, birth month animal, birth month owl, and birth month bug, but cats are particularly brilliant if you want to match a critter up with your personality.

Whether you're a determined January baby, a dreamy June soul or a fiercely independent November personality, there's a feline to match your character. And so, from adventurous Bengals to affectionate ragdolls, here are all 12 birth months matched to the cat breeds that best capture their personality traits.

Grab yourself a packet of catmint seeds, then, and get ready to find out which cat matches your birth month...

If you're a January baby, you're known for being ambitious, independent and determined. It should come as no surprise, then, that the Maine Coon is your birth month cat; after all, these striking kitties have a confident presence, are intelligent and have a reputation for being independent-minded.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A natural leader of the cat world? Sound about right!

February belongs to the Abyssinian, which makes a lot of sense when you think about it. Just like the creative, curious and intelligent people born at this time of year, Abyssinians are famously inquisitive, playful and adventurous.

In other words, these kitties are true free spirits. Sound familiar?

March babies are quiet, sensitive and introspective – but don't let the fact that they're not the loudest in the room fool you. Especially as their birth month cat is an elegant beauty who's often reserved around strangers but affectionate with their trusted people.

Basically, the Russian Blue is a perfect match for March's gentle and imaginative personality for a reason. And, if this has struck a nerve with you, then why not honor your birth month cat further with this Russian Blue Calendar 2027?

Bold, adventurous and full of charisma, April belongs to one of the more unusual members of the cat family: the Bengal. Unlike many cats that absolutely abhor water, these pretty kitties absolutely love it – almost as much as they love exploring. This, coupled with their energetic and confident natures, means they're not exactly known for sitting quietly on the sidelines! (Sound familiar?)

One of the most iconic cat breeds going, May's birth month cat is the sociable, expressive and strong-willed Siamese.

With their bright blue eyes and unusual coloring, these kitties are among the most instantly recognizable breeds in the US. They're also famously vocal and people-oriented, with plenty of personality to keep everyone entertained... just like May babies.

If you're a June baby, you're romantic, sensitive and affectionate. No surprises, then, that your birth month cat is the beautiful ragdoll! These gorgeous kitties are known for their gentle souls, their people-loving natures and their tendency to follow their favorite humans around the house.

Essentially, they're a lovely fit for June's dreamy and sentimental side. And they go all floppy like a ragdoll when you pick them up, making them excellent snugglers, too!

If you're a July baby, you're curious, private and quietly determined – and you tend to prefer a small but loyal friendship group to a big and sprawling one. Enter, then, one of the cutest birth month cats on this list: the Birman!

Loyal, loving and family-oriented. Birmans are often affectionate and sociable without being excessively demanding. They're the comforting presence of the feline family, basically, so lean into it!

Round clusters of white blooms in wetlands or moist areas attract insects and other critters.

Shenandoah Switch Grass adds graceful movement and deep red tips that catch the evening light.

Born in the height of summer, August babies tend to be every bit as sunny-natured as you think they'd be – think confident, outgoing and full of character. No wonder, then, that their birth month cat is the Burmese; these kitties are sociable, playful and love being involved in whatever their humans are doing.

They certainly know how to command attention, and all hail that kind of chaotic energy, quite frankly!

September's long been associated with successful leaders, which means those born under this month tend to be practical, composed and deeply intelligent. Their birth month cats are similar, as British Shorthairs are generally calm, independent and undemanding.

They appreciate a routine and like things just so, but they like it that way for a reason – and it's why they're one of the most popular cats around, as it makes for a cuddly and serene companion.

October babies, assemble! While some might expect those born in the spookiest month of all to be assigned a birth month cat like the hairless Sphynx cat, think again!

Turkish Angoras are intelligent, playful and often quite determined. They have a flair for the dramatic, too, making them an ideal match for passionate, expressive and sociable October-born folk everywhere. (Although, admittedly, this 'I Like A Handful Of Humans And My Turkish Angora' Mug is giving pure Scorpio energy!).

Wannabe witches, rejoice! November babies get the beautiful Bombay cat, which might be the most mysterious member of this list of birth month cats. Why? Well, because with their glossy black coats and striking eyes, these kitties have an enigmatic appearance, while often being deeply affectionate with their chosen people.

If this is your birth month cat, you're mysterious, intuitive and quietly determined... and a brilliant person to have in anyone's corner, quite frankly.

Last but not least, December babies are known for being adventurous, energetic and fun-loving – and generous of spirit enough to be able to deal with the fact that their birthday falls smack-bang in the middle of the holidays.

Somalis, then, make their ideal birth month cat, as they are curious, playful and love exploring their surroundings. (As an added bonus, they're simply stunning, too!).

Ernest Hemingway famously declared that “a cat has absolute emotional honesty: human beings, for one reason or another, may hide their feelings, but a cat does not.” Whichever birth month cat you call your own, then, try to follow its good example and be more in touch with your true feelings and self.

Remember, too, that you don't have to own a cat (does anybody truly own a cat, after all?) to enjoy seeing them in your garden; plant up some cat-friendly plants, and watch the kitties go to town. Just be sure to keep bird feeders up and out of their way, yeah?

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Although hydrangea flowerheads can look pretty framed against a winter landscape, it’s important not to leave them to their own devices this month. Make a little time in November for these care essentials

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As November arrives, backyard activity may be slowing, but beneath the surface, hydrangeas are entering a critical transition. As day length shortens and the air gets fresher and nippier, deciduous shrubs shift their energy into the roots. Understanding exactly what to do (and not do) for hydrangeas now begins with recognizing that dormant plants are still susceptible to moisture stress and sub-zero cold.

Obviously, not all hydrangeas are the same. Some form buds on old wood, which means pruning now is a no-no. Other types are hardier than others, and so need less winter protection. So in order to give hydrangeas the best winter care, you must first know exactly which type of hydrangea you have. However, these November care tips can all help to make a big difference to next year’s display.

Taking action this month gives you enormous benefits in the approach to the colder months ahead. Taking time now can help you shield key dormant buds from bitter cold, adjust water levels, stabilize and protect roots, and ensure your plants emerge stronger than ever next spring. So don’t chance it and leave your favorite shrubs unattended this month. Here are the crucial tasks to do before winter…

Effective fall care lies primarily in knowing your hydrangea type and variety. Varieties that bloom on old wood, such as bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla) and oakleaf hydrangea (H. quercifolia) have already formed embryonic flower buds. If these buds freeze or are pruned off, next year's blooms will be tragically lost before you see them. Conversely, panicles (H. paniculata) and smooth hydrangeas (H. arborescens) produce flowers on new wood grown in spring, making them more resilient to frosts.

Popular bigleaf cultivars such as Nikko Blue or the Cityline series and serrated mountain hydrangeas need bud protection in cold zones. Cold-hardy panicle varieties like Limelight or Bobo and native smooth hydrangeas like Annabelle rarely require insulation, though they still benefit from consistent root hydration.

November hydrangea care also depends on your location, climate and USDA hardiness zone. Gardeners in northern zones 3-5 experience frozen ground and drying winter winds, demanding comprehensive stem barriers and thick thermal mulches. In contrast, those in southern zones 7-9 must contend with erratic temperature swings, where unseasonal late-fall warm spells can trick dormant buds into opening prematurely, only to be sheared by subsequent frosts.

Soil type also matters. Heavy clay soils hold water and risk winter ice pockets around roots, while light, sandy soils drain rapidly and dry out under frozen winds. Before tackling these tasks, it’s worth investing in a soil diagnostic tool with a long probe. The XLUX Deep Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, gives instant readings to make better decisions before the first hard freeze. Don’t forget your trusty bypass pruners to remove any dead or damaged branches safely, plus some isopropyl alcohol to clean blades before and after use. You’re then ready to start…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

One of the kindest things you can do for your hydrangeas this month is to “think twice, cut once” when it comes to pruning. One of the biggest hydrangea mistakes is indiscriminately shearing back during fall cleanups. For old-wood bloomers like bigleaf, mountain, and oakleaf varieties, the buds that produce next summer’s flowers are already set near the tips of the stems. Pruning these in November removes those flower buds, reducing or eliminating next summer's blooms.

For these hydrangeas, you need to resist all structural shaping, topping, or cutting back until immediately after flowering finishes next year. The only exception is removing dead, diseased, or broken stems, which can be cut down to the base at any time. Use sharp bypass pruners like the Felco 2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon, for exceptional clean cuts.

Equally important is leaving the faded, papery flower heads all winter long. While it might be tempting to tidy up dried flower clusters on varieties like Endless Summer or PeeGee, these old blooms act as shields for the tender buds tucked beneath them. So it’s a good idea to leave them in place now. Dried flower clusters also add visual interest to the winter garden, especially when they collect small mounds of snow. Then, in late winter or early spring, as fresh green growth emerges at the base, you can snip the old flower heads off above the first set of green buds.

Hydrangeas need plenty of water, even now. While deciduous foliage yellows and drops, hydrangea roots take up moisture until the soil drops below freezing. Winter air and winds can be drying, and with the ground frozen, the roots cannot replace what gets lost. So don’t be tempted to put your hoses and watering cans away too early. Entering winter in dehydrated soil can lead to brittle branches and dead tips by spring. Get your hydrangeas as hydrated as possible before winter really begins.

If you’re having a rainy fall, you might not need to water hydrangeas, but check the soil and give your hydrangeas a good soaking as needed. If rainfall is sparse, provide a deep, slow soaking every 10-14 days. Aim to moisten the soil 8-12 inches (10-15cm) deep, encouraging roots to settle deeper underground. Prioritize any newly planted shrubs, which need more water as they get established.

Soaker hoses are great options for targeted and controlled watering. You can buy Expert Gardener 50ft Soaker Hoses from Walmart to help you direct the flow wherever you grow your hydrangeas. Stop supplemental watering once morning frosts result in frozen soil.

Soil temperatures fluctuate erratically during late fall and early winter. Rapid freeze-and-thaw cycles cause frost heave, where expanding and contracting soil pushes shallow root crowns above the soil line, exposing roots to drying winds and freezing cold air. You can give key hydrangeas a helping hand by giving them extra insulation this month. This stabilizes soil temperatures, preserves deep moisture, and protects delicate roots through winter.

Start by adding a top-dressing of compost This will slowly break down over winter, releasing micronutrients that enhance soil and slowly feed the roots. A great composting option at this time of year is mushroom compost. You can get lush ready-made bags of Espoma Natural Mushroom Blend Fertilizer, from Walmart, to prime the earth and provide steady support through the colder months.

The compost can do double duty as an insulating mulch, but you can also use other types of mulch, like shredded bark or chopped leaves. Add a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of coarse, loose mulch. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in late-season soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. Always leave a 2-inch (5cm) gap around the woody stems to reduce the risks of fungal rot and gnawing rodents.

If you’re in zones 4-6 growing bigleaf or oakleaf hydrangeas, sub-zero cold and winter winds pose a big threat to next year's blooms. As noted, old wood hydrangeas have flower buds now. While the roots may be hardy to zone 5, flower buds can suffer frostbite below 0°F (-18°C). If stems die back, old-wood varieties will produce foliage during the summer, but zero flowers. So depending on your hardiness zones, consider adding some physical protection if your winters are very cold.

Do this in late November, after the plant drops its leaves and enters dormancy. Drive four sturdy hardwood or metal stakes into the ground around your hydrangea. Keep them several inches clear of the branches. Then wrap breathable fabric around the outside of the stakes to make a wind barrier. Use burlap or jute, such as Wellco Gardening Burlap Roll from The Home Depot, to protect against biting winds while maintaining healthy air flow around the plant. Secure with zip ties or twine.

For extreme northern climates, you can construct a cylinder of wire fencing around the plant and loosely fill with dry pine needles or oak leaves. Just avoid packing the leaves tightly and never use plastic tarps, which trap condensation and bake tender stems on sunnier winter afternoons.

Hydrangeas in outdoor pots, ceramic planters, and decorative troughs require proactive winter care. Unlike in-ground plants, potted roots are exposed to freezing air on all sides. An unprotected container's soil temperature can be 20°F lower than the garden soil, putting roots at risk of freezing and killing the plant outright. Ceramic and terracotta pots also absorb water, making them susceptible to cracking when wet soil freezes and expands. So you’ll need to give your container-based hydrangeas more protection if you have very cold winters.

Begin by grouping potted hydrangeas together along a sheltered, south or east-facing foundation wall, out of wind corridors. Elevate your pots off cold concrete using pot feet or bricks to ensure drainage holes remain clear. Wrap the body of each pot in bubble wrap, thermal burlap, or foam insulation, securing the wrap beneath the outer rim without covering the top soil. You can also pick up floating plant jackets or anti-frost fleece covers, such as the Valibe Shrub Protection Plant Jacket from Amazon, which you can slip over potted hydrangeas in cold snaps.

If you are in zone 6 or colder, move your potted hydrangeas into an unheated garage, garden shed, or cold frame for the winter. These sheltered spaces keep plants dormant while protecting them from sub-zero drafts. Check on them once a month, providing a splash of water so the roots never completely dry out.

As well as the things you should be doing this month, preparing your hydrangeas for the colder months requires knowing what to avoid. We’ve touched on pruning certain hydrangea types. Avoid aggressive pruning on old-wood varieties like bigleaf and oakleaf hydrangeas, which shears away next summer's flower buds. Another thing to avoid doing is allowing roots to dry out prior to ground freeze, as desiccated roots are vulnerable. Keep watering if the soil is dry and remains unfrozen.

Never apply high-nitrogen fertilizers at this time of year. Feeding now forces a flush of soft, tender growth that cannot harden off before freezing weather strikes, causing stem dieback. Don’t use clear plastic sheeting or non-breathable tarps as winter wraps, as they trap humidity, promote mold, and create greenhouse heat spikes on sunny days. This can trick dormant buds into waking prematurely. Finally, don’t just assume all hydrangeas need the same winter protection. Know your hydrangea type, how far north it is hardy, and how far you need to intervene to keep yours healthy.

Taking a little time in November to protect your hydrangeas makes all the difference for the year ahead. By maintaining hydration, shielding exposed old-wood buds from freezing gales, and insulating roots with a mulch blanket, you give your prized shrubs the exact winter protection they need. Come spring, your hydrangeas will emerge from dormancy strong, healthy, and ready to produce a summer display of blooms.

#7832. Wild Bleeding Heart: A Hardworking and Adaptable Beauty

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Here, Melissa Starkey shares about wild bleeding heart, one of her favorite underappreciated native plants to grow.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

This plant is extremely close to my heart because I remember seeing it growing wild in Pennsylvania when I was a child. A great alternative to nonnative common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis and cvs., Zones 3–9), it produces its best flush of heart-shaped flowers in spring but keeps blooming through the entire growing season, even as late as November here at Mt. Cuba Center. Wild bleeding heart also has fernlike foliage, which has a kind of blush tinge.

But all its aesthetic qualities aside, wild bleeding heart is incredibly hardworking and adaptable. It can grow in partial shade and makes an excellent woodland plant. This plant also does quite well out in the sun; it grows naturally on rocky, sunny outcrops. I have seen it growing right out of rocks in the wild. While it does adapt well, its unique flowers require larger pollinators, like bumblebees, that are strong enough to force themselves through its tight petals.

Wild bleeding heart is a bit smaller than common bleeding heart, but it does not go dormant like its nonnative relatives, giving you three seasons of interest. If pink flowers aren’t to your taste, there is a white cultivar available called ‘Alba’ (D. eximia ‘Alba’, Zones 3–9).

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.
