#7774. Prof. Francesca Gino's Contract and Discrimination Claims Against Harvard Business School Dismissed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"In 2021, allegations were brought against [Gino] claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty," and eventually to her tenure being revoked and her being fired.

Some short excerpts from the long decision by Judge Myong Joun (D. Mass.) today in Gino v. President & Fellows of Harvard College:

Plaintiff Francesca Gino is a former tenured professor at Harvard Business School ("HBS") and brings this action against Defendants President and Fellows of Harvard College ("Harvard") and Defendant Srikant Datar ("Dean Datar"). In 2021, allegations were brought against Plaintiff claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty. In March 2023, the investigation committee found, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Plaintiff committed research misconduct…. In May 2025, Harvard revoked Plaintiff's tenure and terminated her appointment with HBS.

Plaintiff claims that Harvard breached its obligations under various policies and procedures governing the investigation of the research misconduct allegations and the tenure revocation proceedings. Specifically, Plaintiff argues that a jury could find that Harvard deviated from its policies and procedures such that Harvard could be found in breach of those agreements, and that Harvard did not carry its burden of proving research misconduct or grave misconduct. Plaintiff also alleges that the proceedings and related findings, including the adverse employment actions taken against her, were pretext for gender discrimination….

In approximately June of 2021, three professors—Leif Nelson, Joseph Simmons, and Uri Simonsohn, who publish under the name "Data Colada"—presented their allegations against Gino to HBS Professor Max Bazerman during a 90-minute Zoom call…. [Eventually, a Harvard] Investigation Committee issued its 41-page Final Report with nearly 1,200 pages of supporting documents, finding by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff committed research misconduct intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly with regard to all five allegations.

The Investigation Committee's Final Report considered and rejected Plaintiff's contentions that unnamed "bad actors," research assistants, or other co-authors might have instead been responsible for the data anomalies. The Investigation Committee concluded that Plaintiff's "repeated and strenuous argument for a scenario of data falsification by bad actors across four different studies," involving "different co-authors, different journals, different lab personnel, and different home institutions" and spanning eight years, was "highly implausible." The Investigation Committee recommended corrections of the scientific record, putting Plaintiff on unpaid leave, and initiation of steps leading to termination of employment….

The court granted summary judgment on all these issues, in Harvard's favor. Here's an excerpt of the discussion of her breach of contract claims:

Massachusetts courts enforce contractual promises made by private universities, while according appropriate respect to their academic and disciplinary judgments. The Third Statute [a Harvard academic policy] permits removal of an officer holding a teaching appointment "only for grave misconduct or neglect of duty." I hold that this is a substantive, enforceable limitation on removal, not a merely aspirational statement.

The limitation does not, however, confer a right to have a federal jury independently determine scientific authorship, data provenance, or the correct weight of forensic evidence after an academic tribunal has considered those matters. Judicial review asks whether Harvard reached its determination honestly and reasonably, upon a rational evidentiary foundation, and in compliance with its enforceable contractual procedures. This is meaningful review: the University's decision does not prevail merely because a committee announced it.

This standard respects both the contractual restriction on removal and the institutional responsibility to adjudicate research-integrity matters. A court may not uphold a decision procured through dishonesty, resting on no reasonable evidence, or reached through a material violation of promised procedures. It also may not choose among plausible competing forensic interpretations merely because a reasonable factfinder could have drawn different scientific inferences. Gino bears the burden of proving breach in this action. The Third Statute Procedures separately placed on Harvard's complainant a clear-and-convincing burden of establishing grave misconduct or neglect of duty; the record must be examined for whether Harvard applied that burden, not treated as though the civil burden had transferred to Harvard….

Harvard's decision had a substantial contemporaneous evidentiary basis. The record describes forensic examination of anomalous data in four research papers; analysis of the history and characteristics of relevant datasets; consideration of Gino's explanations; a faculty investigation finding misconduct by a preponderance of the evidence, and; a subsequent hearing committee finding, by clear and convincing evidence, of misconduct grave enough to warrant revocation. These are not independent judicial findings that Gino altered any data. They establish that Harvard investigated defined allegations and articulated an evidentiary explanation for its decision. The committees' findings alone would not rescue a decision shown to be knowingly false or irrational; the investigative materials, considered together with the contrary submissions, provide the relevant basis for review.

Gino denies intentionally falsifying research data, relies on favorable accounts from coauthors and colleagues, and challenges aspects of the forensic inferences and evidence of access or authorship. I credit these disputes and draw permissible inferences in her favor.

But the question under the contract is not whether a jury could reject some of Harvard's inferential steps or prefer an alternative forensic account. Gino must identify evidence from which a reasonable jury could conclude that Harvard did not honestly believe its determination or lacked a rational basis to make it.

The identified differences over inference, attribution, and scientific weight do not establish that the peer decisionmakers knowingly adopted a false conclusion or acted without a reasonable evidentiary foundation. Accordingly, no triable breach arises merely from the competing interpretations of the underlying research record….

And from the court's rejection of Gino's sex discrimination theory:

Plaintiff points to the following pieces of evidence that she argues supports evidence of discriminatory animus: (1) Harvard deviated from and breached its policies and procedures; (2) Harvard and Dean Datar have historically subjected women to less favorable treatment; (3) Harvard has treated allegations of research misconduct against male professors differently than the allegations against Plaintiff, and; (4) certain statements made by Harvard employees were false and otherwise constitute discriminatory remarks….

Plaintiff relies on similar arguments she raised in support of her breach of contract claims that Harvard deviated from its policies with respect to investigating research misconduct. "Evidence that the employer deviated from its standard procedure or policies in taking an adverse employment action against a plaintiff may be relevant to the pretext inquiry." As discussed, Plaintiff's evidence does not support a finding that Harvard breached its policies. Furthermore, Plaintiff provides no evidence that any purported deviations from Harvard's policies are connected to gender bias….

Plaintiff argues that there is evidence that Defendants have historically treated women less favorably than men. This evidence includes Plaintiff's own testimony and testimony from Plaintiff's colleague at HBS. Plaintiff provided testimony in a sworn declaration that she "personally observed that it was more difficult for women to obtain tenure at HBS than men. Indeed, about three times as many male professors get promoted as compared to female ones. In the Accounting & Management Unit, it's worse: closer to four times as many." She also stated that in 2022, she participated in an Appointment Committee meeting in which "gendered language was used to discuss the work of one female professor in the Accounting & Management Unit." When Plaintiff raised the issue to senior colleagues, one of them told Plaintiff that it "has been that way for a while." Plaintiff's declaration also states that "there had not been a single tenured woman in the Accounting & Management Unit for more than 20 years." Plaintiff's colleague, Professor Frances Frei, also testified to evidence that Dean Datar attempted to prevent another female professor from obtaining tenure.

Plaintiff's evidence is plainly insufficient. This evidence is made up of Plaintiff's own conclusory allegations that it is more difficult for women to obtain tenure, a statement made by an unknown female colleague supporting Plaintiff's belief that obtaining tenure is more difficult for women, vague allegations that unspecified "gendered language" made by unknown speakers was used when discussing an unspecified female professor, and an unsubstantiated statement from a colleague that Dean Datar attempted to "counsel out" another unspecified senior lateral hire. There are no other non-speculative facts—documents, communications, data, or otherwise—that support these conclusions or that tend to show a pattern of gender bias. Indeed, when pressed for further information about Dean Datar's alleged "pattern" of disfavoring women, Professor Frei could not provide a response.

Further, the record does not demonstrate any other evidence of a pattern or practice of discriminatory conduct or unfavorable treatment that can be applied to reasonably infer gender bias against Plaintiff….

Plaintiff points to evidence that Harvard has treated allegations of misconduct against male professors differently than allegations against Plaintiff. Plaintiff points to two examples where male professors were treated differently…. "To successfully allege disparate treatment, a plaintiff must show that others similarly situated to her in all relevant respects were treated differently by the employer." … Here …, there are important differences. For instance, in both the case of Mr. Serafeim and Mr. Soltes [the two examples pointed to by Plaintiff -EV], Harvard found that the complained-of conduct did not fall within the definition of research misconduct….

Additionally, the allegations against Mr. Serafeim had to do with a misleading footnote that was later admitted and explained to be an error, and the allegations against Mr. Soltes had to do with his conduct in connection with subjects that he interviewed. In contrast, the allegations against Plaintiff involved thirteen allegations of data falsification and fabrication in nine papers co-authored by Plaintiff, and after a preliminary assessment, five of those allegations were found to be sufficiently credible to fall within the definition of research misconduct. In short, it is Plaintiff's "burden to connect the dots" between the facts and circumstances surrounding the allegations against her and those of her male colleagues, such that a jury may find that they are similarly situated. Plaintiff has not met that burden here….

Plaintiff points to allegedly false statements made by Dean Datar and other Harvard leaders, as well as a gendered remark by a member of the Investigation Committee, as evidence of unlawful animus. Plaintiff alleges that the following false claims were made: (1) Dean Datar falsely claimed under oath that he did not make any "deal" with Data Colada and Data Colada's allegations against Gino were not brought to his attention until after the Interim Policy was created; (2) Dean Datar falsely denied telling Dean Pisano that Data Colada was pressuring HBS to move the investigation along and accusing it of "whitewashing"; (3) Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino; (4) Professor Amabile falsely claimed under oath that, during the time of the investigation, she was not aware that the allegations brought against Gino were raised by Data Colada, and; (5) RIO Bonacossa falsely claimed under oath that he was not aware of Data Colada's allegations against Gino at the time he was asked to serve as RIO and he did not tell Gino she could not obtain a forensic expert….

The facts presented by Plaintiff regarding the false statements do not prove that the adverse employment actions Harvard took against Plaintiff were motivated by gender bias or that the justification offered by Harvard was a sham. The allegedly false statements about what Dean Datar, Dean Cunningham, RIO Bonacossa, or Professor Amabile knew or when they knew it are not relevant to the reasons offered by Harvard that support their adverse employment decisions.

Additionally, the other fact disputes—whether Dean Datar made a deal with Data Colada and was pressured by Data Colada to move the investigation along, and whether Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino—are not material. The investigation that led to the adverse employment actions taken against Gino took place over nearly 18 months, involved several rounds of review by several different committees, including 26 professors, administrators, and trustees who evaluated documents, research, data, and conducted witness interviews. This investigation concluded in a 41-page report detailing the allegations, investigation process, and reasoning supporting the findings. The Third Statute Proceedings were similarly thorough and resulted in in-depth findings of fact and recommendations. Plaintiff has offered no evidence to demonstrate that Harvard's reasoning is a sham or a pretext for gender bias.

Finally, Gino points to a committee member's observation that she may have experienced professional and personal pressure after her husband lost his job. Although Gino characterizes the comment as reflecting an assumption about gender and family roles, I assume for purposes of the motion that it could carry such an implication. That does not end the inquiry: the remark must be assessed in context, including the speaker's role, whether it informed a disputed factual finding, and whether the record connects it with any adverse decision because of sex. Viewed together with Gino's other evidence, the quoted remark does not, without such a connection, establish that Harvard's stated reasons were a pretext for sex discrimination.

Considering the evidence cumulatively rather than in isolated categories, Gino identifies criticism of the procedures, comments concerning women's advancement, two male faculty members accused of different forms of impropriety, challenged statements by institutional actors, and the committee member's remark. The asserted procedural irregularities do not, without a supported causal connection, compel or permit a reasonable finding that the decisionmakers acted because of her sex. The comparator matters identified above concern materially different charges and screening decisions.

Even assuming that Gino meets the modest prima facie threshold and that some administrative statements are disputed, the total record cited does not raise a genuine dispute that Harvard's articulated research-misconduct basis was a cover for sex discrimination under federal law. Count I's selective-enforcement theory separately fails because the identified male comparators do not demonstrate selective pursuit of comparable allegations on the basis of sex. The Title VII and Title IX claims are against the institution insofar as authorized by the respective statutes; any individual liability asserted against Dean Datar must be evaluated under the applicable state-law provision rather than presumed from the federal employment claims….

Douglas E. Brayley, Jenny K. Cooper, Elena W. Davis, Stephanie D. Porges, and Laura G. Hoey (Ropes & Gray LLP) represent defendants.

#7772. Quartz May Be On Its Way Out—and Here’s How Kitchen Designers Would Replace It

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Quartz countertops have long been a favorite choice of homeowners and interior designers alike due to their strength, nonporous nature, modern look, and uniformity. However, recent discoveries and legal challenges regarding the material’s potential health hazards to fabricators have caused quite a stir and are now reshaping the industry.

The main issue is with crystalline silica that’s a natural mineral found in quartz. When particles are inhaled, they can penetrate deep into a person’s lungs, causing damage that can lead to serious respiratory diseases like silicosis, lung cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). And many workers have become ill from breathing in dust containing crystalline silica while fabricating quartz countertops. Australia has already banned many engineered-stone products, while California is pursuing policy rules that would prohibit fabricating engineered stone containing more than 1 percent crystalline silica.

As a result, more and more people are looking for safer countertop options to use in place of quartz. “We have found some homeowners shying away from quartz surfaces,” says Kaycee Conallen, owner of Kaycee Conallen Design Studio in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania. There are many alternatives to quartz countertops, and designers have helped us identify three top options for your new home or next remodel.

Note: There is no evidence indicating a health concern with already installed quartz countertops, so if you already have one, you don’t need to rip it out.

One alternative to quartz countertops is eco-friendly, silica-free alternatives like recycled glass and paper composites. Both eliminate silica risks while providing unique designs ranging from bold, contemporary glass patterns to sleek, solid-color paper finishes.

Recycled glass countertops incorporate post-consumer or post-industrial glass fragments bound in cement or resin, offering distinct visual textures from fine-ground particles to large, jewel-like shards. Notable glass brands include IceStone, Vetrazzo, Curava, GEOS, and Compac Obsidiana Zero. Glass surfaces are effective at resisting cuts, scratches, and heat, though stain-resistance and maintenance depend on whether a resin or cement binder is used.

Paper-based composites work well for those gravitating towards a solid color and solid surface materials, such as PaperStone, Richlite, and Fenix brands. Surprisingly durable, these heavy-duty panels are made from layers of post-consumer recycled paper or paper from FSC-certified forests, which are compressed under heat and pressure with a silica-free and petroleum-free phenolic resin.

While heat resistant to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit, minor scratches and stains may appear, but can be sanded out. “Fenix is a man-made resin and paper combination originally developed in Italy, and we love that it has a beautiful matte finish, feels soft to the touch, and is very durable,” explains Conallen.

“Sintered stone is another strong option for its resistance to heat, scratches, and stains,” notes Blima Ehrentreu, founder and CEO of The Designers Group (TDG) in New York City and other locations. Using a high-tech process, natural minerals like porcelain and glass are combined under immense heat and pressure to replicate metamorphic rock with minimal to zero crystalline silica.

The non-porous nature of sintered stone makes it resistant to staining, scratches, intense heat, and color-fading from UV exposure. Brands that make this type of surface include Lapitec, Dekton, Neolith, Florim, Sapienstone, and Caesarstone, which are actively eliminating or reducing silica content. In addition, many of these surfaces contain recycled content.

Conallen also loves the look of authentic materials like soapstone. “Each slab of stone carries unique characteristics, personality, and porosity,” she explains. Composed mostly of talc, this metamorphic rock is free of crystalline silica and has a distinctive, velvety feel. Soapstone offers design versatility, as it ranges in color from subtle grays and muted greens to charcoal or deep black, sometimes accented by marble-like veining. Not only does it offer a classic, understated elegance to modern spaces, but it is also a sustainable option given its low-energy extraction process, nontoxic nature, and recyclability.

From a functional standpoint, soapstone is very durable. It withstands heat, so you can set hot cookware directly onto the surface without trivets. It’s also nonporous so it doesn’t get damaged by acidic etching, spills, or bacterial growth. The only drawback is that it’s a softer material than most of the other options mentioned, so it can show minor scratches.

#7770. Journal of Free Speech Law: "Protecting the Thinking Process in Human-AI Interaction: The Forum Interstitiale Between Thought and Expression," by Caroline De Cock

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

International human rights law protects freedom of thought absolutely and freedom of expression subject to limitations. The relevant established doctrine calls the two sides of that line the forum internum and the forum externum. However, the line was drawn when thinking left no trace, and with current technological developments, it no longer holds.

Within the span of six months in 2026, a United States court ordered that 20 million ChatGPT conversations be provided as evidence under ordinary discovery rules, two federal courts reached opposite conclusions on whether a litigant's exchanges with a chatbot were protected at all, and the Supreme Court held that location records kept by a third party remain constitutionally protected. Records of where a person's body had been were protected, while records of how their mind worked were not.

The law currently has no category for the search query, the exploratory prompt, the unfinished draft, or the confession made to a machine. The U.S. answer has been a quarrel about privilege: Courts refuse to grant AI exchanges between users and chatbots protection because the machine is not a professional, like a doctor or a lawyer, and the industry asks for a new privilege because it claims the model behaves like one. Both the courts and the industry assume that protection depends on what the person is using, i.e., what the machine is. This Article argues that it depends on what the person who uses the machine is doing.

It proposes the forum interstitiale, a third zone between the two classical fora, which can protect the thinking process under a standard stronger than ordinary expression law but short of absolute. Every candidate analogy to interactions with AI chatbots in existing law is tested herein, from search queries and confidential dialogue to protected reading, aggregated records, the European law on correspondence and data protection, private diaries and drafts, and neural data. Each fails for the same reason, namely that the protection it offers relates to a relationship, a disclosure, a recording, an addressee, or a data type, and never to the function of the act as thinking.

The interstitial zone this Article proposes only flows upwards. It lifts acts abandoned by the current binary approach into protection and displaces nothing from the absolute core of protected thought. The Article also sets out what acts belong in the liminal zone, five elements of the protection standard, the duties those elements impose on AI providers, and a map of individual AI interactions across the three fora. This classification determines what records of thought can be demanded, kept, filtered, and used against the person who was engaged in the process of thinking.

#7768. The 2027 Colors of the Year Are Here — Here’s What Your Favorite Paint Brands Picked

Paint brands have revealed their 2027 Colors of the Year, from soft greens to deep browns. See which shades could work in your home.

Top paint brands around the world have announced their featured paints for 2027, giving homeowners new options to consider for their next project. This year’s selections cover quite a range, including soft greens and blues, darker earth tones, and even a wood stain.

Each brand has its own approach to what homeowners might want in the coming year.

Sherwin-Williams and HGTV Home by Sherwin-Williams chose Celery (SW 6421), a light green with yellow undertones.

“With subtle yellow undertones, this soft, muted green strikes a perfect balance between an airy pastel and a grounded, herbal hue,” according to Sherwin-Williams.

The color pairs with cream trim and natural wood and works well on walls, cabinets, and ceilings.

Behr selected Grounded (T27-01), a dark olive green with brown undertones inspired by nature.

“The shade’s organic warmth creates a sense of calm and renewal, making every room feel inviting and effortlessly livable,” said Kayla Kratz, Head of Color at Behr Paint Company, in a company release.

Behr recommends Grounded for interior and exterior projects, including living rooms and kitchens.

Valspar chose Cottage Door (8004-38E), a muted blue-gray with warm undertones.

“A cultural shift toward intentional living and self-reflection calls for authentic and heartfelt hues,” according to Valspar.

The color pairs with light neutrals and natural wood, making it suitable for bedrooms and living rooms. It also works on exterior siding and front doors.

Glidden selected Artifact (PPG10-16), a smoky blue-gray with hints of aqua.

“A calm, fresh aqua that feels like a reset for your whole space,” according to Glidden.

The shade works in bedrooms, bathrooms, and living rooms. Glidden also pairs Artifact with lighter blues and earthy greens.

Dunn-Edwards chose French Press Coffee (DEBN07), a dark brown with subtle purple undertones that resemble dark roasted coffee.

“The overall effect is one of layered, lived-in luxury,” according to Dunn-Edwards, describing its 2027 color trends.

The brand recommends French Press Coffee for powder rooms, home offices, and entryways, where its darker color can stand out against lighter finishes.

Dutch Boy selected Deep Rooted (311-7DB), a warm orange that resembles terracotta.

“As paint trends show people seeking more grounding, authenticity, and connection, Deep Rooted brings stability and a sense of calm to the home,” according to Dutch Boy.

The brand suggests pairing the color with soft whites, blues, or greens on walls and furniture.

Clark+Kensington, available at Ace Hardware, selected Vantage Point (38B-4), a rich blue with muted undertones.

“Vantage Point brings a sense of warmth and character to interiors,” said Kim Lefko, Chief Marketing Officer at Ace Hardware, in a company statement.

The brand pairs it with warm neutrals and lighter colors through its Drift and Mellow palettes.

Graham & Brown chose Rose Earth, a soft pink with earthy undertones.

“Rose Earth takes its cue from the natural mineral pigments traditionally sourced from clay deposits in Italy,” according to Graham & Brown.

The brand designed it to complement its Roselle Grove floral wallpaper, though the color also works with greens and warm neutrals.

C2 Paint selected Pueblo (C2-510), a warm shade between dusty pink and terracotta.

“For 2027, we’re looking outward again, toward the things that make us feel alive,” according to C2 Paint.

Pueblo changes with the light, appearing pinker during the day and darker in the evening. C2 Paint suggests pairing it with deep browns, muted greens, and natural materials.

Minwax chose Pickled Oak, a light wood stain with warm undertones, as its 2027 Color of the Year.

#7766. Previous Homeowners May Still Have Access to Your Smart Home — Here’s How To Check

Smart cameras, locks, and thermostats may still be linked to former owners. Experts explain how to check access and secure each device.

Moving into a new property can be a scary and intimidating process. There are so many new things to learn, and the last thing a new homeowner wants to worry about is home security. And while you should absolutely change the locks after moving in, proper safety measures don’t end there.

It’s possible for previous homeowners to still have access to smart home tech they left behind. Security cameras, thermostats, and other smart devices can remain linked to the previous owner’s account without the new homeowner realizing it.

Learn which devices need resetting, and what new homeowners should do to keep their homes secure.

Unfortunately, there’s no easy way to tell just by looking at a device.

“It is much safer to just assume the old owner can still access them,” says Kurtis Baron, an offensive security specialist at the cybersecurity company Echo Secure.

Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology, recommends trying to register each device through its manufacturer’s app. If the app says someone else already owns it, the previous account may still be linked. For example, Ring has an ownership transfer process for previously registered cameras and doorbells. Connell also recommends checking the app’s shared users list for unfamiliar accounts.

“The previous owner, or anyone they shared access with, can still unlock doors, open the garage or watch camera feeds remotely,” Connell says.

Baron recommends resetting all inherited smart devices, including cameras, alarms, locks, thermostats, and connected appliances. Some might be harder to identify than others. According to the Federal Trade Commission, “light bulbs or security systems may be difficult to detect as ‘smart’ devices.”

Homeowners should follow the manufacturer’s instructions to remove the previous account, factory reset each device, and register it under their own account. Google’s moving guide explains how to transfer Nest devices, some of which require the previous owner to remove them first.

“Old PIN codes on keypad locks and alarm panels often stay active too,” Connell says.

Baron recommends getting a new router rather than reusing the previous owner’s equipment. Homeowners should also set up their own Wi-Fi password and check for unfamiliar connected devices.

Some older smart devices may need replacing, especially if the manufacturer no longer provides security updates. Baron recommends replacing anything that can’t be fully factory reset or has become outdated.

A device linked to a previous owner’s account doesn’t always need replacing, though. Some manufacturers offer ownership transfers or can help new homeowners regain control. Until then, homeowners shouldn’t rely on an inherited smart lock or security camera for protection.

Connell recommends asking sellers for a list of every connected device included in the sale, along with manuals, hub information, and account transfer instructions.

The FTC also recommends leaving behind manuals that explain smart features, particularly those that might be difficult for new homeowners to identify. Sellers should confirm they’ve removed their accounts and revoked access for anyone previously authorized to use the devices.

Baron suggests including a requirement in the closing paperwork confirming that the seller has removed access to all smart devices included in the sale. That gives new homeowners a chance to set up their own accounts and passwords without leaving access in someone else’s hands.

Kurtis Baron, offensive security specialist at Echo Secure, a UK cybersecurity and penetration testing company Nathan Connell, founder and editor of Future Technology

Federal Trade Commission, “Buying or Selling a “Smart” Home? Read This” Federal Trade Commission, “Securing Your Internet-Connected Devices at Home” Ring, “Transfer Ownership of a Ring Device” Google Home and Nest Help, “Moving Guide for Google Home and Nest Devices”

#7765. Will Alito or Thomas Retire if Democrats Win the Senate?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

While the Ginsburg example looms in the background, the answer depends on what values the justices are trying to maximize

Will Justice Thomas and/or Alito retire if Democrats take the Senate in tomorrow's election, hoping that the lame-duck Senate will confirm a nominee chosen by President Trump? In recent conversations, I've heard increasing speculation and support for this possibility among some judicial conservatives. And I hear corresponding worry among progressives.

Both sides think the election may create a brief, very consequential window for a Republican Senate to replace two aging justices. The GOP Senate would have to confirm their replacements before January 3, 2027. There would be political costs and procedural obstacles, but it could be done. Justice Barrett was confirmed by a Republican Senate within a month of her nomination on the eve of the 2020 election.

The rationale for retirement is straightforward: Don't get trapped in the actuarial straitjacket Justice Ginsburg found herself in when she failed to retire in 2014 (when she was 81). That was her last clear chance of retiring with a Democratic president and Senate.

Thomas is 78. Alito is 76. Neither has disclosed a serious health risk, and both have indicated they have no plans to retire this year.

But if Democrats take the Senate (prediction markets currently give them a 75% chance to do so) and if they play the sort of constitutional hardball over Supreme Court confirmations that Republicans have played in the past ten years, there's very little chance the new Senate would confirm any likely Trump nominee. Democrats needn't reject every possible Trump nominee--just those who would be likely to satisfy the conservative legal movement. So the president might not get another Supreme Court appointment before he leaves in January 2029. Calls for the eldest conservative justices to retire would surely intensify.

It's worse than that for judicial conservatives. If a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, the next opportunity for a Republican president to make an appointment might not come until January 2033. There are some important "ifs" packed in there, but they are well within the range of reasonable possibilities.

In January 2033, Thomas would be 84, Alito 82. Even assuming both remain healthy and active, that's a substantial amount of succession risk for conservatives to accept when they could potentially lock in their seats for another generation this winter.

A rational justice who prioritizes preserving his seat for something close to his judicial philosophy might well retire. But a rational justice might prioritize (or at least see himself as prioritizing) other things: continued service, jurisprudential influence, institutional reputation, and personal legacy. Justices do not see themselves simply as strategic agents of the political coalitions that produced their appointments.

For purposes of predicting what Alito and Thomas might do, the Ginsburg example cuts both ways. It illustrates the risks of refusing to retire when one's political allies control the presidency and Senate. At the same time, it illustrates the limits of assuming justices will subordinate their personal preferences regarding tenure, legacy, and judicial responsibility to the interests of that coalition.

Like Ginsburg, Thomas and Alito would probably resist renewed and intense calls for their immediate retirement. They might figure that:

(1) one of those additional "ifs" won't come to pass—that Republicans will retake the Senate in '28 or retain the White House;

(2) in any event, they'll outlast whatever period of Democratic control ensues (i.e., the mirror of the Ginsburg gamble);

(3) they've all but publicly committed themselves to staying on for now (Justice Alito says he will stay on through this term and Justice Thomas may want to pass Justice Douglas' record tenure, which would happen in May 2028); and/or

(4) a lame-duck retirement immediately after an electoral defeat would be seen as an unseemly concession to the sort of overtly political behavior by judges they've long publicly decried.

Progressives may dismiss this last consideration. Many critics see Thomas and Alito as essentially unscrupulous political actors who wouldn't hesitate to time their retirements in order to preserve another generation of conservative control. But that assumes they understand their own judicial behavior the way their harshest critics understand it. I doubt they do.

They may regard voting in accordance with their understanding of the Constitution—even when the results consistently advance conservative policy objectives—as fundamentally different from announcing their retirements right after voters have elected a Democratic Senate. On this view, they might think the former is acceptable judicial behavior while the latter is not.

On the other hand, they could see strategic retirements, which are hardly unprecedented among justices, as distinguishable from the politicized judging they've denounced. Choosing the circumstances and timing of retirement is compatible with their judicial philosophies. And many conservatives might well applaud their retirement decisions as responsible constitutional stewardship.

But a retirement announced immediately after the election to permit the outgoing Republican majority to confirm a successor, would be unusually conspicuous. Whatever their views about strategic retirement as a general matter, I'm guessing Thomas and Alito would regard the reputation cost to the Court—and to themselves—under these circumstances as too high.

The irony is that Ginsburg's cautionary example supplies the strongest argument for Thomas and Alito to retire, but also a good reason to doubt they actually will. Justices may be political actors in some respects, but they are not necessarily the political instruments their allies wish them to be.

Don’t let this ice melt’s small bag fool you: This Redmond’s Nature’s Blend is packed with concentrated dye-free, urea-free, and polymer-free nontoxic ice melt chemicals that effectively bust ice and slush over an up to 400-square-foot area. The all-natural blend is certified by the Organic Materials Review Institute (OMRI), making it one of the best snow melts for use around children, pets, vegetation, and waterways. It’s safe and easy to apply via hand, shovel, or cup.

This pick’s unique formulation can melt snow quickly in temperatures approaching 0 degrees Fahrenheit. It works a bit more slowly at more extreme temperatures, but we were impressed by its overall melting capabilities in our tests. The fact that the mild formula is also easy to handle and safe around snow blowers, vehicles, and other sensitive items makes it ideal for residential use.

The Redmond Ice Slicer works well in climates with occasional storms and freezes. If you need something for a more extreme environment, you’re better off choosing another product, as overapplication of this melter can lead to red spots and smears on driveways and walkways. While we didn’t notice any spotting or staining during testing, Redmond’s more aggressive commercial- and industrial-grade ice melts might be better in colder and snowier climates.

Get the Redmond ice melt at Amazon or Ice Slicer.

When people think about removing snow from roofs, they often imagine doing so manually. That’s because few ice melt products are made to address ice buildup on roofs—which is what makes this ice melt such a unique product. The tablets are composed of calcium chloride and designed to be thrown onto roofs to prevent snow and ice buildup from wreaking havoc on gutters and adding weight to vulnerable areas. For those living in areas with heavy snowfall where ice dams often form, they are a worthy investment.

During testing, we aimed for problem spots and tossed the tablets up. While snow began to slough off the roof relatively quickly, we struggled to verify the exact rate at which the tablets melted the ice since we couldn’t see it happening from the ground. Still, for their intended purpose, they worked well.

The Roof Melt tablets aren’t granular or spreadable, so they aren’t compatible with larger surface areas like driveways. You could probably use them on the ground where drainage is constricted and problematic, but other options will be more economical for that purpose. If you deal with dangerous ice dams on your roof, however, these tablets are worth having around to quickly and easily resolve the issue.

The best way to determine how effectively various ice melts perform is to fully test each product. As residents of Montana, we began our testing in the aftermath of a winter snowstorm that turned bitter cold. We applied the products to gravel, pavement, and grass in temperatures as low as -6 degrees Fahrenheit.

As the snow went through several melt/freeze cycles over the coming days, it formed icy spots under our rooflines and in several low spots. We tested the ice melts in freezing temperatures on water drips and overnight freezes that created walking hazards each morning. We analyzed how long it took to apply each product, how quickly they melted ice and snow, their degree of pet friendliness when used around our dogs, and a number of other hands-on factors. Lastly, we compared pricing, packaging, and ease of application.

Ice melt products are designed for use either before or after snow or ice has fallen. Their application prevents ice from forming or melts it into a slush that’s easier to clear with a standard snow shovel. Each type of ice melt will perform differently depending on its form and chemical composition. Other variables, such as temperature, ground type, melting time, and environmental impact are essential to consider before purchasing an ice melt product.

Ice melt is available in solid and liquid formulations, each with pros and cons. Solid ice melt typically comes in pellets and granules. It works well for many applications and is typically the go-to solution for road crews dealing with icy and snowy weather. Pellets and granules are generally less expensive and easier to store than liquid formulas, and they add a “crunchy” texture on surfaces that adds grip for walking and driving. Their main downsides are that they scatter more easily across icy surfaces, making them harder to apply with precision, and that they tend to be slower acting and more likely to clump together, which sometimes makes them less effective.

Liquid ice melt is a wise choice for lower-temperature situations and times when faster results are necessary. That said, some products must be applied before ice forms rather than after. When applied, liquid is less likely to scatter, staying in place for longer-lasting results. Liquid de-icers, which tend to cost more, can be more challenging to transport and store because of their weight. Plus, if heavy rain ensues, the product can get washed away.

Self-heating ice melt, which comes in pellet and granular form, generates its own heat when in contact with ice and snow—a process known as an exothermic reaction. Unlike other products that must absorb moisture to create a brine to melt the ice, self-heating ice melt can get right to work.

Ice melts work by absorbing the moisture on the top of the ice, creating what’s called brine, and working its way down to break the bond between the ice and the surface. This creates cracks and flakes that are safer to walk on and easier to remove. All of these products have a temperature limit. If temperatures plummet beyond a product’s ice melting point, the chemicals will no longer be effective. Here’s what to expect from the various ice melt types available:

Many of the chemicals in ice melts can potentially damage surfaces, so it’s important to consider where the product will be used. The most common areas—driveways, sidewalks, decks, and porches—can be composed of different materials, such as concrete, asphalt, wood, and metal. Packaging and product descriptions of the best ice melts will reveal what materials they can be used on safely, so be sure to read this information prior to purchase. It would be unwise to apply a product that could corrode concrete, rust metal, or damage wood on those surfaces around the home.

The quest for comfort and convenience in frigid weather has led to the invention of such products as heated jackets, heated gloves, and electric snow shovels. Similarly, certain ice melts have been developed to work in colder climates. Some products won’t work in temperatures lower than 20 degrees Fahrenheit. This is acceptable if the temperature in an area seldom gets that low, but these products won’t get the job done if you live in a colder spot. For locations where temperatures can reach less than 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you’ll want to purchase a product specifically made for lower temperatures.

The time it takes a product to melt ice and snow depends on several factors. Liquid ice melters and self-heating ice melters act fairly quickly. Unlike solid melters that take time to absorb moisture and create the brine, liquid products are already a brine. Self-heating ice melters have a similar advantage: Instead of absorbing moisture, the pellets will heat up more quickly and melt the ice and snow faster than other ice melters. Regardless of which form you choose, there will still be some downtime while you wait for it to work, which you put to good use cleaning your windows with an ice scraper.

Longevity refers to an ice melt’s ability to keep working beyond the initial application period. A long-lasting ice melter is especially helpful when snowstorms or icy rain continue throughout the day. Although long-lasting ice melt tends to be more expensive, the cost can even out since smaller amounts of product tend to get the job done.

The chemicals in some ice melters can be hazardous to pets and plants. According to Alex Blutinger, Medical Director of Veterinary Emergency Group in Greenwich, Connecticut, “Melting ice can be very dangerous to animals, specifically because of the harsh ingredients in ice melt products. Ingestion of these chemicals can cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea. It may also irritate the paw pads and exposed areas of the limbs.” Dr. Blutinger says that, if you suspect your pet has been exposed to unsafe deicing chemicals, you should wipe your pet’s paws with a damp cloth or baby wipe to minimize ingestion through liking and reduce the risk of skin irritation. While using a pet-safe ice melt is smart, you can also reduce exposure using paw was or booties.

Certain elements in ice melters can also do environmental damage, such as killing wildlife that may ingest the pellets or aquatic life if the chemicals reach waterways. Many people are concerned about the impact of using large amounts of these products outdoors, so it’s important to read product information carefully to understand the dos and don’ts of using ice melt.

To ensure you get the best performance out of your purchase (or even a homemade ice melt), try the following de-icing tips and tricks.

If you’re not keen to try to melt ice without salt and want more information about ice melts, here are answers to some commonly asked questions.

Ice melters absorb moisture and create a brine that then melts snow and ice. This eventually breaks the bond between the ice and the surface, creating a slush.

Both. Applying ice melt before and after it snows allows the product to work at its best.

A solid, noncorrosive choice for concrete is the Natural Rapport ice melt. This ice melt is made with calcium chloride, which will not corrode concrete no matter how many times it is applied to outdoor surfaces.

It depends. Some but not all ice melt products are formulated to avoid damaging wood, so read product descriptions carefully.

Generally speaking, calcium chloride is better for ice melt. It’s effective at low temperatures, is a good choice for concrete, and comes in pellet, granule, and liquid forms. Since both types can be unsafe for use around plants or waterways, you may want to refer to the Type section above for more information, especially if you intend to use them around pets or kids.

#7762. If You See a Traffic Light With a Yellow Border, Here’s What It Means

Some traffic lights have yellow borders while others don't. Here's why reflective frames matter and why they aren't on every signal.

Traffic lights are something drivers encounter almost every day. And even though they’ve been looked at countless times, most drivers barely even notice some of the subtle details about them.

One detail that stands out at some intersections is a bright yellow border around the traffic lights. It’s a small change to a familiar piece of road equipment, and it can make a difference at busy intersections. Learn what the borders do and why they’re not on every traffic light.

The yellow borders around traffic lights are strips of reflective material attached to a black panel called a backplate. Much like reflective road signs, they catch vehicle headlights and help drivers spot traffic signals at night. The black background also makes the colored lights easier to see against bright skies and nearby buildings.

“This treatment is recognized as a human factors enhancement of traffic signal visibility, conspicuity, and orientation for both older and color vision deficient drivers,” according to the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA).

The borders also help drivers recognize intersections during power outages.

“This countermeasure is also advantageous during periods of power outages when the signals would otherwise be dark, providing a visible cue for motorists to stop at the intersection ahead,” according to the FHWA.

Research suggests the borders can improve road safety. A 2005 study found that adding yellow reflective borders reduced crashes at the intersections researchers examined. The FHWA now recognizes them as a proven safety measure. However, the borders don’t change how traffic lights operate or how long each light stays on. Drivers still need to follow normal traffic rules, including when a signal stops working.

Federal traffic safety standards allow yellow reflective borders, but don’t require them at every intersection. State and local transportation agencies generally decide where to install them. Some intersections may need better visibility because of glare, nearby buildings, or poor lighting. Transportation agencies may also add reflective borders when installing new signals or upgrading existing equipment.

Cost can influence those decisions, too. Adding reflective strips to an existing backplate is relatively simple, but installing a new backplate may require additional support. That’s why two intersections along the same road might have different traffic lights. The lack of a yellow border doesn’t necessarily mean a signal is unsafe.

Everything from the string length to the bulb size and power source can affect the look and feel of Christmas lights. The following considerations are important to take into account before starting to browse for the best indoor Christmas lights for the home.

#7760. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

#7759. Full Court Denies DOJ Petition In California Election Case In About 7 Hours, No Reply Needed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Justice Kagan likely orchestrated the shadow execution before the petition was even filed.

I think we have seen a new record for speed on the emergency docket. Today, shortly before noon, the Solicitor General filed an emergency application in the California election law case. The brief was about 20 pages long. Circuit Justice never even bothered calling for a response. Shortly before 7:00, the petition was referred to the full Court, and was denied.

Rick Hasen calls it a mercy killing. I think shadow execution is more appropriate.

Indeed, this ruling was likely orchestrated by Circuit Justice Kagan before the petition was even filed. The government's case was dead on arrival. And Kagan spared California the fate that befell Missouri, which had to file a pointless brief that no one would read.

NEXT: Will Alito or Thomas Retire if Democrats Win the Senate?

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7758. Pamela Anderson’s Best Garden & Landscaping Tips, Straight From Her Backyard

The actress and activist shows how a thoughtfully designed landscape can create a memorable first impression.

In Pamela’s Garden of Eden, Pamela Anderson transforms her grandparents’ former property into a peaceful, sustainable retreat. In the second episode, Anderson and her team reimagine the landscape surrounding the “roadhouse,” a tree-shaded home with plenty of character but an undefined entrance and overgrown gardens.

By rethinking how visitors move through the space—from the first step onto the property to the front door—they create a lush landscape that’s both welcoming and romantic. Here are a few ideas worth borrowing for your own yard.

A latticed wooden arch sets a clear threshold, making the transition into the garden feel inviting and purposeful rather than purely decorative.

Flagstone pavers set in an irregular pattern create a path that feels naturally worn rather than newly laid.

A landscape refresh doesn’t have to mean starting over. Anderson and her team transplanted existing plants with their roots intact, preserving established growth while reshaping the layout.

What could have been an all-white patio setup is elevated with subtle patterns and soft colors, adding personality without overpowering the space.

Swapping gray trim for white and introducing black window frames adds contrast and gives the exterior an updated look without structural changes or a major investment.

#7754. The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil - and Other Writings on the Ethics of Voting

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Compendium of links to some of my writings on the morality of voting.

Tomorrow is election day. And - to put it mildly many of the options before voters are far from wonderful.  In all too many races, the candidates with a realistic chance of winning are all bad. This situation, like other recent elections, raises difficult questions about such issues as whether people have a duty to vote, whether it is permissible to vote for a badly flawed candidate if the alternative is even worse, and how to balance competing issues in making voting decisions.

I've written about these kinds of issues in some detail, previously, and this post links and and summarizes some of those writings. This is not a post about which candidate you should vote for in any given race. I've already written a post about why - in most cases - the Democrats are the lesser evil in races for federal offices this year (state and local elections are often a different matter). I've also written about why libertarians (like me) should seek political alliances with "abundance liberals" and why the previous "fusionist" alliance with conservatives probably cannot and should not be revived in the near future.

This post doesn't argue for any particular voting choice, but rather compiles pieces about  how we should make such decisions in general - and whether we should make them at all. Much of the post is adapted from a similar one I put up in 2024. Unless otherwise noted, these pieces were all published right here at the VC blog:

1. "The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil"

This post was inspired by the 2016 election, but almost all of it remains relevant today. In it, I explain why it is both permissible and desirable to vote for the lesser evil in an election where all of the viable options are bad. I address a variety of counterarguments, including claims that voting for a lesser evil makes you morally complicit in that candidate's wrongdoing, arguments that it's better to cast a "protest vote" for a candidate that has no chance of winning, arguments based on the very low probability that your vote will be decisive, and more. Here's a brief excerpt:

Imagine an election where the only options are Queen Cersei from Game of Thrones, and Sauron, the Dark Lord from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings. If Cersei wins, she will kill many innocent people, and oppress others. But she will leave much of the population more or less alone (as long as they don't openly oppose her or threaten her family in any way). If Sauron wins, he will kill far more innocent people, and make the survivors his slaves.

You can instead cast a protest vote for a vastly better alternative, such as Gandalf….. But, by assumption, these are purely symbolic options, because they have zero chance of prevailing. If the protest voter would otherwise have backed Cersei, the net effect of his decision to protest is to increase the likelihood of the worst possible outcome: the triumph of Sauron.

Under those circumstances, it seems clear that a person who ensures a Cersei victory has done a good deed. He or she will have saved large numbers of people from slavery or death, even though the Cersei regime would be a deeply unjust one.

The Cersei-Sauron hypothetical was obviously inspired by the contest between Trump and Hillary Clinton, and is an exaggerated version of that tradeoff. But I think it works for many other elections, as well - including many of the choices  voters face this year.

Notice how my logic is different from that of those who say you can only vote for a candidate if he or she meets some minimal threshold of character or good policy. On my approach, it is morally justifiable to vote for almost any candidate - even a cruel despot like Cersei - so long as the only feasible alternatives are even worse.

Canadian columnist John Robson responded to my piece in the National Post, and I, in turn, posted a rejoinder.

2. "Justifying a Moral Duty to Vote is a Lot Harder than You Might Think."

Many people, including some political theorists, believe we have a moral duty to vote. I disagree. Indeed, I think - in many cases - it's better if you don't vote, especially if ignorance and bias make it likely you will make a bad decision. Casting a ballot motivated by ignorance and bias is often worse than not voting at all.

3."Is there a Moral Duty to Vote in an Election Where the Stakes are Unusually High?"

Even if there is no general duty to vote, perhaps we are morally required to do so in situations where the stakes of an election are unusually high. In this post, I explain why I disagree - at least with respect to most voters. There is, however, a limited kernel of truth in this argument. An excerpt:

There is a kernel of truth to the claim that you have a duty to vote if the stakes are high enough. But the resulting moral duty applies far less often than advocates of the argument tend to assume. And the same reasoning actually implies many people have a moral duty not to vote.

Let's start with the kernel of truth. Imagine there's an election for a powerful political office that pits Gandalf (the benevolent wizard in J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings) against Sauron, the despotic dark lord from the same story. If Sauron prevails, millions of people will die or be enslaved, while Gandalf would rule justly if he manages to win. And all you have to do to ensure Gandalf's victory is check his name on a ballot. If you do so, Gandalf wins; if not, Sauron does.

In this scenario, it seems like you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf, at least barring some kind of extraordinary exigent circumstance. In a real election, of course, the odds that your vote will make a difference are far smaller than in this stylized example….

However, a large enough difference between the two candidates could potentially justify a duty to vote for the "right" candidate, even if the odds of casting a decisive ballot are very low….

But notice that the duty in question is not an obligation to participate in the process for its own sake. It's a duty to help good triumph over evil in a situation where you can do so at little or no cost. If you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf in these types of scenarios, it follows that you also have a moral duty not to vote for Sauron. Indeed, the person who votes for Sauron is more worthy of condemnation than the one who merely abstains. The former is actively helping evil win, while the latter "merely" chooses not to help stop it.

While Gandalf supporters may have a duty to vote, Sauron supporters actually have a duty to abstain from doing so. Ideally, they should stop supporting Sauron entirely. But they at least should not take any actions that increase the likelihood of his victory.

All of the above analysis assumes that the voter knows which candidate is superior and to what degree. But, in reality, we have widespread political ignorance, and most voters often don't even know very basic facts about how government and politics work. Most are also highly biased in their evaluation of the information they do know….

Unless and until a voter becomes well-informed about the issues and at least reasonably objective in his or her evaluation of political information, she has good reason to question her judgment about which candidate is superior, much less by how much. Thus, she cannot conclude she has a duty to vote to help the "right" side win. She may instead have a presumptive duty to abstain from voting until she meets at least some minimal threshold of political knowledge….

Later in this piece, I note some possible exceptions to situations to the presumptive duty to abstain; there are unusual situations where ignorant voting really is better than no voting, and even unusual situations where ignorance leads to better decisions than knowledge (I expand on the latter possibility in greater detail in Chapter 2 of my book Democracy and Political Ignorance). I also address some other caveats and counterarguments.

Some steps you can take to be a better voter, building on a helpful article in Scientific American. I think a wide range of people can do these things. You don't have to be an academic or policy expert to undertake the task. But I am skeptical that more than a small fraction of the electorate will ever be willing to put in the time and effort.

In this post, I make a tentative argument for letting children vote, so long as they show they have attained a level of political knowledge as high as that of the average adult voter -which is not that high a standard! I expanded on the idea here. I do note the crucial caveat that it may not be feasible to do this, because it's possible government can't be trusted to come up with an objective knowledge test for the children (though we do in fact impose such a test on immigrants seeking to become US citizens). Letting knowledgeable children vote is one of my least popular ideas (which is saying no little, given how many other unpopular views I hold!). But I remain unrepentant about it. My 11-year-old daughter is one of the relatively few fans of this policy.

My proposal should be differentiated from the idea of letting parents cast votes on behalf of their children, endorsed by Republican VP candidate J.D. Vance, among others.

6. "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance," in Hana Samaržija and Quassim Cassam, eds. The Epistemology of Democracy (Routledge, 2023).

Many of the most serious flaws of voting arise from the fact that most voters tend to be ignorant about government public policy, and highly biased in their evaluation of the political information they do know. In this article, I go over a range of possible strategies for mitigating this problem. Here's the abstract:

There is broad, though not universal, agreement that widespread voter ignorance and irrational evaluation of evidence are serious threats to democracy. But there is deep disagreement over strategies for mitigating the danger. "Top-down" approaches, such as epistocracy and lodging more authority in the hands of experts, seek to mitigate ignorance by concentrating more political power in the hands of the more knowledgeable segments of the population. By contrast, "bottom-up" approaches seek to either raise the political competence of the general public or empower ordinary people in ways that give them better incentives to make good decisions than conventional ballot-box voting does. Examples of bottom-up strategies include increasing voter knowledge through education, various "sortition" proposals, and also shifting more decisions to institutions where citizens can "vote with their feet."

This chapter surveys and critiques a range of both top-down and bottom-up strategies. I conclude that top-down strategies have systematic flaws that severely limit their potential. While they should not be categorically rejected, we should be wary of adopting them on a large scale. Bottom-up strategies have significant limitations of their own. But expanding foot voting opportunities holds more promise than any other currently available option. The idea of paying voters to increase their knowledge also deserves serious consideration.

I expand upon the foot-voting approach to mitigating political ignorance in more detail in my book Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom. I also recently summarized and extended my ideas on this score in "Strengthen Democracy by Empowering People to Vote with their Feet," an article for the NYU Democracy Project, reprinted as a book chapter in Democracy's Challenges: I00 Ideas, (Robert Bauer, Samuel Issacharoff, Richard Pildes, and Rosa Po, eds., NYU Press, 2026).

How to decide which issues to prioritize over others. Not solely about voting. But highly relevant to voting decisions.

8. "If You Don't Vote, You Still Have Every Right to Complain."

Feeling down after considering the above? This piece might make you slightly happier; even if you don't vote, you are justified in criticizing the policies of the winners! I would add that the same logic shows that, if you vote for the winner on the grounds that she is a lesser evil, you are still justified in complaining about her policies. Vote for Cersei over Sauron, when necessary. But then condemn the evil she does. Just make sure not to be at the wrong place at the wrong time when she decides to purge her critics.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7752. 2026 Heating Oil Prices: Are They the Worst They’ve Ever Been, and Is There Any Way to Keep Costs From Skyrocketing?

Published Nov 2, 2026 2:27 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you are one of the 4 million households in the United States that rely on heating oil to power furnaces, boilers, and water heaters, you might be experiencing sticker shock when it comes to heating oil prices this season. The price has risen to about $6 per gallon compared to last year’s $3 per gallon.

According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, the cost to heat a home using heating oil is expected to rise by at least 50 percent across the region, including states like Maine, Massachusetts, and New York. In fact, Maine has been getting a lot of attention lately since the state relies heavily on this type of fuel, and prices have already reached 80 percent higher than just a year ago. Learn why heating oil is so expensive this year and what you can do to manage the “pain at the tank.”

Heating oil prices typically rise during the winter as demand increases heading into the heating season, says Lowell Richard, director of fuel operations at Townsend, a home service company based in New England that offers fuel delivery as well as HVAC and electrical services. “Over the past several months, global events and geopolitical uncertainty have driven significant increases in the cost of heating oil, propane, gasoline, diesel fuel, and other forms of energy,” he explains. With a shift in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war with Iran, the cost of heating oil has gone up. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine has also impacted the global supply, leading to price hikes.

By comparison, propane prices are relatively unchanged from last year because propane has a different supply structure than heating oil. “Propane is a byproduct of both crude oil and natural gas processing, so its price is linked to both—natural gas prices tend to be steadier, while crude oil does fluctuate,” says Richard. “Additionally, propane has lower wholesale prices and adequate inventories. As a result, propane prices are typically steadier than heating oil prices.” It’s worth noting that propane prices vary by supplier and delivery volume, so Richard recommends checking with your local supplier for the current price.

If you are struggling to pay your heating bills, consider tapping into available resources in your area. “Every supplier is unique, but at Townsend, we offer several ways to help our customers spread out or control their costs,” explains Richard. “We have a variety of budget plans to help fit our customers’ financial needs. For example, automatic delivery is something we encourage because it typically offers better pricing and helps homeowners avoid emergency delivery fees.”

Fortunately, there are several ways for you to help offset high heating oil prices on your monthly bill. Try making one or more of the following changes in your home to keep heating costs manageable, and if suspect damage to your oil tank, have the tank checked and replaced if necessary.

Set your thermostat to a comfortable temperature, but keep in mind that setting it even a few degrees lower can save a noticeable amount on your energy costs, says Richard. “Intentionally setting your thermostat 7 to 10 degrees lower when you are sleeping or away can save up to 10 percent on annual heating costs,” Richard explains. Investing in a programmable or smart thermostat will help you set temperature preferences and schedules, even when you are not home.

Check all the doors, windows, and exterior walls for drafts, since your home can lose heat if ‌air is leaking out. “Replace old or missing weatherstripping around doors, windows, and pipe entry points, and seal cracks in your foundation if you have any,” suggests Richard.

Use a space heater so you can lower your thermostat a few degrees. Choose an energy-efficient model that has a thermostat, adjustable heat settings, sleep mode, and auto-off timers to avoid wasting energy. Always turn a space heater off when you leave the room.

Featuring three heating modes, quiet operation, and an attractive look, this efficient space heater earned “best overall” in our hands-on testing.

“Change your air filter every 30 to 90 days,” says Richard. “A clogged air filter will significantly impact how efficient your system is, so make this a regular habit.”

Maintain your heating system to ensure it is running as efficiently as possible, which in turn requires less energy to heat your home. “Get a fall tune-up to catch small problems before they become bigger, and therefore pricier, problems,” says Richard.

“If your water heater runs on heating oil, keep it set to 120 degrees Fahrenheit for safety and to save on energy costs,” notes Richard.
